title: EMERGING MARKETS-Philippine stocks lead losses as inflation hits 6-month high
text:
* BSP reiterates stance on monetary intervention 
    * Thailand March CPI beats Reuters poll
    * Yield curve still remains inverted 

    By Tejaswi Marthi
    April 5 (Reuters) - Philippine stocks fell on Tuesday after
the country's inflation rate exceeded market forecasts, hitting
its highest level in six months, and the peso appreciated even
as the central bank maintained that no policy intervention was
needed for now.
    Stocks in the Philippines gave up 0.7% and
underperformed their emerging Asian peers, while the peso
gained 0.4%.
    The country's consumer price index (CPI) rose 4% in March,
exceeding the 3.7% median forecast in a Reuters poll. Still,
Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) said that monetary policy
intervention was not needed, and that the central bank remained
cautious against possible second-round effects from supply-side
pressures.
    Inflation readings for March exceeded expectations as higher
food prices exacerbated the effects of higher transportation and
utilities costs, Barclays analysts said in a note. They said
they expect the BSP's first interest rate hike in the second
half of fiscal 2022.
    BSP governor Benjamin Diokno said the surge in global oil
prices could make average inflation breach the upper end of the
bank's 2% to 4% target range this year, making it the second
consecutive year of above-target inflation.
    Barclays also raised Philippines' fiscal 2022 inflation
forecast to 4.1% from 3.7%, still lower than the BSP's own 4.3%
forecast.
    Other stock markets in the region were mixed. Indonesian
shares rose 0.1% and Singapore stocks advanced
0.3%, while the benchmark indices in Malaysia and South
Korea fell slightly.
    Most Asian currencies traded largely flat against the U.S.
dollar.
    Oil prices jumped in early trading as uncertainty over
supply loomed after talk of imposing a fresh round of sanctions
against Russia, while Iran nuclear talks stalled.

    The World Bank also cut its growth forecast for East Asia,
especially Thailand, to reflect the impact of the invasion of
Ukraine by Russia, which calls its actions a "special
operation". The bank now expects Thailand's economy to grow 2.9%
this year, down from a prediction of 3.9% in December.

    Thailand's headline CPI for March jumped 5.73%, beating
forecasts, driven by higher prices of goods and energy, the
commerce ministry said on Tuesday.
    Meanwhile, yields on U.S Treasury notes were little changed
but the 2-year/10-year curve still remained inverted, hinting at
a possible recession on the horizon.
    Yields on Singapore's 10-year bond fell for a
second straight day, by 2.3 basis points, to 2.311%, while
Indonesia's benchmark bond yields rose to 6.759%.

East Asia and Pacific (EAP) region

, and Wilcon Depot among top losers

title: JPMorgan Cuts Nippon Steel to Neutral -- Market Talk
text:
1011 GMT [Dow Jones] Nippon Steel & Sumitomo Metal (5401.TO), Japan's steel making giant, slipped Friday on the back of a JPMorgan Securities Japan downgrade from Overweight to Neutral, citing a severe worsening of export conditions, including low steel prices overseas. House analyst Kazuhisa Mori recommends a wait-and-see approach while looking for signs of improvement in external conditions. He also cuts his target price from Y370 to Y350. Shares dropped 0.6% to Y309. (bradford.frischkorn@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: DWT 
 

0000 GMT [Dow Jones]--Aussie-dollar-bashing is the order of the day in the foreign exchange markets. New 2015 lows are being traded in AUD/USD, following the session's breach of $0.7537. Downside targets at $0.7502 and $0.7481 are now sought, and also $0.7306 in the slightly broader-term. AUD/JPY is at its lowest since late April, having breached Y92.68. AUD bears are targeting a 1.618 Fibonacci extension target at Y92.04, while longer-term bears seek Y90.58 on the monthly Ichimoku chart. AUD/USD is at $0.7540, while AUD/JPY is at Y92.70.

0948 GMT With the Greek referendum upcoming, what matters for the rest of the eurozone is that contagion is limited, says David Tan, head of global rates at JPMorgan Asset Management. In particular, he says, depositors and investors must be reassured that the Greek experience cannot be repeated in other single currency area countries. In his view, a 'no' vote is likely to bring the ECB pre-emptively into play. This won't be licence from the ECB for investors to take risks whatever the outcome but a reassurance that they will curtain negative outcomes in financial markets that may stop or reverse the eurozone's recovery. Mr. Tan reckons a 'Grexit' would also provide further impetus to fiscal integration among eurozone countries. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0948 GMT [Dow Jones] The Philippines said Friday it is ready to argue its territorial claims against China in a section of the South China Sea. Lawyers for the Philippines will appear before the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague, Netherlands between July 7 to 13 to persuade the court to take jurisdiction over the case. China has refused to appear before the court and wants the Philippines and other claimants to pursue bilateral negotiations instead. If the tribunal decides that it has jurisdiction over the case, the Philippines will be asked at a future date to present its oral arguments on the merits of the case. (Cris.Larano@WSJ.com) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0943 GMT [Dow Jones] Energy think tank and consultancy firm IHS has urged the Philippines to craft policy that will ensure a balanced power sector fuel mix, underscoring the risk of over reliance on a single fuel like coal. The Department of Energy is aiming for fuel mix of 30% coal, 30% natural gas, 30% renewable energy and the rest for other technologies. However, as matters stand, 42.5% of Philippine power capacity is coal fuelled--a number that could rise to 56% by 2020 as new power plans come on stream; natural gas will climb to 35% of capacity by then. "If coal projects are implemented as planned, Luzon's coal generation share will be over 75% by 2030, and many coal plants will be uneconomic," IHS said, adding: "Without intervention, the Philippines is on the path to having the highest coal share in Asia, despite DOE's intent to have the one-third rule." (Cris.Larano@WSJ.com) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0938 GMT [Dow Jones] India needs more reforms if it hopes to follow in the footsteps of more successful Asian economies, says research firm Capital Economics. To be sure, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government has made some noteworthy progress, such as shaking up the bureaucracy and lifting restrictions on foreign investment. But it has made little headway in implementing other crucial policy changes intended to ease labor and land laws and reform the tax regime. "Unless more is done in these areas we see little prospect of India emulating the likes of China, which managed to sustain growth of around 10% for a number of years." (anant.kala@wsj.com; Twitter: @anantvkala) 


 
Editor JSM 

0925 GMT [Dow Jones]--Eurozone retail sales in May rose 0.2% from April and were up 2.4% from May last year, beating consensus forecasts of a 0.1% monthly gain, Eurostat data shows. Sales volumes in Germany jumped 4.2% from May last year and they rose 3.4% in Spain, indicating that household confidence is holding up despite the threat of Greece leaving the currency area. Retail sales data are notoriously volatile, but Commerzbank economist Christian Weil predicts a healthy pickup in private consumption growth this year. (nina.adam@wsj.com) 


 
Contact us in London. +44-20-7842-9464 
markettalk@wsj.com 

0922 GMT [Dow Jones]--Despite signs that other areas of the economy are staggering, Britain's powerhouse services sector is showing welcome sings of a post-election bounce. The Services Purchasing Managers' Index, a key business survey released Fridayby Markit Economics, rose to 58.5 from a five-month low of 56.5 in May. A range of indicators suggest consumers in the U.K. were more cautious during the campaign for the general election on May 7 and ramped up spending once political uncertainty was left behind: British consumer confidence in June was the highest in the last decade and a half, market-research firm GfK Group said Tuesday. "Since real incomes are now growing strongly, credit conditions are improving and confidence is high, the U.K.'s economic recovery should maintain this strong pace over the rest of the year," said Samuel Tombs, analyst at Capital Economics. (jon.sindreu@wsj.com) 


 
Contact us in London. +44-20-7842-9464 
markettalk@wsj.com 
 

0000 GMT (Dow Jones)--The bull failure high at 116.00 on the September gilt future is back in the immediate picture, following Thursday's impressive strength. Thursday's rejection at 114.41 produced a bullish piercing candle pattern on the daily chart, and the positive picture has been enhanced by further gains during Friday's current session. The 116.00 key high would be opened on a clean break above 115.75, while threatening additional upside scope to a minimum target at 116.35. The mid-June peak at 116.45 would also be opened. Intra-day support lies at 115.49, and only a push into new session lows below 115.33 would concern near-term bulls, exposing 114.84. The September gilt future is at 115.62.

0913 GMT [Dow Jones]--Turkey's annual inflation rate may weaken further in July and August, to slightly below 7%, due to a further correction in food prices, says Selim Cakir, chief economist at TEB. CPI rose 7.20% from a year earlier, but dropped 0.51% from the previous month, the state statistics agency said Friday. "Still, the elevated core and services inflation suggests that once those favourable impacts dissipate, inflation is poised to turn north again. The weak lira, the reversal of oil price base effects and the stickiness of inflation should push inflation back up towards 8% by year end, in our view," he says. He adds that in turn, today's inflation print wouldn't lead to any change to the central bank's policy stance. (yeliz.candemir@wsj.com)

0907 GMT [Dow Jones] BMI Research says the finalization of Islamic banking guidelines in Malaysia will be a positive for the development of the industry and will help the country maintain its dominant position. These guidelines, which are a set of 11 standards, will complement existing guidelines and seek to address the current inconsistencies in the use of Islamic contracts. "As many standards are not legally enforceable, market practices vary across the industry, and the finalization of procedures will help to minimize discrepancies within the industry," BMI says. "While Malaysia's current Islamic banking standards are enforceable and have been in place for many years, they are technical instead of practical and are still open to interpretation." Malaysia is the world's biggest Islamic bonds market and the government projects the sector to grow at an average rate of 18% on-year in the next five years to $296 billion by 2019, compared with $141 billion in 2013. (saurabh.chaturvedi@wsj.com; Twitter: @journosaurabh)

Fitch revised its outlook on Malaysia to stable from negative and reaffirmed the country's long-term foreign and local sovereign credit rating. title: Linkers From Germany, France In Same Week Unusual-Citi- -- Market Talk
text:
0655 GMT [Dow Jones] It is quite unusual for both Germany and France to be active with an inflation-linked government bond auction the same week, says Citi ahead of Germany's EUR1 billion tap of the 0.10% April 2023-dated inflation-linked Bund Tuesday. The German linker, according to Citi strategists, offers little value versus its peer despite a roughly 10 basis points rise in real yields since the auction was announced Thursday. Despite the rise in the yield, the German linker is expensive versus peers cross-country as the coming auction will bring its outstanding volume to EUR16 billion, which is higher than EUR15 billion, which was previously assumed to be an implicit ceiling. Hence, the bond is unlikely to be often reopened in the future, and its price won't face supply pressure. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha) 


 
Contact us in London. +44-20-7842-9464 
markettalk@wsj.com 
 

0654 GMT [Dow Jones] The description of the eurozone in the U.S. Treasury's semiannual currency report, which may come out later this week, will likely provide important material for the future direction of exchange rates, says Daisuke Karakama, chief market economist at Mizuho Bank. The JPY has every reason to weaken, given Japan's trade deficit for three straight years, he says. But on a theoretical basis the EUR shouldn't be declining given that the region has the world's biggest current account surplus. It's only natural for the U.S to think that demand should be stimulated through fiscal action instead of the zone just relying on holding down the currency, he says. (hiroyuki.kachi@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: PJK 
 

0649 GMT [Dow Jones] Australia's equities market rebounded on a rally in mining stocks spurred by a jump in the iron-ore price. The spot price for the steelmaking commodity climbed 4% on Monday. The S&P/ASX 200 ended up 1% at 5207.4, having initially begun the day in the red to build on Monday's close at a fresh eight-month low. Iron-ore producers Fortescue (FMG.AU) climbed 5.5%, Atlas Iron (AGO.AU) surged 15% and Mount Gibson (MGX.AU) rocketed 18%. BHP Billiton (BHP.AU) added 2.6% and Rio Tinto (RIO.AU) put on 4.1%. Still, some question whether the recovery has legs. "Given the recent choppy trade we've been seeing and the fact nothing has fundamentally changed since yesterday's losses, we are just as likely to open with red on the screens again tomorrow as traders sell into strength," says Stan Shamu, market strategist at IG. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; Twitter: @RobbMStewart) 


 
Editor JSM 

0639 GMT [Dow Jones]-SEB thinks EUR/HUF will strengthen as far as 308 in what's left of the year, before the forint gets some strength back, possibly as a result of easier monetary policy from the ECB. That could take the euro down to 303 over the next twelve months, the bank says. SEB also thinks Hungarian inflation has probably bottomed out, and that recovery has taken hold, although policy tightening could yet be some way off. EUR/HUF is now 305.92. (margit.feher@wsj.com @margitfeher) 


 
Contact us in London. +44-20-7842-9464 
markettalk@wsj.com 
 

0636 GMT [Dow Jones] Capital flight from China "could be an outcome" of the Hong Kong-Shanghai stock connect program that is set to allow investors in Hong Kong and Shanghai to buy up shares in each other's stock markets, says Ewen Cameron Watt, BlackRock Investment Institute's chief investment strategist. While many analysts predict that more money will flow from Hong Kong to Shanghai than vice versa, Watt doesn't rule out the reverse happening. He explains that China's huge appetite for gold has already indicated that local mainland investors are eager for ways to diversify their assets. If a significant amount of money rushes from Shanghai to Hong Kong, Watt says that would be in effect a "de facto deregulation" of China's capital account. (chao.deng@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: KLH 
 

0633 GMT [Dow Jones] The Philippines shouldn't make sending medical workers to Ebola-stricken countries its priority, a former health secretary says, rejecting a proposal by the government to send health personnel to West African countries. Dr Jaime Galvez-Tan, who served as health chief under former President Fidel Ramos, says the government's "priority should be to safeguard the country's borders against the entry of the Ebola virus given that many Filipino travelers and overseas workers come from Africa." He says that, while the Philippines remains Ebola-free, the country needs its own professionals to attend to its citizens' health needs. Enrique Ona, the current health secretary, has said the Philippines is considering a request by the U.S. and U.K. for the Southeast Asian country to help fill the gap health personnel in West African countries. The current Ebola outbreak has killed more than 3,800 people, mostly in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to the World Health Organization. The World Bank said the two-year cost to West Africa of the Ebola epidemic--if it spreads in large scale to the big economies in the region--could hit $32.6 billion by the end of 2015. (Josephine.cuneta@wsj.com) 


 
Editor JSM 

0629 GMT [Dow Jones]--UK CPI is expected to have risen 1.4% y/y in September, from 1.5% in August, according to analysts at Barclays, "supporting the market view that the first BoE rate hike will not occur until August 2015." Barclays however continues to see merit in an earlier BoE rate hike given its belief that the central bank continues to underestimate the acceleration of wages, as portrayed by survey measures. UK CPI is released at 0830 GMT. (nick.cawley@wsj.com) 


 
Contact us in London. +44-20-7842-9464 
markettalk@wsj.com 
 

0620 GMT [Dow Jones] The Philippine central bank recently signed an expanded bilateral currency swap agreement with the Bank of Japan, providing it with additional ammunition to deal with future financial shocks. The new currency swap doubles the amount the Philippines can borrow from the Bank of Japan to $12 billion. Japan can borrow $500 million from the Philippines. Japan has similar currency swap deals with other countries in Southeast Asia as part of regional efforts to build a currency firewall to minimize the effects of a future financial crisis, and Japan's own efforts to counter China's growing influence in the region. Southeast Asia was the ground zero of the 1997-1998 Asian financial crisis. (cris.larano@dowjones.com) 


 
Editor: PJK 
 

0619 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/INR began Tuesday on a weak footing after an overnight drop in the benchmark ICE U.S. dollar index, but has since rebounded to an intraday high of 61.10. The daily USD/INR chart suggests the pair is still in a consolidation phase of 60.92-61.55 demarcated by the lower and upper Bollinger bands (standard deviation 1). Indian state-owned banks were said to have been buying U.S. dollars in the spot market, according to an offshore currency trader, likely for funding of energy deals. India relies heavily on imported fuel even though it is an oil exporter itself. Crude oil prices have recently fallen to four-year lows, possibly creating an opportunity for increased stockpiling of oil supplies. USD/INR is now 61.13 from its Monday close of 61.00. (ewen.chew@wsj.com) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0611 GMT [Dow Jones] Taiwan shares end 0.7% higher at 8768.39, as some heavyweights rebound modestly on the back of buying by government-backed funds. First Capital says concerns over global economic growth and lingering food scandals will continue to keep the Taiex trading in a lower range of 8508-9000 in the near term. TSMC (2330.TW) closes up 0.4% at NT$121.00, Hon Hai (2317.TW) gains 0.2% to NT$96.00 while Catcher Technology (2474.TW) adds 2.1% to NT$271.00. Wei Chuan Foods (1201.TW), a unit of Ting Hsin that used substandard oil in some of its lard-based products, falls by 7% (the maximum allowable daily limit) for the second straight session to NT$27.25. (aries.poon@wsj.com) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0559 GMT [Dow Jones] Philippine President Benigno Aquino might soon get his wish for emergency powers from congress to deal with the looming power crisis. The Department of Energy estimates the main island of Luzon, which accounts for more than half of the country's gross domestic product, may face up to 13 weeks of power outages in the summer of 2015. Emergency powers for Aquino would allow the government to lease additional electricity capacity, mainly mobile diesel generators, to fill the supply gap. Philippine laws has left power generation in the hands of the private sector, but the government is allowed to intervene in cases of emergency. Economic growth in the Philippines, one of the fastest in Asia in recent years despite having one of the region's most expensive electricity rates, could stall in the event of severe power shortages and new investment may be delayed, if not cancelled. (Josephine.cuneta@wsj.com) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0549 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/JPY managed to gain on dip buying in Asian trade, but may suffer a setback if U.S. stocks tumble again and U.S. Treasury prices increase, says Toshihiko Sakai, senior manager of forex and financial products trading at Mitsubishi UFJ Trust and Banking. The key is "how much the market has factored into the risk from the U.S. stocks decline," says Mr. Sakai, adding that recent declines in the 10-year Treasury yield to below 2.3% show "we are now coming to the level to think about how far we can go ahead with buying [the dollar] from this point." The USD/JPY is now at Y107.08 after hitting one-month low of 106.76. (hiroyuki.kachi@wsj.com)

title: Southeast Asia's Markets Look to the Fed
text:
Southeast Asian currencies headed south in September, wiping out most of the year's gains, and the flow of money into local stocks became a trickle as investors prepared for U.S. interest rates to rise.

The currencies' swings have investors--some of them still smarting from a wave of selling that struck the region in the spring of 2013--wondering about the safety of holdings in local-currency stocks and bonds.

Whether a slide by Asian currencies might hammer other assets is "the right question to ask," said Jamie Grant, head of Asian fixed income at the Australian fund manager First State Investments, which manages $162 billion. "We've got one eye on [currency volatility] in case it's pointing to something in the future," he said.

But if there is a selloff on the way, it may bear little resemblance to last year's rush to the exits. Then, foreign investors beat a retreat, responding to hints from Ben Bernanke, chairman of the U.S. Federal Reserve at the time, that the central bank would begin to scale back easy-money policies that had channelled cash into emerging markets. .

This year, several Southeast Asian stock markets have been among the world's top performers, thanks largely to reformist drives in countries such as Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines. Worries over shifting U.S. policies have come at a time when investors appear willing to assess each Southeast Asian market on its merits.

There are signs that expectations about what the Fed might do are pressuring regional markets. In September, the dollar surged 4.1% both against Malaysia's ringgit and against Indonesia's rupiah, outsized moves that, for many investors, were an uncomfortable reminder of last spring's selloff.

Stock-exchange data compiled by Credit Suisse Group AG shows that among Asian countries, only Thailand and India received net inflows of funds in September. That cut short an inpouring of cash that had been nearly uninterrupted since the start of the year, a shift that the bank called the "first signs of foreign investor capitulation" to pressure to leave emerging markets as currencies swing more violently.

In the third week of September, the latest for which data is available, foreign investors withdrew a net $45 million from equities in Indonesia, $11 million from the Philippines and $51 million from Thailand, according to EPFR, which tracks flows of money.

In Southeast Asia, where rapid inflows and outflows of speculative funds often roil markets, policy makers are beginning to worry about the potential impact. Indonesian finance minister Chatib Basri said last month he expects that higher U.S. interest rates could send Indonesian markets into worse turmoil than that seen in the spring of 2013. The Philippines central bank warned that it may intervene in currency markets if the peso moves too violently.

Still, share markets in Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines are up more than 20% in the year to date, trading as high as they were before last year's selloff.

Samir Mehta, a senior fund manager at J O Hambro Capital Management Ltd., which manages $25 billion globally, says Southeast Asia has many strengths, pointing to the fact that currencies in the region have fared better against the greenback than the Australian dollar or Japanese yen.

Domestic factors offset some of the global forces at play, economists say. Southeast Asian countries are stronger politically and economically than they were last year. A military-installed government has created some political stability for Thailand, and Joko Widodo, Indonesia's president-elect, is looking to introduce market-friendly economic overhauls.

Indonesia's current-account deficit--a concern for bond investors--has improved. In the second quarter, the figure rose as a percentage of gross domestic product after two quarters at much lower levels, but declined in absolute terms to $9.1 billion from $10.1 billion a year earlier.

The country's central bank has raised interest rates, making Indonesian assets more attractive. Mr. Widodo is expected to continue an effort by the current government to tackle subsidies that have added to the deficit by boosting demand for fuel.

In the Philippines, a stable government led by President Benigno Aquino and one of the fastest economic growth rates in Asia have won over investors.

First State Investments' Mr. Grant said that his investment-grade fixed-income fund will keep steady its holdings of Indonesian U.S. dollar bonds and has been adding to its rupiah-denominated holdings. The higher yields those securities offer relative to U.S. bonds are worth the risk, he said.

"Fears are overdone" about the potential impact of Fed moves, said Pascal Blanqué, deputy chief executive and group chief investment officer at Amundi, which manages around $1 trillion globally. The shifts are likely to create only short-term volatility in Southeast Asia, he said.

Instead of focusing on what the Fed might do, asset managers are looking more closely at developments within individual countries, Mr. Blanqué said.

"Confidence is very much linked to the ability of the authorities to deliver on the fundamentals," he said. "Country risk is back in the emerging space."

title: FACTBOX-Key political risks to watch in the Philippines
text:
MANILA, April 11 (Reuters) - The government and the country's largest Muslim rebel group have agreed a preliminary deal that may end a 40-year conflict that has killed more than 120,000 and displaced 2 million.

President Benigno Aquino hopes this will pave the way for economic growth and development in the south, a poor region but one that sits on considerable resources.

In March it won its first investment-grade credit rating when Fitch upgraded it, coming after Moody's raised its rank for the country last October and Standard & Poor's did in July.

In 2012, the economy grew 6.6 percent, beating expectations and putting its rate of expansion second only to China.

Still, much of the country is dilapidated and vulnerable to natural disaster. Typhoon Bopha killed thousands in the south late last year, and heavy rains in August swamped huge swathes of Manila, killing more than 100 people and leaving hundreds of thousands homeless.

Internationally, by far the greatest concern is the South China Sea, contested waters where the U.S.-backed Philippines are increasingly running up against China.

RATINGS: (Unchanged unless stated:)

S&P: BB+

MOODY'S: Ba1

FITCH: BBB- (Upgraded from BB+ on March 27)

Following is a summary of political risks to watch:

INTERNAL SECURITY

Negotiators from the government and the Muslim rebel group Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) have reached a deal on a roadmap to set up a new autonomous Bangsamoro region in the south of the mainly Roman Catholic state, signalling an end to a long insurgency.

Still, the 11,000-member MILF is not the only active rebel group. Maoist guerrillas have attacked private mining projects on southern island Mindanao, destroying around $70 million worth of equipment, and threatening more attacks. A small al Qaeda-linked Islamist militant group also remains active on remote islands in the southern Philippines, kidnapping foreigners and local traders.

Overall, internal security remains weak, persistently highlighted by foreign embassies in travel advisories, with law enforcement hobbled by corruption, lack of police resources, and easy availability of guns on the street.

What to watch:

- Implementation of the political deal to set up an autonomous region in Muslim-dominated areas in the south. This will include the demobilisation, disarmament and reintegration of former Muslim rebel fighters, imposition of local taxes to cut government subsidies, and revenue-sharing arrangements with oil and gas producers.

- Laws drafted by a 15-member panel of government and rebel representatives that will create a new autonomous government for that region.

- Any more attacks on mines or other businesses, and how investors respond. The Philippine army has said it lacks the resources to contain attacks, so has asked firms to hire private militias to guard their businesses.

- Diplomatic fallout from the peace talks with Muslim rebels after the incursion of 200 Filipinos, belonging to an ancient sultanate, on Malaysia's eastern state of Sabah, which resulted in a bloody confrontation in early 2013.

SOUTH CHINA SEA

The Philippines is at the centre of Asia's most likely military flashpoint: the South China Sea. Last year a regional summit failed to agree a position on the competing claims of various nations, and what appears to be the increasing alignment of Washington with Manila risks infuriating China.

In January the Philippines asked an international tribunal to intervene in its longstanding dispute with China and declare that Beijing's claims are invalid, a move China rejected.

That came soon after U.S. and Philippine officials agreed on an increase in the number of U.S. military ships, aircraft and troops rotating through the Philippines, though officials from both countries say there is no plan to revive permanent U.S. military bases there.

Manila will not surrender claims to its exclusive economic zone, as defined by the United Nations, but it cannot hope to confront China militarily.

Beijing wants one-one-negotiations, but Manila and other claimants prefer a multilateral approach, which opens the way for an indirect role for the United States. China wants the United States to stay out of the dispute.

What to watch:

- New security arrangements between Washington and Manila to increase the U.S. military footprint in the Philippines, the U.S. fighter jets and warships the Philippines is able to buy, and how China responds to any Filipino military buildup.

- Any action taken by the tribunal of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) on Manila's request for intervention.

- Fresh approaches by Manila to pursue its claims on the disputed Spratly Islands. Aquino has said Manila is looking into at least five other options to pursue its claims after China rejected arbitration, including asking for intervention from the International Tribunal on the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) in Germany.

- Commercial activity in the South China Sea. Manila has accepted exploration bids on two oil and gas in the disputed areas, and an Anglo-Filipino company may start drilling oil wells later this year in the Reed Bank, another area claimed by China. Spending on upgrades of air and naval equipment, including radar stations. The Philippines plans to roll out $1.8 billion in defence spending in the next four years, but says its actions are not aggressive.

ECONOMIC GROWTH; CHURCH V STATE?

Fitch's credit rating upgrade is a vote of confidence in the government's efforts curb corruption and increase infrastructure spending, and comes as more and more economies in the West struggle to avoid credit rating downgrades. The move is likely to attract higher levels of investment.

The government has lifted an 18-month moratorium on new resources exploration projects, but commercial operations will not start until lawmakers approve new legislation on mineral revenues and a presidential executive order is signed.

Congressional approval is likely to hold up permits further, stalling up to $12 billion in new investments planned over the next five years, including Southeast Asia's biggest undeveloped copper-gold mine, the $5.9 billion Tampakan project by global miner Xstrata Plc and Australia's Indophil Resources NL

in the south of the country.

Still, the economy is performing well. With 6.6 percent growth in 2012, the Philippines is an example of expansion in contrast to Europe and the United States.

Authorities are struggling to control an inflow of capital that has pushed up the currency and threatens asset price bubbles, and government is concerned about the impact of a strong peso on the competitiveness of its exports, remittances from Filipinos abroad and the growing outsourcing sector.

Separately, Congress approved in December a highly controversial reproductive health bill, requiring the government to hand out contraceptives to poor people, a policy bitterly opposed by the Catholic church. The move, the first time in more than a decade an elected politician has taken on the bishops and won, was a sign of Aquino's confidence and his bedrock of national support, but is unlikely to be the last battle between church and state.

What to watch:

- Whether other ratings agencies follow Fitch in upgrading the Philippines to investment-level ranks.

- Progress on the government's big-ticket infrastructure projects to spur investment, create jobs and further lift the economy.

- How quickly mining firms start work on new projects. [20130411 044911 GMT]

- Growth figures, and central bank policy moves.

- Political fallout from Aquino's challenge to the influential Roman Catholic bishops in pushing reform of contraception laws as his administration faces mid-term elections in May.

- A Supreme Court ruling on the reproductive health law after Catholic lay groups won a temporary restraining order on the law's implementation.

(Editing by Daniel Magnowski) [20130411 044911 GMT]

That came soon after U.S. and Philippine officials agreed on an increase in the number of U.S. military ships, aircraft and troops rotating through the Philippines, though officials from both countries say there is no plan to revive permanent U.S. military bases there.

Manila will not surrender claims to its exclusive economic zone, as defined by the United Nations, but it cannot hope to confront China militarily.

Beijing wants one-one-negotiations, but Manila and other claimants prefer a multilateral approach, which opens the way for an indirect role for the United States. China wants the United States to stay out of the dispute.

What to watch:

- New security arrangements between Washington and Manila to increase the U.S. military footprint in the Philippines, the U.S. fighter jets and warships the Philippines is able to buy, and how China responds to any Filipino military buildup.

- Any action taken by the tribunal of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) on Manila's request for intervention.

- Fresh approaches by Manila to pursue its claims on the disputed Spratly Islands. Aquino has said Manila is looking into at least five other options to pursue its claims after China rejected arbitration, including asking for intervention from the International Tribunal on the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) in Germany. Commercial activity in the South China Sea. Manila has accepted exploration bids on two oil and gas in the disputed areas, and an Anglo-Filipino company may start drilling oil wells later this year in the Reed Bank, another area claimed by China.

- Spending on upgrades of air and naval equipment, including radar stations. The Philippines plans to roll out $1.8 billion in defence spending in the next four years, but says its actions are not aggressive.

ECONOMIC GROWTH; CHURCH V STATE?

Mining firms want the Philippines to lift an 18-month moratorium on new projects, but this will not happen until lawmakers approve new legislation on mineral revenues and a presidential executive order is signed.

Congressional approval is likely to hold up permits further, stalling up to $12 billion in new investments planned over the next five years, including Southeast Asia's biggest undeveloped copper-gold mine, the $5.9 billion Tampakan project by global miner Xstrata Plc and Australia's Indophil Resources NL

in the south of the country.

Still, the economy is performing well. With 6.6 percent growth in 2012, the Philippines is an example of expansion in contrast to Europe and the United States.

Authorities are struggling to control an inflow of capital that has pushed up the currency and threatens asset price bubbles, and government is concerned about the impact of a strong peso on the competitiveness of its exports and the growing outsourcing sector.

Separately, Parliament approved in December a highly controversial reproductive health bill, requiring the government to hand out contraceptives to poor people, a policy bitterly opposed by the Catholic church.

The move, the first time in more than a decade an elected politician has taken on the bishops and won, was a sign of Aquino's confidence and his bedrock of national support, but is unlikely to be the last battle between church and state.

What to watch:

- Possible ratings upgrades after the passage of new alcohol and tobacco sales tax rates. The tax reform measures are likely to push the Philippines towards investment grade.

- When the mining moratorium is lifted, and how quickly resources firms start work on new projects.

- Growth figures, and central bank policy moves.

- Political fallout from Aquino's challenge to the influential Roman Catholic bishops in pushing reform of contraception laws.

title: UPDATE: Philippine  Central Bank  To Review BOP Target As Jan Surplus Surges
text:
--Central bank to review BOP surplus target

--BOP surplus in January at $2.043 billion, more than triple December surplus


 
    By Rhea Sandique-Carlos 
 

MANILA-Intervention by the Philippines' central bank in currency markets and a surge in income from its investments abroad swelled the country's balance of payments surplus in January and may prompt a revision of the bank's forecasts.

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Tuesday said January's BOP surplus was $2.043 billion, more than triple the $640 million surplus registered in December 2012 and well above the $864 million surplus in January 2012.

The substantial increase in January's surplus was mostly supported by the central bank's foreign exchange operations as well as income from investments abroad, said BSP Governor Amando Tetangco .

The central bank has been intervening in the currency market to keep the peso from appreciating sharply. Despite the bank's support of the dollar, the peso appreciated 6.4% against the greenback in 2012. That intervention has led to a buildup in the Philippines' foreign exchange reserves and those reserves are mostly parked in U.S. Treasurys, providing income for the BSP.

The government is planning to revisit its projection for a BOP surplus of $3 billion for 2013, Mr. Tetangco said. When the forecast was made last year, "the expectation was that, among others, the country will have a larger trade deficit, as imports will recover, in line with a recovery in the export market, given the expected improvement in the external environment," he said.

"If the EU recovers as the ECB [European Central Bank ] anticipates, and if the U.S. economy remains on track, we should see some easing in the capital inflows," Mr. Tetangco added.

One of the factors for the peso's strength over the last year has been capital inflows as investors look for higher returns amid near-zero interest rates in developed nations.

"The desire [of the BSP] is not to manipulate but to temper the strengthening of the peso," said Emilio Neri , an economist with Bank of the Philippine Islands . He added that if capital inflows continue, the central bank may need to further intervene in currency markets and keep the peso from appreciating more substantially.

Mr. Neri expects the BOP surplus this year to range between $10 billion-$11 billion.

The country had a BOP surplus of $9.236 billion in 2012, compared with $10.179 billion the previous year.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Philippine peso up after Moody's; exporters lift won, Taiwan dlr
text:
* Moody's upgrades Philippines to Ba1

* S.Korea intervention caution caps won's upside

* Taiwan dlr up on exporters; importers limit gains

(Adds text, updates prices)

By Jongwoo Cheon

SINGAPORE, Oct 29 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso turned higher on Monday after Moody's upgraded the country's sovereign ratings, while the South Korean won and the Taiwan dollar gained on month-end demand from exporters amid subdued trading.

The peso initially weakened to 41.275 per dollar during morning trade, but it reversed direction in the afternoon session after the rating agency's move.

Moody's Investors Service upgraded the Philippines' foreign and local currency long-term bond ratings by one notch to Ba1 from Ba2, citing the country's improved economic performance and continued fiscal revenue buoyancy.

"At the moment, the market is looking for a catalyst to push the peso. Dollar/peso would be vulnerable to further downside with lack of corporate demand," said a European bank dealer in Manila.

The dealer expected the central bank to intervene to stem the peso's strength, but added: "one thing is clear that any upside (in dollar/peso) will be heavy."

The peso has gained 6.5 percent against the dollar so far this year, becoming the best performing emerging Asian currency, Thomson Reuters data showed.

That came even as the central bank has been spotted slowing down its appreciation along with intervention by other central banks, which has curbed the peso's upside.

"Emerging Asian currencies have lost much of their appreciation momentum on sustained worries about intervention. They also technically appeared to have risen too much, so more investors may want to take profits," said Yuna Park, a currency and bond analyst at Dongbu Securities in Seoul.

Investors were not confident enough about the global economic recovery despite signs of stable U.S. growth and due to uncertainty over the euro zone's debt crisis.

Traders await Spain's request for a bailout, which would initiate the European Central Bank's bond-buying programme and could push the euro out of its recent range.

Investors also kept a wary eye on Greece, after the country's opposition leader said his party would vote against an austerity package expected to go before parliament this week.

WON

The won hit 1,094.6 per dollar, its strongest since Oct. 28 last year on demand from exporters for month-end settlements.

But traders took profit on caution over possible intervention by the foreign exchange authorities to slow down the won's strength. Trading was also thin.

President Lee Myung-bak said in a speech that South Korea's comparative economic strength has been pushing the local currency higher. This appreciation "makes difficulties for exporters," he said.

"The won may see short-term resistance around mid-1,090 once exporters' month-end deals are cleared this week," said a senior foreign bank dealer in Seoul.

TAIWAN DOLLAR

The Taiwan dollar rose slightly on exporters' demand for settlements, while importers' bids for greenbacks limited the local unit's upside.

Interbank speculators hesitated to build up aggressive bets either way as overseas markets, especially in New York, are unlikely to provide market-moving factors due to Hurricane Sandy.

The storm is expected to slam into the U.S. East Coast on Monday night. Market participants in the New York area see a light trading day on Monday -- and possibly through Tuesday -- with some U.S. markets closed, as some offices in lower Manhattan's Financial District are in an evacuation zone.

RINGGIT

The ringgit eased as traders covered dollar-short positions on a weaker euro, dealers said.

The Malaysian currency came under more pressure from some dollar demand from importers, they added.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Profit-taking weighs on Asia  FX , but set for weekly gains
text:
* Ringgit down on dlr-short covering

 * Philippine peso eases on rate cut speculation

 * Won turns higher on exporters 

(Adds detail, updates prices)

 By Jongwoo Cheon

 SINGAPORE, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Most emerging Asian currencies eased on Friday as investors took profits after disappointing earnings from U.S. technology giants, although they were mainly poised for weekly gains amid signs the global economy is stabilising.

 The Malaysian ringgit lost 0.4 percent as interbank speculators covered dollar-short positions, while the Philippine peso slid on speculation of a rate cut by the central bank next week.

 Regional stocks also eased as weaker quarterly results from Google Inc and Microsoft hit technology names in the area.

 But the retreat in emerging Asian currencies is simply a correction on profit-booking, dealers and analysts said.

 Regional units are also expected to move higher against the yen if the Bank of Japan takes another easing step at a policy meeting on Oct. 30, they added.

 Most local currencies in Asia have already gained versus the Japanese unit with the South Korean won hitting a six-month high.

 "Still, U.S. funds are looking for attractive places for yields next year. We will see more inflows to emerging markets towards the end of this year, especially after the U.S. election and China's transition of power," said a European bank dealer in Singapore.

 The dealer said those funds are likely to look to South Korean and Malaysian bonds.

 Most emerging Asian currencies were on course for weekly gains as economic data from the United States and China earlier this week alleviated concerns over a slowing global economy.

 Some U.S.companies also delivered solid earnings, supporting risk appetite, although Asian currency authorities such as central banks in the Philippines, Singapore and Taiwan were spotted intervening to stem rises in their currencies, dealers said.

 The South Korean won led weekly gains among emerging Asian currencies with a 0.7 percent climb against the dollar. Offshore funds and domestic exporters chased the local currency.

 The Taiwan dollar has risen 0.4 percent against the greenback so far this week, while the ringgit and the Chinese yuan have both gained 0.3 percent, according to Thomson Reuters data.

 The Singapore dollar has advanced 0.2 percent, the data showed.

 But the Indian rupee has lost 1.7 percent as higher-than-expected inflation data undermined hopes for a rate cut to boost the economy. Indian oil companies also bought the dollar to make payments.

 RINGGIT

 The ringgit earlier weakened past 3.0476 per dollar, the 38.2 percent retracement of its appreciation since Oct. 10 on dollar-short covering.

 Technical charts indicated that the Malaysian currency may head to 3.0543, the 50.0 percent retracement, if it ends the day weaker than the 38.2 percent level.

 However, some traders have been buying the ringgit on dips, limiting its depreciation.

 "Besides Google, the market is in a risk-on mode. I will try to sell dollar/ringgit between 3.055 and 3.060," said a Malaysian bank dealer in Kuala Lumpur.

 PHILIPPINE PESO

 The Philippine peso slid as interbank speculators took profits from the second-best performing emerging Asian currency this year.

 It also came under pressure from speculation the central bank may cut interest rates at its policy meeting on Oct. 25.

 Investors remained cautious over possible intervention by the central bank as well, especially after it was spotted buying dollars below 41.20 earlier this week, dealers said.

 "We will not tolerate excesses in exchange rate movements and will not hesitate to consider other tools in our policy tool kit," Governor Amando Tetangco said in an email.

 Still, the local currency found some support at 41.45 per dollar on expectations of remittance inflows, dealers said.

 "The peso can correct up to 41.57 and 41.75 if the BSP cuts in policy rates," said a European bank dealer in Manila, referring to the central bank.

 "But for now 41.45 would be strong support, given that there is not enough negative news to reverse the recent risk rally."

 WON

 The won turned higher as exporters including shipbuilders and electronics companies bought the local unit to settle payments. Custodian banks also purchased the South Korean currency, dealers said.

 The local unit started the day softer and weakened to 1,106.5 per dollar as some offshore funds and domestic interbank speculators sold.

 But exporters did not miss the chances to buy the won on dips, especially around 1,106, dealers said.

 "Given growing expectations for further appreciation in the won, exporters snapped it up whenever it weakened," said a South Korean bank dealer in Seoul.

title: EM ASIA  FX -BOJ gives another boost; won, Sing dlr at 4-1/2-mth high vs yen
text:
* Philippine peso up on medium-term funds, macro accounts

* Won turns higher on BOJ easing; intervention caution grows

* Rupiah down on Indonesian corporate dollar demand

(Adds text, updates prices)

By Jongwoo Cheon

SINGAPORE, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Most emerging Asian currencies rose on Wednesday as Japan's central bank joined other major policymakers in launching fresh stimulus to shore up growth, bolstering risk sentiment and hopes for more capital inflows to the region.

The South Korean won and the Singapore dollar

hit their highest levels versus the yen in about four and a half months after the Bank of Japan (BOJ) eased monetary policy by stepping up asset purchases by 10 trillion yen ($127.21 billion), double the usual amount.

The move invigorated emerging Asian currencies, most of which started the day slightly weaker against the dollar on worries about Spain's apparent reluctance to apply for financial aid. Asian shares also rebounded from initial losses.

"We got another excuse to get bullish here," said Andy Ji, Asian currency strategist for Commonwealth Bank of Australia in Singapore.

"There is already enough liquidity around and all it takes for those to come to the region is some feel-good stories," said Ji, picking up the won as the best choice for investors.

Emerging Asian currencies have appreciated so far this month as the Federal Reserve introduced a third round of quantitative easing and the European Central Bank launched a fresh bond-buying programme to ease the three-year old debt crisis.

Still, Asian policymakers may not necessarily welcome those measures as they risk inviting hot money into their economies, and stronger regional currencies are likely to hurt export competitiveness at a time when global growth is faltering.

Business sentiment among Asia's top companies fell for the second straight quarter, dragged down by export-orientated economies such as China and Japan, while domestic spending helped boost Southeast Asia's outlook, according to the latest Thomson Reuters/INSEAD Asia Business Sentiment Survey published earlier.

Some authorities such as central banks of Philippines and Taiwan have been recently spotted intervening to curb appreciation of their currencies, dealers said. Investors remained wary of similar moves by central banks in the region.

Investors are also awaiting the latest data on Chinese manufacturing, with the HSBC flash purchasing managers' index (PMI) due on Thursday.

PHILIPPINE PESO

The Philippine peso gained on demand from medium-term funds and macro accounts, and extended strength to hit a session high of 41.57 per dollar.

But the peso's gains were limited as domestic interbank speculators took the gain as chances to book profits, they added.

With traders seen still holding short dollar positions to cover, the peso is unlikely to extend gains here, a foreign bank dealer in Manila said.

WON

The won started local trade weaker against the dollar, but turned firmer after the BOJ eased policy.

The South Korean currency hit 14.0644 versus the yen, its strongest since May 3.

The strength further boosted caution over possible intervention by the foreign exchange authorities, especially as major South Korean companies such as Hyundai Motor Co

compete with Japanese peers including Toyota Motor Corp in overseas markets.

"Few will ignore the authorities and push up the won here, especially as yen/won collapsed," said a South Korean bank dealer in Seoul.

TAIWAN DOLLAR

The Taiwan dollar was firmer than the previous close, which dealers said the central bank weakened through intervention, and exporters' demand for settlements.

On Tuesday, the island's central bank was spotted buying U.S. dollars to stem the local currency's strength not only in the main foreign exchange market but also in the smaller market , dealers said.

In the prior session, the Taiwan dollar closed 0.2 percent weaker at 29.460 to the greenback, while it strengthened to 29.250 before the central bank stepped in the market.

RUPIAH

The rupiah lost 0.5 percent against the dollar on domestic corporate bids for the greenback and as the central bank was not been spotted in the market.

Some state-run banks bought the rupiah, but dealers said Indonesian exporters were behind the demand, rather than the authorities.

While most other emerging Asian currencies benefited from the BOJ's move, the rupiah did not much recover its losses.

"The rupiah will appreciate only when trade deficit narrows and growth numbers come out better," said a Jakarta-based dealer.

title: DJ UPDATE:  Philippines  Fires Warning Shot On Strengthening Peso
text:
--Philippine central bank intervenes as peso hits 4-year high

--Bank warns speculators it may curb NDFs

--Official moves may have only limited impact as investors flock to peso

(Combines previous stories, recasts throughout.) 


 
   By Martin Vaughan and Cris Larano 
 

The Philippine central bank signaled Wednesday it's leery of the peso's recent surge and may increase its efforts to curb the currency's rise.

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas sold pesos for dollars in the market, traders said, and the bank announced it will review rules on nondeliverable forward contracts, a tool traders use to speculate on the direction of emerging-market currencies.

Manila's authorities stepped in as the peso hit a four-year high, with the dollar falling to PHP41.60. The U.S. currency rebounded after the central bank announcement to PHP41.83 late in Asia trade. The bank's moves came before Standard & Poor's Ratings Services upgraded the government's debt by a notch to just below investment grade.

Central bank Gov. Amando Tetangco soft-pedaled the moves, saying the peso's recent action is in line with a broader pick-up in appetite for risky currencies.

"It's appreciating just like most (currencies) in the region are, although admittedly it has moved more than the others in recent days," Mr. Tetangco told Dow Jones Newswires in a text message. "We are monitoring price action and market behavior to determine (any) unusual activity."

The peso is up 5% against the dollar this year and his risen 4.5% since May 24 alone. That's in sharp contrast to most of its Asian peers, weighed by global risk aversion as the euro-zone debt crisis has roiled markets in recent months: Indonesian rupiah is down 3.0% this year, while the Malaysian ringgit and Thai baht are roughly flat.

Investors have been drawn to the peso for a number of reasons. The Philippine economy grew at a standout pace of 6.4% in the first quarter, and reforms by President Benigno Aquino III have narrowed the fiscal deficit. The peso's gains have been driven by foreign buying of Philippine shares, which increased 59% in the first half of the year.

Thomas Harr, Asia currency strategist at Standard Chartered, said the Philippines "is having a little bit of a moment similar to what Indonesia had between mid-2009 and mid-2011," when that country's assets, such as bonds and the rupiah, posted big gains on expectations of sovereign credit upgrades.

The Philippine central bank may struggle to curb the peso via NDF restrictions since it can only directly control what domestic banks do in this offshore market. "Any rule changes will be modest and limited and will have only a short-term impact on the peso," Mr. Harr said.

Mr. Tetangco said the central bank will review regulations on NDFs and "special deposit accounts"--fixed-term deposits by banks, trust entities and other financial institutions, used primarily to manage liquidity due to foreign exchange inflows--"because these two can be possible entry points for speculation."

Those statements are a "warning shot" to let markets know the central bank is watching, said Credit Suisse economist Santitarn Sathirathai.

But while the Philippine central bank was in the market Wednesday, it typically doesn't intervene as aggressively as its counterparts in such places as Indonesia, South Korea and Taiwan.

And the Philippine authorities aren't greatly concerned about supporting the country's exports, Mr. Santitarn said, because inflation remains low, keeping the peso competitive in inflation-adjusted terms.

Rather, he said, what worries the central bank is the exchange rate's impact on remittance flows from overseas workers. A growing segment of the population depends on those flows to purchase daily necessities, and a weakening dollar means the paychecks from overseas will translate into fewer pesos.

A Manila-based currency trader said the central bank may consider cutting interest rates to lessen the peso's attractiveness, especially if June inflation, out Thursday stays below the bank's 3%-5% target range.
