title: WSJ BLOG/Real Time Economics: Look Back: Broad Economic Concerns Mount World-Wide
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's Real Time Economics blog at http://blogs.wsj.com/economics .)

The U.S. and world economies are in danger again as financial leaders gather in Washington for the International Monetary Fund's annual meetings. Markets are falling world-wide due to broad economic concerns that go beyond a hangover from the crisis and extend to policy dysfunction in the U.S., Europe and developing nations. This post followed developments from the annual meetings and the latest readings on the economy for Thursday.

4:22 pm | by Jamila Trindle

The European debt crisis highlights the need for the Dodd-Frank law's changes to financial regulations, Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chairman Gary Gensler said Thursday.

"Twenty-first century finance knows no true geographic border as money and risk can move around the globe with a touch of a button," Gensler said at a conference on regulation at Georgetown University.

Last year's Dodd-Frank law gave the CFTC the bulk of responsibility to oversee the over-the-counter derivatives market and the agency is still in the process of writing new rules for that market.

Gensler said that there are people who would like to roll back the rules, which would continue "the regulatory environment that led to the crisis three years ago."

Gensler also said that the CFTC is coordinating with foreign regulators to make the rules consistent and will seek public comment on the agency's jurisdiction over international transactions.

4:11 pm | by Paul Vieira

A coalition of advanced and emerging economies -- among them Britain, Canada and Indonesia -- sought Thursday to urge Group of 20 leaders to implement a coordinated strategy to rescue a weakening economy, according to a foreign-policy analyst who closely tracks the international forum.

A letter released Thursday from Britain, Canada, Mexico, Australia, Indonesia, and South Korea to French president Nicolas Sarkozy said the lack of visible political will in Europe over the summer, and the failure to find a lasting solution to sovereign debt problems, had damaged confidence and held back the recovery.

John Kirton, who heads up the University of Toronto's G20 research group, said the letter is an attempt by these countries to put together a deal. To their advantage, they are not linked to the big developed economies -- the United States and the euro zone -- or the so-called BRICS group of large emerging economies.

The joint letter also has an air of desperation, he added. "These leaders don't believe they can wait for Cannes," Mr. Kirton said, in reference to the G20 leaders summit scheduled for early November in the French city known for its film festival.

Mr. Kirton added that the euro zone, the United States, and the BRICS group -- China, Brazil, India, Russia and South Africa -- are at odds about what is required, highlighted by a tense encounter between Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner and his euro peers in Poland last Friday.

Mr. Kirton added countries like Canada and Australia, which have relatively sterling balanced sheets, could agree to provide more fiscal stimulus, so long as the euro zone and the U.S. attack their large deficits and the BRICS come up with some form of financial assistance.

"But I am a bit pessimistic about such a deal," he said.

3:47 pm | by Anjali Cordeiro

Philippines Finance Secretary Cesar Purisima said Thursday that it is in the country's greater interest to focus on economic fundamentals and leave the level of its currency up to markets.

His comments come as emerging-market currencies, including the Philippine peso, are seeing big drops on rising risk aversion.

Purisima said at a Washington speech that the central bank allows markets to determine the value of its currency, intervening mainly to smooth out any disruptive movements.

"Outside of that the best thing we can do is invest in fundamentals," he said.

His comments would suggest that Philippines policy makers aren't inclined toward any dramatic intervention to shore up the currency, but would rather make smaller moves when needed to smooth out volatile swings.

"The best thing is really to leave it up to the markets," he said.

The government is keeping its budget deficit target at 3% of gross domestic product, he said, adding that the "official" estimate for 2011 growth has been 5%.

3:32 pm | by Phil Izzo

Nomura economists look at today's mostly flat jobless claims and sees no positive signs for employment. They write:

The overall picture of the labor market can best be described by the word "stagnant". Business confidence surveys have indicated that while businesses, at least outside of the financial industry, have not turned to conducting large-scale layoffs, they have suggested that a general lack of sales and uncertainty over the economic outlook are impeding hiring plans.

3:28 pm

Paul Krugman looks at the market tumble, and is in "I told you so" mode. He writes:

"When the 2008 crisis struck, it was immediately clear that this was what we had been afraid of. And it was desperately important that policy makers realize that we were in a world where the usual rules no longer applied.

But they didn't. The banks were rescued -- but as soon as that happened, the moralizers and deficit worriers, the people who see hyperinflation lurking under every bed, took over. Warnings that we were repeating not just the mistakes of Japan but the mistakes of Hoover and Bruening were waved away as the squeaking of people of no consequence, never mind the fact that some of us had pretty fancy credentials.

And now we are exactly where I feared we'd be, repeating all the old mistakes and experiencing all the old consequences."

Read the whole post here.

3:23 pm

So it is a puzzler why markets, having gotten the stimulus they expected, are now selling off. The sense of panic was such some analysts were already beginning to talk about whether the Fed would need to expand its balance sheet further to aid growth. The market unrest raises questions about how the Fed deals with markets, and whether monetary policy can really do anything for an economy where access to credit on affordable terms isn't the main thing holding the nation back.

Perhaps the biggest problem for the Fed is the idea that in ratifying the market's expectations so closely over recent years, policymakers may now be in the position of chasing their tails. In both Operation Twist and the recently ended bond buying program known as QE2, markets priced in the impact of the policies before they were actually implemented. It remains to be see what Operation Twist's fate will be, but bond markets sold off after QE2 instead of rallied, as many would have expected.

Read the whole post here.

3:15 pm

MarketBeat is liveblogging the close with the DJIA currently down more than 450.

From the liveblog:

3:12 pm

Zero Hedge has a post up from Peter Tchir of TF Market Advisors, who is skeptical about the euro zone's recapitalization move reported by the FT:

"Europe is going to bail out the 16 weakest banks? Banks that are in trouble because the PSI for Greece is worse than any stress they ran. Plans should be getting made for these banks to die but to possibly save the creditors and limit systematic risk.

The focus should be on putting together plans for the big banks that pose real systematic risk. The market knows the stress tests were a farce, so why make a plan to save those that barely survived that low hurdle. Didn't they learn anything from dealing with Greece. Giving minimal help to the worst institutions is NOT going to solve anything and just shows how far behind they are in their thinking."

Read the whole post here.

3:00 pm | by Jean Yung

Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa must consider together raising resources for solving global issues, China's central bank governor said Thursday, reiterating a point raised in a joint statement by the emerging-market countries.

However, financial support from an individual country will vary depending on each country's situation, Zhou Xiaochuan said without elaborating.

The specifics of boosting support for the global recovery effort still requires wider discussion by the Group of 7 and Group of 20 nations, Zhou added.

He was speaking to media after a meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors of the BRICS.

2:45 pm | by Margit Feher

The European Central Bank's sovereign-bond purchases and liquidity-providing measures launched to prevent a contagion of deteriorating financial market conditions are temporary and do not replace the need for fiscal discipline, Vitor Constancio, the bank's vice president, said Thursday.

The ECB remains committed to its primary mandate of maintaining price stability, he said. Using inflation to reduce debt would undermine the ECB's credibility, Constancio added.

"Inflating the debt away would unduly jeopardise the most precious capital of the ECB and of any independent central bank, namely its credibility," Constancio said in a speech the ECB released on its website. "The ECB will never debase the currency. As our record shows, we have remarkably preserved both internal and external value of the euro by keeping inflation low and inflation expectations well-anchored."

2:39 pm

You can read the transcript from IMF chief Christine Lagarde's press conference here.

2:29 pm

The Financial Times is reporting that EU is looking to speed up bank recapitalization for the 16 banks at risk during the stress tests. From the FT:

"European officials look set to speed up plans to recapitalise the 16 banks that came close to failing last summer's pan-EU stress tests as part of a co-ordinated effort to reassure the markets about the strength of the 27-nation bloc's banking sector. [ 09-22-11 1636ET ]

A senior French official said the 16 banks regarded to be close to the threshold would now have to seek new funds immediately. Although there has been widespread speculation that French banks are seeking more capital, none is on the list. Other European officials said discussions were still under way."

Read the full article.

2:24 pm | by Phil Izzo

The Atlanta Fed says that despite the growing economic concerns, the probability of deflation in the U.S. remains low -- 16% as of yesterday:

"Prices of Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) with similar maturity dates can be used to measure probabilities of a net decline in the consumer price index over the five-year period starting in early 2011. One measure of this deflation probability was 16 percent on September 21, unchanged from a week earlier. This deflation probability has leveled off after increasing from 12 percent to 18 percent in the first three weeks of August. An alternative lower bound on the probability of deflation was 1 percent on September 21, also unchanged from a week earlier."

2:17 pm | by Jared A. Favole

President Barack Obama told European leaders that they need to take "forceful and decisive" action to deal with the euro zone debt crisis, the White House said Thursday.

President Obama met Wednesday with British Prime Minister David Cameron and French President Nicolas Sarkozy while at the United Nation's General Assembly. They discussed an array of foreign policy and economic issues.

White House Press Secretary Jay Carney said Thursday President Obama said Europe needs to take "forceful and decisive" action to deal with the crisis. Carney, speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One while en route to Ohio with the president, said Obama also reiterated that he believes Europe has the capacity to deal with the debt crisis.

2:06 pm

European markets are closed. So what's the damage? From MarketBeat:

FTSE 100 , down 246.80 points, or 4.67% to 5041.61.


   -- Down 322.10 points, or 6.01%, over the last two trading days. 
 
   -- Largest two day point & percentage decline since Monday, August 08, 2011. 

Stoxx Europe 600 , down 10.44 points, or 4.63%, to 214.89.


   -- Down 14.21 points, or 6.20%, over the last two trading days. 
 
   -- Largest two day point & percentage decline since Monday, September 05, 
      2011. 

1:53 pm | by Phil Izzo

IHS Global Insight economists Nariman Behravesh and Sara Johnson say recession risks in the U.S. and euro zone are "uncomfortably" high amid disappointing economic data, political paralysis and the potential for a serious policy mistake. But they say this won't be a replay of 2008 financial crisis. They write:

"While the risks of recessions in the United States and Europe have risen, a repeat of the financial meltdown of 2008 and the ensuing 'Great Recession' does not seem likely. Emerging markets will almost certainly continue to grow, albeit more slowly. Central banks stand ready to -- once again -- deploy unorthodox policies, if needed. That said, a financial shock emanating from the Eurozone could do a lot of damage."

1:47 pm | by Nathalie Boschat and Gabriele Parussini

The euro zone could look in the future at leveraging the resources of its bailout fund to increase its capacity to respond to systemic crises, French Finance Minister Francois Baroin said Thursday, although he cautioned this isn't a priority for now.

The euro zone could in the future look at "how to give meaning to this fund by leveraging its resources to give it a systemic power," Baroin told reporters at the beginning of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund.

Baroin insisted, however, that the immediate priority is for euro-zone countries to get a July 21 accord through national parliaments to stabilize the euro zone. The agreement will expand the capabilities of the bloc's rescue fund by allowing it to act in a preemptive manner, buy sovereign debt on the secondary markets and recapitalize ailing banks.

"It wouldn't make sense to have an alternative strategy" until the July 21 agreement is in place, Baroin said. "We can't have a plan B until the plan A has been implemented."

1:36 pm | by Jonathan Cheng

From MarketBeat:

Unlike other recent, ugly trading sessions that come to mind -- say, August 8's crazy 635-point Dow disaster, or Aug. 10's 520-point bloodletting, or even Aug. 4's 513-point slide -- this week's ugliness hasn't been punctuated by equally jarring moves to the upside. Nope, this week the stock markets have just kind of slid lower and lower.

For a sense of how gruesome things are, WSJ's helpful Markets Data Group reckons we're on pace for our worst stock-market week since October 2008, when we managed to lose 18% in five days. We're already below our August nadir, putting us at a one-year low. And gold, that heroic metal in times of ill times, is on track for its biggest dollar decline (-$81 so far) since 1980, and its worst in percentage terms (-4.5%) since Feb. 2009.

Stay tuned, folks. We still have, of course, about 10 hours to go in the week.

1:30 pm | by Phil Izzo

Earlier this morning, the Conference Board release its index of leading indicators for August, which showed a 0.3% monthly gain. But economists Josh Shapiro at MFR Inc. warns that the underlying data aren't so encouraging. Stock prices and consumer expectations dropped and the positives came from two places that are artificially inflated. He writes:

"Abstracting from the yield curve slope component, which is influenced by the Fed's abnormally low federal-funds-rate target, and the recent jump in the M2 money supply component which is due to safe-haven inflows to the U.S. banking system from Europe as well as from money market funds, the overall signal from the LEI is in all likelihood misleadingly benign at the moment."

1:25 pm | by Karen Talley

Port of Long Beach, Calif., key way station for goods shipped in from Asia, is not expecting an overly merry holiday season.

Figures to be released next month are likely to show trade numbers for September were relatively flat vs year ago, as major retailers wait as long as possible to make decisions regarding their holiday season inventories, a spokeswoman said.

Retailers haven't ordered as many goods heading into the holiday season as they have in past years, also illustrating that there's still uncertainty about the overall economy, the spokeswoman said

1:22 pm | by Ian Talley

The European economic union is facing the threat of failure unless officials there quickly move to boost the firepower of its bailout facilities, U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner said Thursday.

"What Europe is trying to do is build the fiscal budget and financial complements to the initial Maastricht treaty," Geithner said. The Maastricht treaty is the euro-zone agreement that created the euro common currency.

"Without the broader fiscal and financial elements, their framework is not going to work," he said. "Europe's leaders recognize this is an existential threat to the endeavor of the euro," he added.

Given the risk to the euro, Geithner said he's confident Europe will move ahead in the coming weeks to strengthen its backstop funds.

"We are going to see them act with more force in the coming weeks or months," he said.

His comments come as world financial leaders and central bankers gather in Washington for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, and Group of 20 nations talks. Officials will focus on encouraging Europe to act swiftly and decisively to stem the crisis.

The U.S. and emerging markets have expressed frustration at the sluggish pace of efforts in Europe to respond to their crisis. European Union leaders agreed in July to make their bailout funds more flexible but have yet to ratify it.

Geithner said some countries have room economic space to encourage growth.

"Some countries are going to need to move more quickly, and have no alternative," he said. "But many of the other economies have more room, more choice, to soften that path of consolidation so they're not hurting the economy as it recovers."

The Obama administration for example, wants to enact a $447 billion stimulus package to boost employment. Economists say Germany can do more too.

Geithner reiterated a call for China to pick up the pace of appreciating its yuan. A higher currency value could boost global demand, he said.

He spoke at a National Journal event.

1:05 pm | by Arild Moen

Immediate action is needed to restore confidence in political decision-making and to stop the euro-zone debt crisis from spreading beyond its borders, European Central Bank Governing Council member Erkki Liikanen says in an interview to be published in Finnish magazine Suomen Kuvalehti Friday.

He also says it is crucial that changes to the euro-zone's rescue fund -- the European Financial Stability Facility -- are fully implemented and that it comes into force soon.

"Right now there is a great risk that we won't be able to stop the European debt crisis from spreading into a global crisis," says Liikanen, who is also the Governor of the Bank of Finland.

1:04 pm | by Laurence Norman and Ian Talley

The euro zone needs to look at leveraging up its bailout fund once it has implemented agreed-upon reforms, European Union Commissioner for Economic and Monetary Affairs Olli Rehn said Thursday.

Speaking on a panel ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meetings in Washington, Rehn said he hoped to see current reforms to the region's bailout fund, the European Financial Stability Facility, completed by the second half of October.

However he went on to say that it is "very important to look at the possibility of leveraging the EFSF resources and funding to have a stronger impact and make it more effective."

12:57 pm | by Bob Davis

The deputy governor of China's central bank on Thursday said that China would continue to buy European government debt, which he said could do "quite a bit at the margin to help" Europe handle its sovereign debt crisis. [ 09-22-11 1636ET ]

Speaking at a panel during the International Monetary Fund's annual meeting, Yi Gang said that finance ministers and central bankers gathered for the IMF meeting and also a session of the Group of 20 nations need to "discuss the world situation and come up with a feasible package that can increase confidence in the world." Yi didn't propose any specific solutions and other top officials say they doubt the weekend's meeting will produce any concrete outcome.

He said that the chance of another global recession "is still rather limited."

12:51 pm | by Ben Lefebvre

What's going on with oil? Oil prices have been swinging like a 1970s house party, and Goldman Sachs says it knows why.

Investors are trying to square resilient U.S. crude oil demand -- the Department of Energy yesterday reported a 7.3 million barrel draw in crude reserves last week amid increasing U.S. demand -- with a broader economic outlook that's still gloomy for Europe and US.

In addition, demand for U.S.-made refined fuel is strong, helping the domestic refining industry. In all, the "U.S. oil market [is] facing same level of overall demand as it did prior to the 2008 financial crisis," Goldman says in a note.

U.S. benchmark crude recently down nearly $5.00 at $81.22/barrel.

12:38 pm

Berkley economist Brad DeLong posts some dire charts with the headline:

Another Slow-Moving Run on the Banks...

12:31 pm

I'm worried and scared - Mohamed El-Erian

"When I'm scared, that means a global recession is a certainty - we don't want to get there" - Mohamed El-Erian

12:29 pm

"Today's problems are largely economic, but the solutions are largely political" - Christine Lagarde

12:26 pm | by Corey Boles

Amid all the economic turmoil, the last thing the U.S. needs right now is another fight that threatens to shutdown the U.S. government. House Speaker John Boehner promises that won't happen, despite the House defeat Wednesday night of a spending to bill to keep the government funded until mid-November.

Mr. Boehner said that GOP leadership would gather with the Republican rank-and-file members to present them with options for changing the spending bill later Thursday.

But crafting a deal may not be easy. It is doubtful that the speaker will be able to lower the overall spending figure in the bill as that would then jeopardize its passage in the Senate, which must also approve it in order to avert a possible shut down of non-essential government operations.

The other, and considerably simpler, option would be for Republicans to either increase the level of natural disaster relief funding in the bill, or to remove a measure stripping funding for a program boosting the development of cleaner-emission vehicles that is popular with Democrats. These were both reasons given by Democratic leadership for the fact that virtually every one of their members voted against the spending bill.

In doing so, they would likely win the support of enough Democrats in the House to pass the measure, but would run the risk of angering their own lawmakers even further.

12:20 pm | by Anjali Cordeiro

More from Greenspan:

Former Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said Thursday that markets are signaling worries that something could "break" and it appears that Greece could default in coming weeks without a new tranche of money.

Global financial markets and particularly riskier assets have fallen sharply on worries about global growth and the euro zone's growing debt problems. The market selloff worsened Thursday.

Markets "are fearful something will break and clearly Greece is weeks away from default unless there is a new tranche," Greenspan said speaking at a panel in Washington.

Separately, referring to the Federal Reserve's QEII bond buying program to boost the U.S. economy, Greenspan said it had one positive effect of weakening the dollar. But he also noted that the euro also declined, limiting the benefits of the weaker dollar.

Now, if the Federal Reserve wanted to, it could "unwind things with little economic consequence," he said. The Federal Reserve could do an "off market transaction" with the U.S. Treasury department acting as an intermediary, he said.

Ultimately if the Fed wanted to "they could unwind the whole thing with very little economic consequence," Greenspan said. The Fed could use certain "off market transactions" that have the U.S. Treasury department acting as an intermediary, Greenspan said.

12:18 pm | by Phil Izzo

Dropping consumer sentiment in Europe has some disturbing echoes, notes Francois Cabau of Barclays:

"Euro area September "flash" consumer confidence dropped to -18.9 from -16.5 in August, coming halfway between our and market expectations (BC: -20.0; consensus: -18.0). After last month's record 5.3 point plunge, today's 2.4 point drop is smaller but nevertheless significant. In fact, we find it interesting that last time the euro area consumer confidence number dropped by more than 5 points, it then declined by 2.1 points the following month, before falling 4.4 points the next. Those three months were October, November and December 2008."

12:01 pm | by Matt Day

Is copper trying to tell us something? Comex December copper was recently down 8% at $3.461/pound after earlier hitting the lowest level since August 2010. The contract has slid 18% this month.

"Copper is telling you that the odds of a recession are increasing," says MF Global's Adam Klopfenstein. "It's hard to paint a positive picture" for the industrial bellwether with the current slate of worries about the global economy, from slowing manufacturing in the euro zone and China to Europe's debt woes.

Commodities in general have taken a hit today amid the increased economic concerns.

11:58 am | by Laurence Norman

EU Commissioner for Economic and Monetary Affairs Olli Rehn disputed numbers the IMF is using to detail challenges facing Europe's banks. "It is essential that we continue to work in order to ensure the sufficient recapitalization of European banks. In this regard, we do not share the numbers of the IMF...but we share their same concern, and, I can just say that this is a work in progress," he said. The IMF has estimated that European banks have already lost 200 billion euros from the debt crisis and face potential losses of 300 billion euros. It has urged European authorities to ensure the quick recapitalization of the region's banks. Rehn, who was speaking at a question-and-answer session at the Peterson Institute in Washington, also dismissed concerns about Italy needing a bailout program.

11:54 am | by Ainsley Thomson

Euro zone countries and institutions must act swiftly to resolve the euro crisis and all European economies must tackle their budget deficits to prevent contagion to the wider global economy, the leaders of six countries from the Group of 20 industrialized and developing nations said Thursday. In a joint letter, the U.K.'s Prime Minister David Cameron, Australia's Prime Minister Julia Gillard, Canada's Prime Minister Stephen Harper, Mexico's President Felipe Calderon, Indonesia's President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, and South Korea's President Lee Myung-bak said the lack of visible political will over the summer, and the failure to find a lasting solution to sovereign debt problems, had damaged confidence and held back the recovery.

The letter said euro-zone countries must look at "all possible options" to ensure long-term stability in the world's second largest international currency.

11:44 am

Former Fed chief Alan Greenspan weighs in on the turmoil, saying that markets are fearful that something will "break." He blames much of the crisis on Europe, saying that without Europe a U.S. double dip would be unlikely and noting that Greece appears weeks away from default without a new tranche of aid.

11:37 am | by Michael R. Crittenden and Nathalie Boschat

World Bank President Robert Zoellick, speaking earlier today, said the world remains in a "danger zone."

"I still think a double-dip recession for the world's major economies is unlikely, but my confidence in that belief is being eroded daily," Zoellick said. He cautioned that the situation for emerging markets "may be changing for the worse," potentially threatening the global economic recovery.

"Falling exports were already a worry, now falling markets and declining confidence could prompt slippage in developing countries' investment and a possible pullback by their consumers too," he said. "A fall in developing countries' domestic demand would mean we'd lose their economic engines as drivers of global recovery."

11:30 am | by Phil Izzo

In a sign of the flight from risk sparked by economic concerns, the yields on 10-year Treasurys have plummeted to under 1.8% - the lowest levels since the 1940s.

11:23 am | by Thomas Coyle

Employees the world over are feeling depressed, according to a survey by the consulting firm rogenSi. Job insecurity among workers this year is about where it was in 2009, when the global economy was still reeling from the U.S. financial crisis of 2008. Meanwhile 92% of those polled said their sense of self worth now stems from pleasing bosses, not intrinsic things like work ethic and self-belief. That's in keeping with the "culture of fear" that has held sway for businesses since the economy went rogue a few years ago, says rogenSI's Alex Jacobson.

11:21 am | by Nathalie Boschat, Ian Talley and Gabriele Parussini

Christine Lagarde, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, opened the annual meetings with a warning that world leaders need to take more decisive action to pull the global economy out of the current crisis. "There are signs of hope. It's just a question of having a little bit of patience and pushing leaders in the direction where they need to take more action than they have so far," the IMF chief said.

"In 2008 we managed to avoid protectionism and kickstart recovery. They don't have as much ammunition now," she said, referring to world economic leaders.

11:19 am | by Phil Izzo [ 09-22-11 1636ET ]

The day began with varied worrying economic signals. The euro zone posted disappointing manufacturing numbers, giving rise to renewed fears of a double-dip recession. Economic bellwether FedEx echoed recent warnings that global trade has slowed and Asian shipments have been particularly weak. Meanwhile in the U.S., initial jobless claims fell a bit but remain at an elevated level that shows continued weakness in the labor market.

22 Sep 2011 14:40 EDT DJ  Philippines Fin Min: Best To Leave Currency Issues To Markets

WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--Philippines Finance Secretary Cesar Purisima said Thursday that it is in the country's greater interest to focus on economic fundamentals and leave the level of its currency up to markets.

His comments come as emerging-market currencies, including the Philippine peso, are seeing big drops on rising risk aversion.

Purisima said at a Washington speech that the central bank allows markets to determine the value of its currency, intervening mainly to smooth out any disruptive movements.

"Outside of that the best thing we can do is invest in fundamentals," he said.

His comments would suggest that Philippines policy makers aren't inclined toward any dramatic intervention to shore up the currency, but would rather make smaller moves when needed to smooth out volatile swings.

"The best thing is really to leave it up to the markets," he said.

title: Emerging Market Debt,  Currencies  Echo Rebound In Risky Markets
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market currencies and credits took a bit of a break from their recent declines Thursday, as so-called risk assets recovered on news that five major central banks are working together to provide liquidity for crisis-embroiled European banks.

Latin American and Eastern European currencies were slightly stronger against the dollar and euro, while sovereign credit spreads tightened with U.S. Treasury yields rising. The joint announcement from the European Central Bank, the Federal Reserve, and three other key monetary authorities that they are going to coordinate efforts to provide euro-zone banks with dollar funding, lifted investors sentiment.

"People are feeling a little better about Europe from the ECB announcement, so emerging markets are largely up," said Win Thin, senior currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman. "But I'm still skeptical because not much about the underlying dynamic has changed."

The risk premium, or spread, on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global was six basis points tighter to 385 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, the index was down 0.23%.

Emerging-market currencies, which rallied early this year, have fallen sharply in recent days due to worries about global growth and contagion from the euro zone's debt problems. Now central banks in these countries are in the position of having to hold them up rather than find ways to weaken them, as was the case earlier in the year.

"By year-end, all these guys will probably be cutting rates," Thin said.

Chile's central bank rate decision is due later Thursday and it is widely expected to keep its target policy rate unchanged at 5.25%. Its spread on the Embig tightened five basis points to 1.59%, but fell a fraction in price terms.

The Bank of Indonesia was suspected of intervening to shore up its currency. Traders also said that the Philippines central bank appeared to have intervened to support its currency. Peru has been working on extending stimulus from the fiscal side and said Tuesday that it will adopt measures to speed public sector investments.

Indonesia may need to introduce fiscal stimulus next year to help shield its economy from a potential global economic slowdown, senior officials said Thursday. Finance Minister Agus Martowardojo told a parliamentary hearing that the country may need to issue a fiscal stimulus package in the first half of next year.

While growth across Asia appears relatively resilient, the outlook in emerging Europe appears to be headed for a slowdown given its ties to the beleaguered euro-zone bloc. The deteriorating sovereign debt problems there are expected to dent the export demand for goods produced by these highly open economies such as Hungary and the Czech Republic.

The Hungarian currency and credit markets have been coming under excruciating pressure in recent days as investors reel from new government proposals that could hit the country's banks. The forint has fallen particularly hard recently after Prime Minister Viktor Orban announced controversial plans Monday to help struggling households by locking in exchange rates on mortgages denominated in foreign currencies, particularly Swiss francs.

But the forint and Polish zloty recovered ground against the euro Thursday on the coordinated move by the central banks to provide dollar funding to European banks. That alleviates some pressure, for now, that has been mounting for euro-zone banks to raise short-term funding because investors fear their exposure to the region's debt crisis.

The zloty strengthened to PLN4.3284 per euro from PLN4.3809 to start the day, while the forint gained to HUF284.94 a euro from HUF287.06. Emerging Europe's region index on the Embig lost 0.08% in price, while its spread narrowed seven basis points to 3.45%.

title: UPDATE: Philippines Comfortable With Peso Level; Monitoring For Disruptive Moves
text:
-- The Philippines is comfortable with current level of its local currency, finance secretary Purisima says

-- The Philippines is closely monitoring movements of peso against Asian peers

-- The Philippines aims to step up spending on infrastructure, social sector

(Rewrites first paragraph, adds finance secretary's comments on the local currency in the second and fourth paragraphs and budget deficit in the fifth and sixth paragraphs, background on suspected currency intervention by the Philippines in the third paragraph)


 
   By Gaurav Raghuvanshi 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Philippines is comfortable with the current level of its currency and is monitoring for any disruptive movements of the peso, the nation's finance chief said Thursday, less than a month after the central bank reportedly intervened to boost the U.S. dollar from a three-year low.

"Right now we believe that we are within the comfortable band of exchange rate that moves within (the currencies of) our peer countries. We cannot stop appreciation (of the Philippine peso). Most of the currencies of the world are appreciating against the U.S, dollar and that's something that we need to adjust to," Cesar Purisima, the finance secretary, told reporters in Singapore. "What we are trying to monitor closely is disruptive movements."

On July 26, the Philippine central bank was estimated to have bought as much as US$200 million at various levels as the peso climbed to its highest in three years. The U.S. dollar hit a low of PHP41.90 on Aug. 1 but has since recovered a bit, trading at PHP42.50 at 0750 GMT Thursday.

Purisima, who is also a member of the monetary board of the Philippine central bank, said the nation's authorities are monitoring the movements of the peso's peers in the Asian region and that "we let the market determine the peso-dollar exchange rate."

He also highlighted how the government racked up a budget deficit of only PHP17 billon in the first half of this year, much smaller than the target of about PHP150 billion for the period.

"That shows that we are way ahead of our (budget deficit) program. We're doing so much better. In fact, our challenge is how to spend more," he said, adding that the government is trying to build capacity in its institutions to step up spending on infrastructure and social sector.

Earlier, addressing delegates at an investor conference organized by Credit Suisse, Purisima said financial markets are likely to remain turbulent until global issues, such as the U.S. debt burden and the sovereign debt crisis in Europe, are addressed.

"If you see what happened on Wall Street last night, the market turbulence of the last week appears far away. But we will get more turbulence unless the problems are addressed," he said.

Purisima also said that the Association of Southeast Asian Nations should work on relying less on exports to the U.S. and Europe and focus more on increasing domestic consumption.

-By Gaurav Raghuvanshi, Dow Jones Newswires; +65 64154 152; venkat.pr@dowjones.com [ 18-08-11 0827GMT ]

title: CORRECT: Asia Central Banks  Intervene  To Curb  Currency  Gains As Dollar Slides
text:
("Asia Central Banks Intervene To Curb Currency Gains As Dollar Slides," at 0839 GMT, misstated the level at which the Bank of Korea was suspected of intervening in the fourth paragraph. The correct version follows:)

-- Central banks in South Korea, Thailand and the Philippines intervene to slow gains in their currencies

-- U.S. debt ceiling impasse propels Asian currencies upward

-- Philippines' Purisima says U.S. debt imbroglio speeds the dollar's decline

By Martin Vaughan

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Several Asian central banks were seen intervening in currency markets Tuesday, as the U.S. political stalemate on increasing the government borrowing cap caused the dollar to tumble against regional currencies.

Philippines Secretary of Finance Cesar Purisima said U.S. failure to reach a debt deal is causing a "loss of confidence" in the dollar and could "accelerate the search for an alternate reserve currency."

Purisima said U.S. leaders are "missing the point" and are endangering the dollar's preeminent status, used as the default currency across the globe in trade and finance.

The Bank of Korea was suspected of buying around $300 million in an attempt to slow the won's rise, said traders in Seoul. The bank may have been trying to defend the psychological level of KRW1,050 to the dollar, the traders said.

The Philippine central bank was estimated to have bought as much as $200 million at various levels as the peso climbed to its highest mark in three years. The dollar hit a low of PHP42.22.

Bangkok dealers said the Bank of Thailand also engaged in mild dollar buying to curb the baht's rise, as the greenback slipped to THB29.68, its lowest since November 2010.

"The idea that we're seeing intervention is a consistent theme across Asian currencies right now," said Robert Rennie, chief currency strategist at Westpac Institutional Bank.

After notching substantial gains in the first four months of the year, the riskier currencies of emerging Asia had been hemmed in recently by fears surrounding sovereign debt in the euro-zone periphery. Those fears were to some extent calmed by the announcement last week of a second bailout for Greece, setting the stage for Asian currencies to strengthen.

Asian currencies were further boosted Tuesday as the dollar sank on comments from President Barack Obama and House Speaker John Boehner which revealed that any deal to cut spending and raise the U.S. debt ceiling remains far off. U.S. officials have said they have only until Aug. 2 to raise borrowing limits or risk missing debt servicing payments.

-By Martin Vaughan; +65 6415 4033; martin.vaughan@dowjones.com

title: Asian  Currencies  Resume Climb, Prompting  Intervention
text:
-- An ebb in euro-zone worries, strong US data lift Asia currencies

-- Central banks in South Korea, Philippines intervene, traders say

-- Singapore dollar climbs, resuming record highs after two months


 
   By Martin Vaughan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian currencies have snapped a two-month funk, testing recent highs and prompting some intervention from central banks Friday as investors put Europe's debt crisis behind them for the moment and as encouraging U.S. data spurred regional share gains.

Central banks in South Korea, the Philippines and Taiwan apparently sold their currencies to slow the resumed gains, local traders said. Most of the region's authorities had been sidelined since early May, when Greece's fiscal crisis flared up, sapping demand for risky assets.

With the next bailout payment apparently headed toward Athens, risk appetite has perked up in recent days, boosting Asian currencies. Strong U.S. job data Thursday helped propel them back toward their highs, with the Singapore dollar resuming its record run against the U.S. currency.

Craig Chan, Asian currency strategist at Nomura Bank in Singapore, predicted the Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah will be among the biggest gainers in coming months, as global growth picks up again and the region's authorities allow more appreciation to counter rising inflation.

Asia's central banks have tolerated significant gains in their currencies as the region has led the global economic recovery, but they still step in when they feel the rises are too abrupt or out of line with the trends of their trading partners.

"It's too early to say that we're at the end of the solvency issue for Greece," said Nomura's Chan. "But now there seems to be a little bit more clarity, and people are getting more hopeful that we're moving through the soft patch."

The U.S. private sector added 157,000 jobs in May, well above the forecast 95,000 increase, said payroll giant Automatic Data Processing Inc., boosting expectations that Friday's closely watched nonfarm payrolls will also be strong.

With investors bidding up the Singapore dollar along with other Asian currencies Friday, the U.S. dollar slid below its May 2 record low to S$1.2177. It had traded above $1.2500 several times in May as global risk aversion sent investors into the safe-haven greenback.

As the won climbed to its highest since the U.S. subprime crisis went global in August 2008, the Bank of Korea bought an estimated $200-$300 million, apparently in a bid to defend the KRW1,057.00 line after the dollar fell to the day's low of KRW1,056.20, traders said.

The head of the BOK's foreign-exchange market team declined to comment.

Seoul traders predicted the authorities will be less aggressive than in recent forays into the market, probably because a strong won helps to keep imported inflation from feeding the rapid rise in domestic consumer prices.

Traders in Manila said the Philippine central bank appeared to buy $50-$100 million, but the dollar still ended at a two-month low of PHP42.75. Taiwan's central bank appeared to buy the U.S. currency around NT$28.760, Taipei traders said.

The Philippine and Taiwan central banks couldn't immediately be reached for comment.

--By Martin Vaughan; +65 6415 4033; martin.vaughan@dowjones.com

(Min-Jeong Lee in Seoul, Phisanu Phromchanya in Bangkok and Fanny Liu and Aries Poon in Taipei contributed to this article). [ 08-07-11 0943GMT ]

title: DJ Asian  Currencies  Surge in Line With Euro, Prompting  Intervention
text:
-- Asian currencies surge as euro climbs on ECB, dollar slumps on budget

-- Intervention spotted in Philippines, Malaysia, Korea, Indonesia, Thailand, India

-- Singapore dollar logs record high, Australian dollar highest since 1983 float, Korean won 2.5-year peak

-- No letup seen for dollar weakness until the Fed ends QE2 in June 


 
   By P.R. Venkat 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian currencies surged Friday as the euro climbed on an interest-rate hike and the dollar languished on a potential U.S. government shutdown, prompting several central banks in the region to intervene to curb their currencies' gains.

Among the sharp gainers, the Singapore dollar broke from its recent stagnancy to pop to a record high against the U.S. currency, the Australian dollar again notched its highest level since being floated in 1983 and the South Korean won hit a two-and-a-half-year high.

Central banks in the Philippines, Malaysia, Korea, Indonesia, Thailand and India apparently bought dollars to keep the advance in their own currencies under control, local traders said.

Traders began the day expecting the dollar might rise against Asian currencies, as investors looked set to take profits on recent dollar declines to square their positions heading into the weekend.

Instead, the U.S. currency remained weak as the euro added to gains from Thursday's rate hike by the European Central Bank, its first tightening since 2008. Many Asian currencies take their cue from the euro, which has acted as a barometer of global risk appetite.

The dollar fell against most major and regional currencies as hopes faded that Republicans and Democrats in Washington could agree on a budget deal before the U.S. government runs out of operating cash at midnight Friday.

"The tightening cycle in Europe has clearly started, and the rate-differential argument is pertinent here," while U.S. budget worries weighed on the dollar, said currency strategist Nizam Idris at UBS in Singapore.

Asian central banks may try to cushion the dollar's fall against their currencies but know they can't stop the trend, and are simply trying to keep their export-reliant economies roughly competitive with their neighbors'. The authorities seldom comment on intervention, but officials at several central banks in recent days have said they will act to prevent excessive volatility.

The region's currencies have surged over the past year as Asia has led the global economic recovery and as low interest rates in the richest countries have spurred a flood of investor capital into Asia seeking higher returns.

Asian currencies also got a boost as the People's Bank of China fixed the tightly controlled yuan higher Friday for a sixth session, setting the dollar's central parity rate at a record low CNY6.5420.

Expectations that Beijing will allow faster yuan gains sent the yuan sharply higher in the market for nondeliverable forwards, an offshore venue where investors can bet on future moves. The 12-month dollar/yuan contract sank to a three-year low bid quote of CNY6.3620, from CNY6.4000.

The region's currency authorities are generally tolerating greater appreciation these days to help them battle rising inflation, said Thomas Harr, head of Asia currency strategy at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore. The dollar will likely remain weak until at least June, when the Federal Reserve is slated to end its "quantitative easing" policy of buying government bonds, he said.

Friday's euro ascent kick-started the Asia rally. The common currency had come off Thursday's highs as the ECB's quarter-percentage-point rate hike was almost universally expected and central bank chief Jean-Claude Trichet said the ECB hadn't decided to embark on a series of rate increases.

Nonetheless, the euro took off in the Asia morning on the view that the ECB may tighten every quarter, and the currency never looked back.

The euro's rise to a 2011 high above $1.44 spurred accelerating gains among Asian currencies, notably the Singapore dollar. The U.S. dollar had been largely holding above support around S$1.26 for the past two weeks, but the euro's climb helped break through that level. At 0945 GMT, the euro was at $1.4399, and the U.S. currency bought S$1.2571.

"Whoever is long dollar will be suffering here," said Idris.

The ICE Dollar Index, a broad measure of the currency's value against the currencies of America's main trading partners, was at 75.185 late in the Asian session. That was down from 75.534 late in New York and threatened a slide to its November 2009 low of 74.17 in coming weeks.

To tame the peso at five-month highs, the Philippine central bank apparently bought $600 million between PHP43.05 and PHP43.00 in heavy trade, defending the U.S. currency around the psychologically important PHP43.00 line, Manila traders said. Bank Negara Malaysia apparently twice sold the ringgit, which has benefited as a proxy for the rising Chinese currency, Kuala Lumpur traders said. They spotted the central bank buying dollars at MYR3.0210 late in the day after a defense at MYR3.0220 failed.

The Bank of Korea apparently bought an estimated $1 billion as the dollar fell to 1,082.00, its lowest since August 2008, when the global financial crisis was escalating, Seoul dealers said.

In a bid to curb the rising rupiah and baht, Bank Indonesia apparently bought an estimated $100 million at IDR8,653, while the Bank of Thailand apparently bought dollars around THB30.03, local dealers said. After the rupee hit a six-month high, the Reserve Bank of India was seen apparently buying dollars at INR43.98, local traders said.

title: WSJ: Philippines Ayala Corp. CEO Sees Continuing Peso Appreciation
text:
11 Mar 2011 03:50 EDT  WSJ: Philippines Ayala Corp. CEO Expects Inflation To Remain Manageable

11 Mar 2011 03:50 EDT  WSJ: Philippines Ayala Corp. CEO: Central Bank Intervention To Slow Peso Rise Supports Remittance-Driven Spending

11 Mar 2011 03:50 EDT  WSJ: Philippines Ayala Corp. CEO Sees Continuing Peso Appreciation


 
   By James Hookway 
   Of THE WALL STREET JOURNAL 
 

MANILA (Dow Jones)--Philippines-based conglomerate Ayala Corporation expects the local peso currency to continue rising this year as mounting inflationary pressures compel the country's financial authorities to raise interest rates.

But its chief executive said the nation's expanding import bill could temper the peso's gains as oil prices continue to rise.

Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala, also the company's chairman, told The Wall Street Journal in an interview Thursday that surges of investment into emerging Asian markets over the past year or so "are generally considered a positive development in the region, but they sometimes have some unintended side-effects such as currency overvaluation, excessive monetary and credit expansion, or even unsustainable asset-price inflation," Mr. Zobel said.

To cope with the appreciation of the Philippine peso, which has advanced 2.5% against the U.S. dollar this year and about 6.5% since the beginning of 2010, some of Ayala Corp.'s export-driven businesses such as semiconductor firm Integrated Micro-Electronics Inc., or IMI, and its business process outsourcing unit LiveIt Investments Ltd. use "simple hedges" which he didn't specify to make their revenue streams more predictable.

At the same time, other Ayala businesses, such as its telecommunications business Globe Telecom Inc. and utility provider Manila Water Company Inc., have benefited from a stronger peso, providing the parent company, Ayala Corp., with a more balanced revenue stream. Both Globe and Manila Water have seen a stronger peso reduce the cost of their imports, such as components and equipment, Mr. Zobel said.

Still, if it weren't for the intervention of the Philippine central bank to slow the ascent of the peso in November last year, Mr. Zobel said the appreciation of the local currency could have eroded demand among some of its consumer-related business, such as retail banking or shopping malls. That's because the Philippine economy is heavily dependent on the remittances that Filipino expatriates send home to support their families. Some 10 million Filipinos work abroad, including many in the United States, Europe and the Middle East, where their salaries convert into fewer pesos than before when they are sent back home.

Without the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas intervening to buy dollars towards the tail end of last year, Mr. Zobel says the peso could have strengthened by as much as 10% in 2010.

Ayala Corp. is one of the Philippines' oldest and most successful companies, operating real estate, banking and automobile businesses in addition to its telecoms, outsourcing and utilities businesses. In the coming year, Mr. Zobel said the company would be keen to bid for a series of new public-private partnerships being launched by Philippine President Benigno Aquino III's government. Many of the tenders involve contracts to build and operate major infrastructure projects such as toll-roads, railway lines and other, similar big-ticket ventures designed to upgrade the Philippines' economic potential.

Going forward, "we think there will continue to be appreciation pressures for the Philippine peso as rising global commodity prices could compel our local monetary authorities to tighten policy later this year. Our economic managers may also opt to use the exchange rate to anchor domestic inflation" by letting the currency appreciate a bit more, Mr. Zobel said.

"However, currency appreciation could be pared as the country's import bill could balloon amidst rising global oil prices just as geo-political risks threaten to soften remittances from overseas Filipinos this year."

Government officials say around 3 million Filipinos work in the Middle East, which has been unsettled this year by a wave of political upheavals.

On inflation, Mr. Zobel said the situation was becoming "a bigger concern but does not seem to be as serious as the 2008 episode," when prices last spiked. He drew a distinction between the forces driving prices in his business environment, the Philippines, and other, more developed countries.

"In the U.S. and in most developed economies, higher oil prices tend to affect a bigger portion of the population as motor vehicle use is high," Mr. Zobel said. "In contrast, only a small portion of the population own motor vehicles in developing economies like the Philippines. So, while rising oil prices exert upward pressure on overall prices and tend to dampen consumption in the Philippines, food prices--particularly rice--tend to have a larger impact on the spending behavior of consumers."

For Ayala Corp., rising inflation--the Philippines' consumer price index reached 4.3% on year in February, the highest rate in nine months--"could pressure the cost of credit to rise while softer consumer demand could soften our top line growth somewhat," Mr. Zobel said.

-By James Hookway, The Wall Street Journal; James.Hookway@wsj.com

title: EM ASIA  FX -Rupiah at 4-yr high on c.bank; intervention  caps gains
text:
* Indonesia c.bank sees more room for rupiah's rise

* Intervention from Indonesia, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand spotted

* Won, Taiwan dlr at 2-wk high (Updates with text, prices)

By Jongwoo Cheon

SINGAPORE, March 4 (Reuters) - The rupiah hit a near four-year high against the dollar after the central bank signalled on Friday it was willing to use the currency's gains in its battle with inflation even though it was seen buying dollars in an effort to control the rupiah's rise.

The central bank kept its benchmark rate on hold at its policy meeting, but said that it would gradually lift borrowing costs in the future and that it saw room for the rupiah to strengthen further without hurting export competitiveness.

"The bank confirmed today that the currency strength is helping the inflation problem," said Christopher Gothard, chief currency strategist for Brown Brothers Harriman in Hong Kong.

"BI is still attempting to manage the rupiah's gains, with interventions designed more to slow the gain and make it more orderly, rather than stop it altogether," Gothard said.

Central banks in other Asian countries, such as Singapore, Philippines and Thailand, were also spotted buying dollars. Dealers said the interventions seemed designed to slow their currencies' gains rather than to weaken them because that would exacerbate inflation pressures.

RUPIAH

The Dollar slid by up to 0.3 percent against the rupiah to 8,780, the rupiah's strongest level since June 2007, from Thursday's close of 8,803.

Foreign investors continued to sell the pair, which has room to fall to 8,755, the low in June, but the central bank was on guard, dealers said.

Earlier, the central bank kept its overnight interest rate at 6.75 percent as forecast by a slender majority of economists, saying it would adjust the rate in stages if necessary and closely monitor rising core inflation.

"Today's decision implies BI will be more comfortable doing the tightening via FX. But slowly,, as they will continue to intervene," said a strategist of a U.S. Bank in Singapore.

TAIWAN DOLLAR

Dollar/Taiwan dollar slid to a two-week low as foreign investors sold the pair and on foreigners' continuous stock purchases.

Dollar/Taiwan dollar touched 29.310, the lowest since Feb 18.

WON

Dollar/won hit a near two-week low as continuous foreign purchases of Seoul stocks prompted stop-loss dollar sales.

The pair fell to as low as 1,114.1, the lowest since Feb. 21, but it found support from caution over dollar-buying intervention by South Korea's foreign exchange authorities and importers' demand around mid-1,110.

"They (the authorities) don't want it to go above 1,130, but they will buy dollars at 1,110 anyway even if the Bank of Korea raises interest rates," said a dealer in Singapore.

Foreign investors reported their biggest net buying of local stocks in two months.

PESO

Dollar/peso edged down on fixing demand and profit-taking from the peso's recent gains, but the Philippines's central bank was spotted buying dollars to check the peso's strength.

Bangko Sentral Pilipinas (BSP) was seen intervening at around 43.25-27, dealers said, even though it said higher February inflation supported its view that the scope for keeping rates steady has narrowed.

"All central banks in Asia, including the BSP, are facing the same dilemma -- how to check inflation and to support exports at the same time," says a senior European bank dealer in Singapore.

Philippine February inflation hit its highest since May, raising the likelihood the central bank will lift rates this month for the first time since the global financial crisis.

Dollar/peso may break through its support at 43.25, the low of on Feb 21 and the 61.8 percent of the November-January rise, if the central bank take actions to curb inflation.

A break of this support will see a decline to 42.90, the 76.4 percent of the rise. Strong resistance for pair is seen at 43.60 and 43.90.

title: EM ASIA  FX - Intervention  seen as won, peso hit 11-week highs
text:
* Won, peso lead most Asian FX higher against dollar

 * Intervention seen in Korea, Thailand, the Philippines

 * Dlr/yuan NDFs off 2-week low amid policy uncertainty

 By Kevin Yao

 SINGAPORE, Aug 3 (Reuters) - The South Korean won and Philippine peso hit 11-week highs on Tuesday as upbeat U.S. factory data and European bank earnings buoyed risk-taking, but their gains were curtained by official intervention.

 Asian stocks rose to their highest in nearly three months and turned positive for the year, while the dollar hovered near a three-month low against a basket of currencies <.DXY>.

 Earnings from big European banks BNP Paribas  and HSBC  topped forecasts as bad debt fell sharply.

U.S. manufacturing grew in July for a 12th straight month, an industry report showed on Monday. Although growth slowed, it was still stronger than had been expected. [ID:nN02170396]

 WON

 The won <KRW=> gained as much as percent 1,159.9 per dollar, the highest since May 19, but later pared most gains as the authorities were spotted buying dollars, causing some investors to cover dollar-short positions.

 Still, traders expect the won <KRW=> to rise further.    "Intervention from the beginning prompt some offshore players to buy dollars, preventing the won's further gains. But it is unlikely to get back to the 1,170 levels after breaking through major resistance lines," said a foreign bank dealer.

 Another foreign bank dealer said: "It is difficult to buy the won further as the authorities may -- be able to intervene more easily once exporters deals are completed."

 Foreign investors bought a net 132.7 billion won worth of stocks on the main exchange, helping the benchmark KOSIP <.KS11> rise nearly 0.5 percent.

 PESO

 Dollar/peso NDFs fell across the curve as hedge funds and other offshore investors were seen dumping dollars, particularly in short tenors.

 "Offshore investors expect lower spot rates," said a NDF trader.

 The most liquid one-month dollar/peso NDFs <PHP1MNDFOR=> hit a 2-½   month low at 45.32 from 45.39 late on Monday, while one-month onshore forwards <PHP1M=> fell to 45.365 from 45.496.

 The onshore/offshore spread narrowed to 45 points from 106 points on Monday.

 Spot peso <PHP=> gained 0.4 percent to 45.13 to the dollar, the highest in 11 weeks, but it later pulled back to 45.20 as traders spotted dollar-buying intervention by the central bank.

 Dollar/yuan NDFs <CNYNDFOR=> dropped to a two-week low but later rebounded slightly as uncertainty over China's yuan policy kept markets trading within an established range.

 "People are more willing to take risk but there are still no signs China will speed up appreciation in the yuan," said a trader at an Asian bank in Hong Kong.

 He said activity remains thin and driven by trade-related hedging rather than speculation.

 One-year NDFs bounced to 6.6744 from two-week low of 6.6560 in early trade and from late-Monday's 6.6645 to price in 12-month yuan appreciation of 1.47 percent.

 The one-year NDF has fluctuated in a range of yuan appreciation between 1.3 percent and 1.9 percent since late-June.

title: ASIA LOCAL BONDS-Yields rise as  currencies  sag
text:
* Indonesian, Philippine bond yields inch higher

* Thailand bond yields turn lower

By Saikat Chatterjee

HONG KONG, May 25 (Reuters) - Asian local currency bond yields rose on Tuesday as weakening currencies took some sheen off Asia's high-performing debt.

A strong rebound in growth in the continent's economies, rising currencies and low debt-to-GDP ratios have fuelled demand among global funds for Asian government debt in recent months.

But the euro zone's debt problems have triggered a wave of risk aversion in world markets leading to a marked slowdown in new capital inflows, which in turn has sapped the rally in emerging market currencies.

The ringgit <MYR=>, which is the star performer in Asia, up by more than 8 percent until the end of April, has seen its year-to-date gains cut sharply to a little above 2 percent.

Central banks in Indonesia and Philippines were seen intervening to support their currencies, both of which have fallen to their lowest in several months. [ID:nSGE64O03Q]

By early afternoon, the ten-year Indonesian bond yield <ID10YT=RR> was up six basis points at 9.03 percent, while the four-year bond yield in the Philippines <PHBD0567=> was two basis points higher at 5.94 percent, traders said.

"Risk aversion is still there and that has reduced the flows into local currency bonds," said Lum Choong Kuan, head of fixed income at CIMB Investment Bank. "Although there has been some selling in Thailand, we are still seeing a lot of demand for rupiah and ringgit assets."

Thomson Reuters data shows Indonesian local currency bonds in dollar terms have lost more than 2 percent in the past month cutting their year-to-date returns to 10 percent.

The latest EPFR data shows foreign fund inflows into emerging market bond funds have slowed to a trickle in recent weeks, a far cry from more than $1 billion per week seen in March.

In Thailand, however, yields fell as investors expected the central bank to keep rates on hold next week because of the negative impact of months of political unrest on its economy.

DBS expects the economy to contract 9 percent on a seasonally adjusted annualised rate in the second quarter after expanding at 15 percent in the March quarter because of the riots.

The five-year bond yield <TH5YT=RR> eased by six basis points to 3.11 percent, just shy of its lowest level since end April.

A two-month political standoff ended last week but economists said it could take months for the economy to get back to rates of growth seen in the March quarter. This puts any chances of a near-term rate hike in the freezer for now.

"While we believe the central bank is still keen to raise interest rates to a more neutral level, this will require a more stable political backdrop ... the situation remains fluid, but the possibility of fresh elections in the fourth quarter may allow them to begin tightening," Standard Chartered Bank said. (Editing by Chris Lewis & Jan Dahinten)

title: UPDATE 2-Indonesia, Manila prop up  FX  as emerging markets tumble
text:
JAKARTA, May 7 (Reuters) - Central banks in Indonesia and the Philippines intervened to shore up their sliding currencies on Friday as worries about Greece's debt crisis spurred investors to dump emerging market assets.

The high-yielding rupiah <IDR> has tumbled 3 percent against the dollar this week, among the worst hit in Asia, while the peso has skidded 2.7 percent as part of a broad sell-off in Asian currencies and a move into safer assets.

Though worries about Greece's problems spreading to the rest of Europe are likely to persist for some time, Indonesia's central bank said the country's solid fiscal and economic fundamentals would support for the rupiah in the long run.

"We don't see (the weakening rupiah) as too worrying because fundamentals are still good. This will just be temporary,"Darmin Nasution, Bank Indonesia's senior deputy governor, told reporters on Friday.

But he said the central bank has been closely following the rupiah's moves since earlier this week.

"The central bank is always in the market," he added.

In the Philippines, central bank Deputy Governor Diwa Guinigundo offered similar reassurances to nervous investors, saying the country can withstand shocks in financial markets as domestic consumption remains healthy and its foreign reserves are at a comfortable level.

"In case there is a double dip, we are well placed to absorb the shocks. On balance, we have what it takes to weather another crisis," Guinigundo told reporters.

The rupiah fell just over 1 percent on Friday to 9,300 per dollar, a two-month low, but later pared some of the losses on suspected cental bank intervention.

But the currency is still up 2 percent against the dollar so far this year. It had gained nearly 6 percent through April before Greece's debt crisis escalated and profit taking set in.

Investor sentiment toward Indonesian assets was also undermined by Finance Minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati's decision on Wednesday to resign, as she played a key role in improving the economy.

Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist at BNP Paribas in Singapore, expects the rupiah to find support near 9,400/9,500.

"The rupiah has lost ground on unwinding of risk exposures, including liquidation of Indonesian bonds, on the global stock rout as well as the finance minister's resignation," she said.

"But the fundamentals for Indonesia remain positive and we expect the rupiah to be sought after again when the dust settles."

One of the central bank deputy governors, Budi Mulya, echoed Bank Indonesia's vigilance.

"Bank Indonesia (BI) will continue to ensure a stable rupiah that reflects its underlying fundamentals," Mulya said in a phone text message.

"At times of substantial capital inflow, BI safeguarded rupiah stability through its sterilisation, and that has built up foreign exchange reserves to more than $78 billion. Similarly, in the event of capital outflows, BI is also committed to safeguard the rupiah's stability."

The central bank also reiterated its commitment to ensure a free capital market and dispel concerns of any capital controls.

In the Phillipines, the central bank also sold dollars to slow the peso's decline, traders said.

The peso <PHP=> was down 0.9 percent at 45.78 per dollar despite the interventions.

Among other Asian currencies, the South Korean won <KRW=> fell 4.1 percent on the week, its biggest weekly fall since February 2009.

Foreign investors had flocked to emerging Asian assets earlier this year as the region's economic growth far eclipsed that of the West, but a spike in volatility in recent weeks has prompted some to scale back their positions and book profits. (Reporting Gde Anugrah Arka, Sonya Angraini and Kevin Yao; Writing by Yoko Nishikawa; Editing by Sara Webb & Kim Coghill)

title: UPDATE: Asian Shares Come Off Lows; Exporters Hurt Tokyo
text:
(Adds information, quotes, updates/adds market levels)

By Shri Navaratnam and Philip Vahn

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian shares recovered some ground Friday as investors were soothed by the realization that a trading glitch was partly behind Wall Street's slide overnight and began to bargain hunt.

However, concerns that Greece's debt problems could engulf the weaker European countries continued to linger.

In Tokyo, the market remained under pressure as the recent gains in the yen damped exporter stocks.

Jonathan Barrett, managing director at Commodity Broking Services in Sydney, referring to the early drop in Asian markets, said investors may have overreacted.

"People are factoring in a disaster scenario. If that contagion fear (of the Greece fiscal crisis spreading to other European countries) is real why did European markets only fall 1.0% to 1.5%?" he said.

In a note to clients UBS analysts said: "In our view, the lack of a clear 'end game' for sovereign risk in Europe means that despite recent sharp declines in markets, this is not a buying opportunity. Positions may still be unwound."

Japan's Nikkei 225 was down 2.7% while Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was down 0.8% at 4547 after hitting an eight-month of low 4427.30 earlier. South Korea's Kospi Composite fell 2.0%, Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index lost 0.8%, Taiwan's main index was off 0.4% and the Shanghai Composite index was down 0.3%.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were up 65 points in screen trade.

The euro, which plumbed 14-month lows of $1.2510 against the U.S. dollar Thursday, recovered some ground in Asian trade although analysts expect more pain ahead for the single currency. The Korean won bounced back after hitting a three-month low against the U.S. dollar of KRW1,169.5 earlier. It was trading at KRW1,163.9.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average at one point on Thursday skidded as much as 9.2%, the biggest intraday drop in its history, before closing down 3.2%. The intraday dive appeared to be triggered in part by a breakdown of trading systems.

In Tokyo, Sony was down 5.3% while Panasonic lost 5.1%, Honda Motor was off 4.8% and Toyota Motor dropped 2.8%. Fast Retailing slipped 5.9% after saying late Thursday April same-store sales at its Uniqlo casual clothing chain fell 12.4% on-year.

Nintendo fell 10.0% after the video game giant said Thursday its net profit dropped to Y228.64 billion in the fiscal year ended March 31, from Y279.09 billion a year earlier; it also expects profit and sales to fall in the current year.

Metal plays were leading losses in China, hurt by sharp declines in metal prices in Asian trade. Baoshan Iron & Steel lost 4.0% and Yunnan Copper fell 4.0%.

Shanghai benchmark copper futures were trading 3.3% lower at CNY54,980 per metric ton. The red metal was also down 2.0% on the London Metals Exchange.

Financial stocks led the Australian market lower, with ANZ off 3.1% and Westpac down 3.5%. In the resources sector, BHP Billiton lost 1.3% and Rio Tinto was off 2.0%.

Financials were also weaker in Seoul. Shinhan Financial lost 3.7% while tech bellwether Samsung Electronics gave up 2.7%. Daewoo Shipbuilding slipped 2.5%, but was outperforming its peers after the Financial News reported it had won a $1.6 billion contract to build a floating production storage and offloading vessel.

In Hong Kong, Swire Pacific rose 2.4% after its property unit Swire Properties said Thursday it has shelved its US$3.09 billion Hong Kong initial public offering. Traders said the move was viewed positively, given prevailing weak property market conditions in the city state.

"Some investors were also concerned with the dilution effect of Swire Pacific's holding in its property unit's spinoff, which may also hurt investment value of Swire Pacific in the long-term," said First Shanghai's Linus Yip.

Elsewhere, Malaysian shares were 0.6% lower, Singapore's Straits Times Index fell 0.8%, India's Sensex was down 1.1% and New Zealand's NZX-50 was 1.5% lower.

In foreign exchange markets, the euro was at $1.2712, compared with $1.2599 late in New York, and was fetching Y117.55 against the yen, from Y113.26, but well below Y120.12 on Wednesday. The dollar was at Y92.51, from Y89.92.

Despite the steadier euro, "it only seems a matter of time before the key (1.2500) support level breaks" against the dollar, said Mark Smith, an economist at ANZ bank in Wellington.

"On the face of it, the overnight market reaction may have been overdone. But the question increasingly asked is where the mark-to-market losses on European debt will ultimately reside, and this is looking to be mostly in European financial institutions. We have now moved beyond a mere Greek debt crisis," Smith said.

Markets are also watching the outcome of Thursday's U.K. elections, with results so far showing the opposition Conservative Party leading the seats-count but could fall short of a majority, leading to a hung parliament. The British pound was at $1.4903, up from $1.4832 late in New York.

The sharp falls in Asian currencies prompted some central banks in the region to intervene in currency markets to slow the greenback's rise. The central banks of Indonesia and the Philippines intervened to support their currencies, local traders and dealers said.

Bank Indonesia sold some $150 million to support the rupiah, while the Philippine central bank sold $50 million to $100 million for pesos, market participants estimated.

Japanese government bond futures were sharply higher on stronger U.S. Treasurys. The lead contract was up 0.19 at 140.5 points after briefly tapping 140.10, the highest level since March 10.

Spot gold was at $1,199.00 per troy ounce, down $9.80 from the New York close.

Nymex June crude oil futures were down 41 cents at $76.70 a barrel on Globex, after falling 3.6% Thursday to the lowest close since mid-March.

* Dollar/won NDFs jump, won vols pick up

 * C.banks in Indonesia, Philippines intervene

 * Swiss c.bank intervenes to weaken its currency

 * Investors jittery ahead of U.S. jobs data, G7

 By Kevin Yao

 SINGAPORE, Feb 5 (Reuters) - The South Korean won led Asian currencies lower on Friday as investors dumped riskier assets on jitters over debt problems in Europe, prompting central banks in Indonesia and the Philippines to intervene to support their currencies.

 Asian stocks dipped, while dollar extended its gains from the previous day due to investor anxiety about sovereign debt in Greece, Portugal and Spain sparked a sell-off in the euro.

 But the euro leapt against the Swiss franc as the Swiss central bank intervened to weaken its own currency. The ero earlier plunged to a 15-month low against the franc <EURCHF=>. [ID:nTOE614043]

 Weakness in the Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso prompted their central banks to intervene, traders said.

"I would place them in the category of Asian central banks that are genuinely concerned about volatility of their illiquid currencies so would not be at all surprised if they stepped in to calm rupiah and peso on what is a very nervous count-down to payrolls," said Westpaccurrency strategist Sean Callow.

 Asian central banks usually intervene by buying dollars to limit the rise in their currencies to support local exporters, but also step in to smooth sharp currency falls.

 WON

 The spot won <KRW=> tumbled about 2 percent in early trade to 1,176.9 per dollar but later steadied near 1,170.

 The won, which has lost more than 4 percent since Jan. 11, faces further weakness after a dip below the 100-day moving average at 1,162 on Friday.

 Offshore dollar/won NDFs <KRWNDFOR=> jumped amid jitters over sovereign debt risks in Europe, but they later trimmed gains as Korean exporters start selling.

 One-month NDFs steadied near 1,170 after hitting as high as 1,178.6 compared to Thursday's close at 1,174.

 "We see strong selling by exporters, funds are staying aside now. It was a drama last night, with euro collapsing and everything squeezed. I think all want to take a breath before U.S. non-farm payrolls and G7 meeting this weekend," said a Singapore-based NDF trader.

 Manwhile, won's implied volatilities <KRWVOL> hit 15 percent from 14 percent on Thursday as the spot dips.

 "BI (the central bank) is interferring in the market just to stabilise the rupiah -- they are selling dollars at 9,410," said a trader in Jakarta.
