title: EM ASIA  FX -Rupiah jumps,  intervention  suspected as peso rises
text:
* Rupiah, ringgit lead Asian currency rally against dollar

* Philippine central bank seen trying to cap peso

* Baht falls amid concerns over Thai king's health

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, Oct 15 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah and Malaysian ringgit led Asian currencies higher against the beleaguered dollar on Thursday, but the baht came under selling pressure amid concerns over the Thai king's health.

Central banks in Taiwan, South Korea and the Philippines were suspected of intervening to curb the rise in their currencies.

The dollar fell to a 14-month low against a basket of major currencies <.DXY> as comments by the head of Australia's central bank encouraged investors to buy the higher-yielding Australian dollar, which helped buoy emerging Asian currencies.

"Dollar weakness, positive commodities and emerging market sentiment from overnight promise further heaviness for the regional currency pairs today," Emmanuel Ng, strategist at OCBC Bank, said in a note.

RUPIAH, RINGGIT

The high-yielding rupiah <IDR=> jumped 0.8 percent to 9,290 per dollar, the highest since September 2008, as foreigners continued to buy stocks and bonds.

The rupiah, the top performer in Asia, has gained 18 percent against the dollar so far this year.

Some traders cautioned that the central bank, which has been tolerating the sharp gains to help check price rises, may intervene if the rupiah rise further.

The ringgit <MYR=> rose as far as 3.347 per dollar, up 0.6 percent from Wednesday's close, the highest since August 2008.

"Obviously, the broad dollar weakness continues," said a trader.

PESO

The peso <PHP=> gained 0.4 percent to 46.25 per dollar, highest since Sept. 2008, as the dollar falters globally.

"BSP (the central bank) abandoned its support at 46.45 and is now at 46.25," said a Manila-based trader, who added that offshore NDFs <PHPNDFOR=> pointed to more dollar depreciation.

A second trader believed the official dollar-buying intervention on Thursday was not as aggressive as the previous day. "As always, I think they've been trying to support dollar/peso slowly," said the trader.

BAHT

The Thai baht <THB=> resumed its slide in line with heavy losses in Thai stocks on concerns over the health of Thailand's King Bhumibol Adulyadej. The baht hit a two-week low at 33.51 per dollar.

"There has been more dollar buying. We think the FX market is largely taking a lead from the fast-sliding stock market in contrast with most rallying Asian bourses," a dealer said.

The health of the king is improving but he needs time-consuming physical therapy, a palace official said on Thursday after concerns over his health sparked a second day of foreign selling in Thailand's financial markets. [ID:nBKK412913]

ING was cautious about Thai markets.

"We view political risk as elevated, which leads us to recommend investors avoid all Thai financial assets," analysts at ING said in a note. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0555 GMT

title: WSJA: Asian Shares Drop,  Currencies  Sharply Lower
text:
OF THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA 
 

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Asian stocks were sold off heavily Thursday, knocking many of the region's currencies sharply lower and prompting governments to intervene.

Markets in Tokyo, Hong Kong and South Korea fell in response to a broad selloff overnight in the U.S. Tokyo's benchmark index fell 6.9%, while Hong Kong and Seoul were down 4% and 6.7% respectively. Australia's major benchmark dropped 4.2% and Shanghai fell 1.7%. Mumbai and Singapore were down 4.1% and 2.8% late Thursday. Jakarta was down 2.8% late.

The selling continued in Europe, where the DJ Stoxx 600 index was 3% lower. U.S. stock futures were down 1% to 1.5% in screen trade.

The stock hits reflect fears of deflation in the U.S., a major market for Asia-made goods, and the impact of a slowdown on commodity-rich nations like Australia and Indonesia.

That has led to a flight to safer investments typically denominated in U.S. dollars and the Japanese yen, taking money out of Asian markets and contributing to a drop in local currencies.

"It's part of the wholesale destruction of wealth across the planet," said Patrick Bennett, a strategist with Societe Generale in Hong Kong. "With asset and equity prices tumbling, investors are being encouraged to cut exposure completely."

Weaker currencies can boost big exporting nations because it makes their goods cheaper to sell in other markets. But declining currencies also hit countries with extensive foreign borrowing needs, can drive up inflation by making imports more expensive and can scare off foreign investment.

Among the hardest hit, Indonesia's rupiah and South Korea's won fell to their lowest level against the U.S. dollar since the Asian financial crisis a decade ago.

Thailand's baht fell to its weakest level since March 2007, while Taiwan's dollar hit a three-week low and the New Zealand and Australian dollars also weakened further.

The central banks of South Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Singapore and India intervened to defend their currencies, local traders said. Australia's central bank issued data that showed it plowed A$3.15 billion into currency markets last month to defend the Australian dollar against a sharp decline.

Japan and Hong Kong have defied the trend, the former because its currency is seen as a safe haven and the latter because it is pegged to the value of the appreciating U.S. dollar. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the city's de facto central bank, put roughly HK$15 billion into the market Thursday to bring the currency's value within its trading band with the U.S. dollar.

Economists cautioned that the current environment hasn't reached the point of the Asian currency crisis, when domestic funds followed foreign investors as they ran for the exits. Most governments have moved to back bank deposits to reassure consumers. Regional financial institutions have cleaner balance sheets than a decade ago, and bad loans have so far had only a minor effect on regional banks.

Still, continuing hits to currencies continue could erode consumer confidence, leading locals to consider moving their money elsewhere. "The impact on confidence could become a much bigger problem," said Sim Moh Siong, an economist at Citigroup in Singapore. "If this goes beyond how much money foreigners remove from Asia, the situation could broaden out."

In Tokyo, the Nikkei Stock Average of 225 companies ended down 6.9% at 7703.04. Shares of major banks and brokerages were hammered, with Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group tumbling 10% to Y281,500 and Nomura Holdings ending down 11% at Y666.

Shares of nonlife insurers dropped after sector companies reported dismal fiscal first half results Wednesday and sharply reduced their earnings forecasts for the full fiscal year ending March.

Although most of the bad news had already been factored in by investors, forecast revisions confirmed the grim outlook. Tokio Marine Holdings went limit-down at Y2,220, and Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance Group Holdings also went limit-down at Y2,035.

Real estate stocks also sank, dogged by credit concerns, with Mitsui Fudosan skidding 14% to Y1,070, and Mitsubishi Estate falling 13% to Y1,077.

In Seoul, the Korea Composite Stock Price Index, or Kospi, finished down 68.13 points, or 6.7%, at 948.69, based on skepticism over conditions in the U.S., particularly among financials.

Shinhan Financial Group declined 9.7% to KRW26,400, and KB Financial Group plunged by the daily limit of 15% to KRW24,550. Among builders, Hyundai Engineering & Construction and GS Engineering & Construction both dropped by the daily 15% limit to KRW42,100 and KRW45,200, respectively.

In Shanghai, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index, which tracks both A and B shares, ended down 1.7%, or 33.71 points, at 1983.76. Railway companies and insurance companies fell on profit-taking.

China Railway Group Ltd. dropped 4.1% to CNY5.82 after gaining 4.7% Wednesday, while China Life Insurance Co. fell 4.0% to CNY20.24 after rising 6.1% in the previous session.

-By Carlos Tejada, The Wall Street Journal; carlos. tejada@wsj.com

(Takashi Mochizuki and Takashi Nakamichi in Tokyo and Rosalind Mathieson in Singapore also contributed to this article.) [ 20-11-08 0946GMT ]

title: Emerging  FX -Central banks step in as Asia loses ground
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Asian currencies slid against the dollar on Monday as investors dumped assets amid heightened fears of a global downturn, forcing central banks in Indonesia and the Philippines to intervene.

The high-yielding Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> bore the brunt of the selling, briefly hitting as low as 10,800 per dollar but later steadied near 10,600 thanks to official intervention.

The rupiah's drop of around 3.5 percent on Monday took its cumulative decline so far this year to 11 percent.

"They (the central bank) are selling the dollar at various levels from 10,300," said a trader in Jakarta.

A second trader said state banks were selling dollars at 10,600.

The Philippine peso <PHP=> lost 0.8 percent to 49.385 per dollar, its weakest since December 2006, despite dollar-selling intervention by the central bank to set a floor for the unit.

Some traders said they expected the peso to test the 49.50 level in the near term unless the central bank intervened more aggressively.

The Philippine stock index <.PSI> tumbled 10 percent on Monday, triggering an automatic suspension of trading.

The MSCI index of Asian stocks outside Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> fell for a fourth consecutive session, losing 4 percent as of 0520 GMT, marking its lowest since June 2004.

Meanwhile, the South Korean won <KRW=> dropped as low as 1,447.9 per dollar as investors shrugged off the central bank's 


move to slash its key interest rate by 75 basis points -- the
biggest rate cut ever -- to calm the jittery market.


Analysts at Goldman Sachs said the won, which has lost 35 percent against the dollar so far this year, would face further selling pressure in the near term amid the global market turmoil.

"However, we continue to believe that the won/dollar has overshot on the downside and expect the won to strengthen beyond the near term," they said in a note.

The Japanese yen climbed towards a 13-year peak against the dollar <JPY=> and an all-time high against the Australian dollar <AUDJPY=R>, as a slide in Tokyo shares overshadowed a G7 warning about excessive yen volatility.

The Group of Seven big industrialised economices said on Monday that a rapid rise in the Japanese yen was bad for both markets and the economy and that it would watch developments accordingly.

Elsewhere, the Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> was virtually flat at 6.8476 per dollar while the Hong Kong dollar <HKD=> eased slightly to 7.7535 per U.S. dollar after the central bank injected HK$7.75 billion ($994 million) into the market.

Hong Kong's central bank bought U.S. dollars against the Hong Kong dollar last Thursday for the first time in nearly a year to stem a rise in the Hong Kong dollar.

The Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the U.S. dollar and can trade between 7.75 and 7.85 to the U.S. dollar.

title: Emerging  FX -Asians plumb multi-year lows on growth fears
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 23 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah hit its lowest level in nearly three years as Asian currencies fell to new multi-year lows on Thursday, hit by investor fears over global growth and persistent selling of risky assets.

 A day after Hungary raised rates by a hefty 3 percentage points to defend its currency, risk aversion was elevated in Asia with stock markets in Korea, Indonesia and the Philippines falling between 4 and 7 percent.

 The rupiah <IDR=> hit its lowest in nearly 3 years at 9,950 a dollar, the Philippine peso weakened to its weakest since early 2007 at 49 per dollar while the Malaysian ringgit fell to 3.5771, a nearly 2-year trough.

 The broad selling in emerging markets seemed to have sucked Asia in deep, even though it is backed by better fundamentals, such as ample reserves and growth estimates in higher single digits even in dismal global circumstances.

 "The nasty part is that deleveraging/balance sheet hole-plugging can produce indiscriminate selling, so Asia can be swept up even though its fundamentals are better," said Sean Callow, a strategist at Westpac Bank

 Central banks in India, Indonesia, Korea and the Philippines have been intervening to slow their currencies' decline and some of them were suspected of being in the market on Thursday.

 Analysts reckon policy makers are however merely smoothing the currency depreciation, and are tolerant of the weakness at a time when the risks of recession in Asia's main export markets are as high as that of heavy capital outflows triggered by the credit crisis.

 "Adding liquidity to increasingly thin and volatile markets is a valid policy decision, and note that FX reserves of most economies are ample," Patrick Bennett a strategist at Societe Generale said in a note.

 "We would only become concerned with a central bank attempting to defend a particular level, or one which was clearly acting contrary to economic fundamentals."  CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR  Change on the day at 0526 GMT

title: UPDATE 2-Eyes on S.Korea as Asian c.banks defend  currencies
text:
(Updates levels, adds Philippine intervention)

 SINGAPORE, Sept 2 (Reuters) - Central banks in Malaysia, India and elsewhere in Asia defended their weak currencies on Tuesday, but analysts suspected that South Korea's hands-off stance may deter others from standing firmly in the way of their falling currencies.

 The Bank of Thailand said it had sold dollars to put a floor under the baht <THB=TH>, which hit a one-year low of 34.49 per dollar on growing political tensions.

 Thai Prime Minister Samak Sundaravej declared a state of emergency in Bangkok on Tuesday and gave the army control of public order after overnight clashes between pro- and anti-government protesters.

 Market participants also reported interventions in India, Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia as currencies there buckled under the U.S. dollar's broad rally, the latter hitting an 8-month high against a basket of major currencies as oil prices fell.

 "All central banks are trying their best to stop the flood of outflows," a trader in Singapore said.

 In South Korea, where the won <KRW=> has been plumbing multi-year lows, the authorities restricted their efforts to meetings, warnings. Dollar-selling intervention, if any, was light as the volatile currency hit a new 4-year low near 1,134 per dollar.

 No one is sure why the Korean authorities have loosened their grip and let the won weaken, but market participants believe it is either because they want to shore up exports or out of reluctance to spend reserves against an inevitable dollar rally.

 Analysts said Korea's indifference to won weakness could weaken the resolve of other central banks.

 "It's very difficult if one goes, particularly if it's a large and important third-markets competitor for the rest of the region, like Korea," said Simon Flint, a strategist at Lehman Brothers. "It becomes difficult for the others to resist depreciation from a trade-weighted perspective.

 "Secondly, it weakens people's belief in the ability of the central banks to intervene effectively once they have seen one central bank can't do as they have apparently said they will do."

 INDIA ALSO STEPS IN

 The Reserve Bank of India was also spotted selling dollars but the rupee <INR=IN> still continued falling to hit a new 1-½   year low of 44.35 per dollar.

 The Malaysian central bank may have sold dollars at 3.4190 and 3.4180 per dollar, a trader in Kuala Lumpur said, but the ringgit persisted with its decline.

 The rupiah <IDR=> hit a low of 9,196 per dollar, its weakest since Aug. 19. A trader in Jakarta said the central bank sold dollars from 9,190.

 "It's not large. I think they realise that there is no point intervening aggressively in a dollar bull market all over the place," said one trader in Jakarta.

 In the Philippines, the central bank was seen selling dollars as the peso <PHP=> reached 46.60 per dollar, its weakest in almost a year.  (Reporting by Vidya Ranganathan; Editing by Jan Dahinten)

title: Emerging  FX -Asia dips further on credit worries, strong dollar
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 26 (Reuters) - The South Korean won hit a fresh four-year low in weaker Asia on Tuesday as the U.S. dollar rose against the euro due to fears of a euro zone slowdown, while renewed concerns over credit markets stoked risk aversion.

The U.S. dollar climbed towards a six-month high against the euro <EUR=> as investors waited for European data releases later in the day for evidence of the health of the euro zone economy. The dollar also neared a two-year high against the pound <GBP=D4> hit on Monday.

The South Korean won <KRW=> fell by 1 percent to 1,089.40 per dollar, its weakest since mid-November 2004, as investors increased their short won positions on growth worries, undeterred by a prospect of intervention.

"Since the market sees that government actions are now useless, everybody is on the (dollar) bid side," a trader in Seoul said.

South Korean authorities were suspected of intervening to support the local currency in recent weeks, but the won is still the biggest loser among the Asian currencies, having lost 14 percent this year.

In Malaysia, traders said the central bank was spotted selling dollars to put a floor under the ringgit <MYR=>.

The ringgit fell as low as 3.393 per dollar to hit a nine-month low against the dollar, hurt by the central bank's decision on Monday to leave rates on hold despite rising inflation.

"CPI is so high but they haven't done anything to contain the inflation while other central banks in Asia are hiking rates," said one trader in Kuala Lumpur.

"And there is the Anwar election today. A lot of event risk," he said, referring to a by-election that opposition leader Anwar Ibrahim is contesting as he seeks to return to parliament.

MORE INTERVENTION

Traders in the Philippines also suspected authorities had intervened to support the peso <PHP=>, which fell 0.8 percent to an 11-month low of 46 against the broadly stronger dollar.

"The central bank was in the market at 45.88 and 45.98 per dollar, and now they are defending 46," a trader in Manila said.

Two other traders in Manila also confirmed the intervention.

"I think there's still demand for dollars. The market would rather hold dollar than peso," a second trader said.

Analysts at Lehman Brothers said they were watching several factors to determine currency movement in the region.

"For the rest of the week the focus will mainly be on testing key central bank intervention levels, the political theatre in Malaysia and Thailand, central bank meetings in Thailand and the Philippines, and slowing growth indicators," they said in a note.

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> extended early losses and dipped 0.6 percent to 1.4263 as market players speculated the central bank may shift its monetary policy away from battling inflation towards one more supportive of growth. title: ANALYSIS-UPDATE 1-Philippine peso's rally on rate hike may fade
text:
(Updates with Standard Chartered forecast)

SINGAPORE, July 18 (Reuters) - The Philippine central bank's hefty rate rise and its hawkish stance will bolster the ailing peso in the short term, but more tightening may hurt the economy and undermine the currency in the longer run, analysts said.

Also, concerns about a fallout from lofty global oil and food prices on the economy may not recede quickly though the market expects further interest rate rises to help restrain prices.

Some analysts raised their outlook on the peso following the central bank's aggressive 50-basis-point rate hike on Thursday and hints of further tightening, but most have maintained their forecasts on the currency.

Analysts at UBS said they expected the central bank to raise rates by a total 200 basis points in the coming months to fight inflation, which hit a 14-year high of 11.4 percent in June.

That included the latest rate rise of 50 basis points and an earlier increase of 25 basis points in June.

Consequently, UBS has raised its one-month and three-month peso forecasts to 44.50 per dollar each -- little changed from the current level, analysts said in a note.

"Definitely, the 50-basis-point rate hike gives a more positive tone to the peso in the near term," said Callum Henderson, chief currency strategist at Standard Chartered Bank.

"But over the longer term, the more they tighten now, the greater the chance of further growth deceleration and further peso weakness in the first half of 2009," he said.

Standard Charted Bank has raised its peso forecast to 44.75 per dollar by the end of September from 45.50 and raised its end-2008 outlook to 45 from 46, analysts at the bank said in a note.

The peso <PHP=>, among Asia's worst performers this year, jumped 1 percent to a 3-week high of 44.44 per dollar in onshore trade, buoyed by the rate rise and falling oil prices.

It has lost 7.3 percent against the dollar so far this year, after it gained 19 percent as the region's top performer in 2007.

The peso rose as high high as 44.41 per dollar in one-month offshore non-deliverable forwards <PHP1MNDFOR=>, a one-month high, and hit 44.65 per dollar in three-month NDFs <PHP3MNDFOR=>, its strongest level since early June.

OUTLOOK UNCERTAIN The Philippine economy expanded a robust 7.2 percent last year, but a global economic slowdown and soaring costs have cast a pall over this year's prospects.

A Reuters poll this month forecast annual economic growth to slow to 5.1 percent this year and ease to 5.0 percent in 2009.

The market had been dumping the peso in recent weeks as the currency is seen heavily exposed to high oil prices, prompting the central bank to intervene to prop it up.

The Philippines imports nearly all of its crude oil needs and is the world's biggest rice importer. Its trade deficit this year is set to expand by a third to about $11 billion, the highest in at least nine years, central bank documents show.

Oil prices <CLc1> bounced above $130 a barrel on Friday, having risen almost 37 percent so far this year.

Grappling with slowing growth but more concerned about inflation, the central bank raised interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point in June. Before that, it cut interest rates by a total of 250 basis points since July 2007.

Higher interest rates may help limit the peso's further weakness as the cental bank appears determined to prop up the currency to help contain imported inflation, analysts said.

"Overall, the technical environment appears conducive for a near-term dollar/peso reversal. Outstanding positions appear net dollar long, carry attraction to short dollar/peso is high, rates are higher and the BSP (central bank) has been capping spot upside," JPMorgan strategist Claudio Piron said in a note.

"That said, a more sustained spot descent will likely be contingent on further policy follow-through on the hawkish BSP rhetoric," he added.

Analysts at DBS Bank maintain their year-end forecast at 47 per dollar, citing persistent inflationary risks.

"With BSP looking for double-digit inflation to persist in the first quarter of 2009, the real policy rates in deep negative, the stock market and bond market will not be in a hurry to rally," they said in a note.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia trades narrowly, supported by  intervention
text:
SINGAPORE, July 1 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies traded narrowly on Tuesday as investors warily held back following decade-high inflation rates in Thailand and South Korea, while authorities were suspected to have intervened in some currencies.

Foreign exchange authorities in Indonesia, Malaysia, India and the Philippines were suspected to have intervened to support their currencies.

South Korea's annual inflation in June rose to 5.5 percent from 4.9 percent in May, hitting its highest in almost 10 years.

Subsequently, the Korean won <KRW=> weakened to 1,048.75 per dollar, 0.3 percent lower than its previous close of 1,046 <KRW=KFTC>, while market players kept a look-out for possible dollar-selling intervention.

Earlier on, several currencies in the region were buoyed by a pullback in oil prices <CLc1>, which hit a record high above $143 per barrel on Monday, but these currencies gave up gains as oil prices rebounded to around $141 per barrel on Tuesday.

Still, the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> inched up by 0.1 percent to 9,215 against the dollar and held around those levels throughout the day.

Traders in Jakarta said the authorities had sold dollars everyday for the past few weeks to support the rupiah, and were doing the same on Tuesday.

"The government cannot subsidise our local oil, and this has caused higher inflation, so another way to (support growth) is to maintain the dollar/rupiah pairing at a cozy rate so our industries can run well," an Indonesia-based trader said.

Indonesia's annual inflation rate rose to a 21-month high of 11.03 percent in June, due largely to the lifting of fuel subsidies in the country.

The country's policy setting meeting will take place on Thursday, and Robert Prior-Wandesforde at HSBC said he expected a 25-basis-point hike in the present interest rate of 8.5 percent.

"We are expecting another quarter-point move on Thursday and a total of 125 basis points of hikes by the end of this year, taking the policy rate up to 9.75 percent," the economist said.

Thailand's consumer prices in June rose 8.9 percent from a year earlier, higher than the expected 8.5 percent polled in a Reuters survey. However, markets in Thailand were closed for a mid-year holiday.

MORE INTERVENTION CITED

The Indian rupee <INR=IN> fell to a 15-month low of 43.437 on heightened concerns over the impact of rising oil on the economy's growth. Traders said they suspected the central bank had been selling dollars early in the day.

Traders in Manila also cited intervention by the Philippine central bank to support the peso <PHP=>, which hit a 9-month low of 45.02.

"The central bank is protecting the peso around 44.99 to 45 per dollar," a trader said.

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> steadied around its previous closing levels of 3.265 per dollar, and traders said they suspected the Malaysian central bank had sold dollars to support the ringgit at 3.267-per-dollar throughout the day.

"Seems foreigners are not willing to touch this currency in the short term until political news is gone," a trader in Kuala Lumpur said.

title: TABLE-Asia ex-China's  FX  reserves fall $9 bln in May
text:
SINGAPORE, June 10 (Reuters) - Asian holdings of foreign exchange reserves, excluding those of China's, fell for the second staight month, central bank data showed, as some central banks sold dollars to support their weakening currencies.

 Asia's reserves, excluding China's, in May fell by nearly $9 billion from April to $2.54 trillion, following a $10 billion decline in April from March, the data showed.

 The overall decrease was led by an $6.86 billion dip in Japan's reserves, the second straight monthly decline, as higher U.S. yields cut the value of bonds in Japan's reserves while the euro's fall versus the dollar also dented the stockpile.

 South Korea's reserves fell by $2.28 billion, possibly due to the dollar-selling intervention by the authorities to prop up the won <KRW=>.

 Other central banks in the Philippines, India, Thailand and Indonesia have also intervened in the market in recent weeks to limit the declines in their currencies out of concern that further weakess could stoke inflationary risks.

 That marks a shift from Asian central banks' traditional dollar-buying intervention to keep their exchange rates competitive, resulting in the rapid build-up of their reserves.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia rises in cautious trade as oil prices ease
text:
SINGAPORE, May 28 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose on Wednesday as investors, encouraged by a drop in oil prices, cautiously moved to take profit on the dollar's steep gains in recent sessions.

 Market talk that Malaysia may announce new measures to liberalise trade in the ringgit, additionally helped buoy the tightly managed currency after recent losses.

 The Thai baht <THB=TH> rose as far as 32.15 per dollar, up almost half of a percent from late Asian trade on Tuesday.

 "There have been some dollar selling this morning to take profit after the dollar gained too much yesterday," said a trader in Bangkok.

 On Tuesday, the baht fell about 0.6 percent to its weakest level since May 16, in step with other Asian currencies hit by worries about the economic fallout from record high oil prices. The declines spurred authorities into action and central banks in South Korea, Indonesia and the Philippines were seen intervening on Tuesday to support their currencies.

 But a retreat in oil prices <CLc1> to below $127 per barrel on Wednesday from records above $135 hit last week offered markets some relief.

 The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> hit a one-week high at 9,295 per dollar, up 0.5 percent from late Asian trade on Tuesday.

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> also rose almost 0.5 percent to 43.55 per dollar.

 "Oil prices came off overnight, which put some downward pressure on the dollar versus the peso," said a dealer in Manila.

 A second trader said he expected the Philippine central bank to check on the peso's weakness for fear of fuelling inflation.

 "They will come into the market if needed," he said.

 The peso, has lost 5.5 percent against the dollar this year, trailing behind the South Korean won's 10 percent decline and the Indian rupee's 8 percent drop.

 OUTLOOK UNCERTAIN

 The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> hit 6.9421 per dollar, up a fifth of a percent from Tuesday's close and bringing its gains so far this year to 5.2 percent.

 The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> briefly rose to 30.493 to the U.S. dollar, cementing its position as the best performer in emerging Asia with gains of about 6.4 percent so far this year.

 However, currency investors remain wary after the recent sell-off.

 "The near-term outlook will be uncertain and range-bound," said Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist at BNP Paribas.

 "A lot depends on commodity prices currently, if the prices head up, the FX rebound today may be temporary," she said.

 Meanwhile, the ringgit <MYR=> rose as far as 3.225 per dollar, up 0.4 percent from late Asian trade on Tuesday after three sessions of losses.

 Some traders said renewed speculation that Malaysia would allow offshore trading in its currency again underpinned the ringgit.

 A central bank spokesman declined to comment and investors hoped the central bank governor's news conference on first quarter gross domestic product data would provide some clues whether any currency policy change was in fact on the cards. title: Emerging  FX -Asia listless amid uncertainty,  intervention
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were steady on Thursday as investors held back because of uncertainty over the outlook for the U.S. economy and rate decisions due in Europe later in the day.   

 Traders said the market was also cautious because central banks in the Philippines, Malaysia, India and Singapore were suspected of having intervened this week to curb strength in their currencies.   

 The U.S. dollar recovered against the yen and other major currencies overnight and held near a nine-month high against sterling <GBP=> in Asia.   

 But Asian stock markets <0#.INDEXA>, where foreigners have been heavy net sellers this year, barely moved, giving little direction to currencies.   

 The South Korean won <KRW=> initially rose 0.3 percent to hit 934.0 per dollar as local equities <.KS11> rallied, but it soon pared the gains to trade around 937.   

 A trader in Seoul said the won was stuck between 933 and 945 per dollar.   

 "There's a solid bottom for the dollar at 930 because oil companies are buying more dollars and equity outflows are continuing," the trader said.   

 "But there's also interest from shipping companies to hedge their earnings above 940 and exporters are selling options," she said.   

 Another trader felt the won would weaken to around 970 per dollar over the next few weeks, owing to outflows for dividend payments and  SK Telecom's purchase of a stake in Korean broadband provider  hanarotelecom , valued at nearly $1.2 billion.   

 SK is buying the stake from a consortium led by  American International Group and private equity fund Newbridge Capital.   

 Options traders said there was demand to sell won around 940 for one month and up to 1,000 per dollar through one-year options.   

 Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> was steady around 1.4310 per U.S. dollar while the Philippine peso <PHP=> fell half a percent from its previous close, backing off the highest level in nearly eight years hit on Wednesday.   

 In a volatile session, the peso rose from a low of 40.78 per dollar to hover around 40.60 before slipping again in late trading as the dollar gained against sterling and the yen.   

 "I think the peso will still appreciate. Any dollar upticks will be sold," a trader in Manila said.   

 But some analysts said the peso's long rally may have run its course for now.   

 They said a report earlier on Thursday showing Philippine exports in November fell 2 percent from a year earlier raised worries the currency's 20 percent appreciation in the past 12 months may be hurting the economy.   

 Many investors kept to the sidelines ahead of meetings by the European Central Bank (ECB) and Bank of England (BoE), and a speech by Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke later on Thursday.   

 Analysts expect the ECB to hold interest rates steady at 4.0 percent but see the BoE cutting rates due to weak consumption, which has sparked fears of a slowdown in the economy.   

 The next Fed rates decision is due on Jan. 30 and market expectations are shifting increasingly towards a cut in the Fed funds rate of as much as 50 basis points, although the majority in a Reuters poll still expected a more modest 25 basis points.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia rebounds on Fed move, but caution remains
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 20 (Reuters) - Asian currencies bounced back on Monday as regional stocks rallied after the U.S. Federal Reserve cut its discount rate in a surprise move on Friday, but the spectre of a credit market squeeze still weighed on sentiment.   

The Korean won <KRW=> steadied near 943 per dollar after hitting 939.9, which was up about 1 percent from late Asian trade on Friday.   

The high-yielding Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> rose as far as 9,380 per dollar, up nearly 1 percent, although it remains the worst performer in Asia this year with a loss of 4.2 percent versus the dollar.   

A Jakarta-based trader doubted that the rupiah would sustain its rally in the near term, given continuuing jitters about the U.S. subprime market crisis.   

"The subprime issue is still not finished -- there is still some doubt about it. If the subprime woes turn up again, I'm afraid the rupiah will go down again," he said.   

But Indonesia's central bank would want to stop the rupiah falling below the 9,500 level, traders said.   

Last week, central banks in Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines were reported to have intervened to support their currencies as investors fled risk amid credit market turmoil.   

MSCI's measure of Asia Pacific stocks excluding Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> jumped 5.5 percent following a rebound in U.S. stocks on Friday after the Fed cut its discount rate.   

Leading the pack, Indonesian stocks <.JKSE> jumped 6.6 percent, while South Korean shares <.SK11> surged 5.7 percent.   

NOT OUT OF THE WOODS   

Rising local stocks helped drive the Singapore dollar <SGD=> as far as 1.5240 per U.S. dollar, up almost 0.9 percent from late Asian trade on Friday and its strongest in nearly a week.   

Elsewhere, the Thai baht <THB=THB> rose as high as 34.30 per dollar, up more than 0.8 percent, while the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> gained about 0.6 percent to 3.491 to the dollar.   

Philippine markets were closed for a public holiday.   

Many analysts remained cautious as fears of a global credit squeeze persisted, even though the Fed's statement accompanying its discount rate cut fuelled expectations that it could be moving towards lowering its benchmark fed funds rate target.   

Thomas Harr, a currency strategist at Standard Chartered Bank, said he would refrain from telling his clients to buy into Asian currencies for now, despite the recovery in Asian stocks.   

"I think what we are seeing today is obviously a little bit of recovery, which is natural given that the Fed at least did something by cutting the discount rate on Friday," he said.   

"But the feeling in the market is that this may not improve liquidity that much. It's not clear that we are out of the woods yet and we expect the market to be choppy in the coming days." The Japanese yen, which has moved in the opposite direction to most emerging Asian currencies in recent sessions as investors unwound carry trades, eased against the dollar <JPY=> after pulling back from a 14-month high on Friday. title: Emerging  FX -Asian high-yielders buckle under credit fears
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 15 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso, Indonesian rupiah and Singapore dollar hit multi-week lows on Wednesday as investors extended their aggressive sales of risky assets on fears U.S. credit market woes were spreading overseas.   

The high-yielding peso <PHP=> fell 0.8 percent to 46.27 per dollar, a five-week low, while the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=>, another high-yielder, fell to 9,412 per dollar, its weakest point since June 2006.   

Traders in Jakarta said Bank Indonesia must have sold between $800 million and $900 million as it tried to brake the rupiah's decline and stop it from slipping beyond 9,400 per dollar. Central banks in Malaysia and the Philippines were also suspected of intervening to support their currencies.   

The euro <EUR=>, sterling <GBP=> and Australian and New Zealand dollars fell as investors moved out of higher-yielding assets and bought back the low-yielding yen <JPY=>. The yen hit a 4-1/2-month high against the dollar.   

A Reuters poll showed market participants were pushing back the possibility of a rise in official Japanese rates to September from August. The euro has also been hurt by a paring of the chances of a rate rise by the European Central Bank next month.   

"Indonesia will, of course, be an issue when you have this kind of risk aversion because of the high yields," said UOB Bank strategist Jimmy Koh.   

Koh said he was more worried about other asset markets than about currencies.   

"So far it has been an issue of market sentiment. But it can become a fundamental issue if there is a sharp pullback in liquidity and that introduces a risk premium into other sectors of the economy, thereby dampening consumption," Koh said.   

POSITIONS UNWOUND   

Markets in South Korea and India were closed for holidays. The Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell more than half a percent to the weaker side of 1.53 per U.S. dollar. The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> hit 3.4930 per dollar, its weakest since the end of June. "Currently, we're having a bit more pressure on the Asian currencies as a result of base dollar strength, not so much against the yen but more against European currencies," said Thio Chin Loo, a currency strategist at  BNP Paribas.

"It's just a symptom of unwinding of risk across the board and this has affected Asian currencies as well," she added.   

The flow of bad news from credit markets has not abated.   

Concern grew after a U.S. investment firm wanted to halt redemptions on Tuesday and a Canadian trust couldn't find funds to repay some short-term debt.   

Wal-Mart , the world's largest retailer, cut its profit forecast and Swiss Bank  UBS warned that market turmoil was likely to hit its investment banking business.   

"We continue to see price action driven primarily by crisis management and position liquidation rather than active decision making," said  Bank of America strategist Christy Tan.   

"We're still in the midst of a deleveraging environment," she said.

title: Asian c.banks step in to support  currencies -traders
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 15 (Reuters) - Central banks in Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines were suspected of intervening once again on Wednesday to smooth declines in their currencies as fears of a wider credit crisis led to a heavy sell-off.   

The ringgit <MYR=> fell to a five-month low of 3.4920 per dollar, succumbing to the broad selling of high-yielding currencies and stock markets.   

A trader in Kuala Lumpur said the central bank had been suspected of providing dollars through state-run banks at levels from 3.4840 to 3.4920.   

"They are just smoothing the depreciation process, I think," he said.   

The Philippine peso <PHP=> fell 0.8 percent to a one-month low of 46.25 per dollar, its fall cushioned intermittently by central bank intervention at various levels, traders said.   

Traders in Jakarta said Bank Indonesia had also sold dollars and that had stemmed the rupiah's <IDR=> decline at a June 2006 low of 9,405 per dollar.

title: UPDATE 1-FACTBOX-How central banks have acted to inject funds
text:
(Updates with no action from Fed)   

FRANKFURT, Aug 14 (Reuters) - Global central banks are withdrawing much of the extra cash they have injected into banking systems to calm panicky credit since last Thursday.   

Below is a list of central bank actions since the credit markets upheaval turned nasty last week.   

EUROPEAN CENTRAL BANK

Aug 9 - 94.8 billion euros ($129.8 billion) in a one-day tender on Thursday, the largest amount ever.   

Aug 10 - 61.05 billion euros ($83.61 billion) in a three-day tender on Friday to cover the weekend,   

Aug 13 - 47.67 billion euros ($65.29 billion) in one-day money on Monday   

Aug 14 - 7.7 billion in one-day money on Tuesday. The ECB also added an extra 73.5 billion euros in one-week money more than its estimated liquidity needs for banks during its main refinancing operation.   

Trichet also issued a statement on Tuesday calling for investors to stay composed composure in face of market volatility and a repricing of risk.   

The ECB's injections exceed those that it flooded into markets immediately after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks on the United States. At that time, 69.3 billion euro in overnight money was allocated on Sept. 12, 2001, followed by 40.5 billion euros the next day.   

U.S. FEDERAL RESERVE   

Aug 9 - $24 billion during its regular market operations, only slightly above the usual allocation.   

Aug 10 - Added $38 billion through three separate repurchase agreements, its biggest single-day cash injection since Sept. 19, 2001. The repos brought down the federal funds rate, the cost of overnight loans between banks, to the Fed's target rate of 5.25 percent.   

Aug 13 - Added $2 billion of temporary reserves to the banking system through overnight repurchasing agreements.   

Aug 14 - The Fed took the unusual step of refraining from an open market operation at 9:30 a.m. (1330 GMT), when daily operations are usually conducted. In an earlier statement, the Fed said it was evaluating whether or not to conduct an operation at that time and said it stood ready to conduct additional operations later in the day as needed.   

BANK OF JAPAN   

Aug 10 - Added 1.0 trillion yen ($8.45 billion) at its regular money market operation on Friday after a slight rise in the benchmark overnight call rate, the highest amount in about six weeks. Traders said the amount was at the higher end of market expectations, but was not a major surprise.   

Aug 13 - Added 600 billion yen ($5.1 billion) into the banking system in a one-week operation.   

Aug 14 - Drained 1.6 trillion yen ($13.6 billion) in two operations.   

BANK OF ENGLAND   

The Bank of England said banks hit by tough credit conditions could use its emergency lending facility, which is routinely available and priced at 100 basis points above the bank's 5.75 percent policy rate.   

BANK OF CANADA   

Aug 9 - Injected C$1.64 billion ($1.55 billion) on Thursday, saying it was in contact with other central banks on the global situation and stood ready to add money as needed.   

Aug 10 - Injected a total of C$1.685 billion ($1.605 billion)   

Aug 13 - Injected C$670 million.   

THE RESERVE BANK OF AUSTRALIA   

Aug 10 - The RBA added more than twice the usual amount of money into the banking system, injecting A$4.95 billion ($4.19 billion).   

Aug 14 - The RBA added A$2.6 billion ($2.2 billion) in its regular morning money market operation, slightly higher than average.   

SWISS NATIONAL BANK   

Aug 9/10 - The SNB offered banks money at a below-market rate of 2.6 percent on Thursday and Friday, adding a total of 3.1 billion Swiss francs ($2.57 billion) <CHF=>. It since has started to drain the extra liquidity.   

Aug 13/14 - Traders said the SNB drained liquidity as overnight rates remained low after the previous week's liquidity-providing actions.   

CENTRAL BANKS OF MALAYSIA, INDONESIA, PHILIPPINES

Traders said the Asian central banks intervened in foreign exchange markets on Friday to support their currencies by selling U.S. dollars. Malaysia's central bank chief Zeti Akhtar Aziz said on Monday there was sufficient liquidity in its financial system, but that it was monitoring the situation.   

BANK OF KOREA   

South Korea's central bank said on Friday it was ready to add funds to markets if needed.   

CENTRAL BANK OF NORWAY   

The central bank said Thursday's loan of 45 billion crowns ($7.80 billion) gave ample liquidity to banks and it would continue to ensure orderly operations in the money market.

title: Indonesian rupiah, peso off lows,  intervention  cited
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 28 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso were pushed off their lows on Wednesday by suspected central bank dollar selling, but both currencies remained weak amid heightened risk aversion in global markets.   

Traders said the Indonesian and Philippine central banks sold the dollar for their local currencies which had come under pressure as investors unwound yen-funded carry trades following a steep sell-off in global stock markets.   

By 0315 GMT, the rupiah was quoted at 9,175 per dollar <IDR=>, down 1 percent from levels seen late in Asia on Tuesday, but off a three-month low hit earlier at 9,195.   

The peso <PHP=> stood at about 48.60 to the dollar, down about 0.4 percent and just off a three-week low of 48.65. "They just want to smooth the movement, nothing more than that," said a trader in Singapore, referring to the suspected intervention in Indonesia and the Philippines.   

Dealers said they suspected that Bank Indonesia had bought the rupiah around the 9,200 level against the dollar, while a trader in Manila said the central bank there stepped into the market when the peso weakened to 48.65 per dollar.   

"They were just there to dampen the volatility and prevent things from getting out of hand," the trader said.   

"The market does seem to have settled down a bit and I don't think there is any panic."

title: Emerging  FX -Rupiah leads weak Asia on equity falls
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 28 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah led the decline in Asian currencies on Wednesday as regional stock markets fell and investors unwound yen-funded carry trades following a steep sell-off in global stock markets.   

Traders said the Indonesian and Philippine central banks sold the dollar for their local currencies as the rupiah and peso led a broad decline in most Asian currencies.   

The rupiah <IDR=> recovered from a three-month low of 9,195 per dollar, but was still down about 0.8 percent at 9,150 per dollar. The peso <PHP=> was near 48.50 per dollar, down a quarter of a percent and just off three-week lows.   

The South Korean won <KRW=> fell a third of a percent to 941.6 per dollar, while the Singapore dollar <SGD=> also dipped nearly 0.3 percent to around 1.53 per U.S. dollar.   

Analysts remained bullish about the underlying strength of Asian currencies in general, citing the region's solid economic growth and hefty balance-of-payment surpluses.   

"I think what we see right now in the market is just a reaction to what happened yesterday, so you see people starting to get a bit risk averse again," said Magnus Prim, chief Asia currency strategist at SEB.   

"But I see the fundamentals are still pretty good and the falls should prove to be a short-term correction," he said.   

The yen <JPY=> fell against the dollar, taking a breather after surging to 10-week highs in the previous session as investors unwound risky trades on fears of rising volatility.   

A tumble in global stock prices including the biggest daily fall in Chinese stocks in a decade, soft U.S. economic data and growing tensions with Iran jolted investors from complacency and prompted them to cut exposure to risk.   

The Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index, or VIX <.VIX>, rose 70 percent on Tuesday in another sign of investor jitters. The VIX typically rises as investors become anxious about the stock market and tends to fall when fear subsides.   

Asian equity markets <.MSCIAPJ> were weaker on Wednesday, but Chinese stocks <.SSEC> rose about 4 percent on Wednesday after falling nearly 9 percent on Tuesday.   

China's yuan <CNY=CFXS> hit a new intraday post-revaluation high of 7.7378 per dollar, extending the previous day's gains.   

RUPIAH, PESO FACE BIGGER PRESSURE   

Aslim Tadjuddin, a deputy Indonesian central bank governor, said that the bank views a sharp fall in the rupiah as temporary and will do "everything necessary" to defend the currency.   

But traders said the central banks would not over-react.   

"They just want to smooth the movement, nothing more than that," said a trader in Singapore, referring to the suspected intervention in Indonesia and the Philippines.   

JPMorgan analysts Claudio Piron and Yen Ping Ho said in a research note that the rupiah, the peso and the Indian rupee would face greater pressure as investors had borrowed the cheaper yen to build long positions in the units.   

"While we struggle to identify fundamental changes in the external backdrop that warrants a fundamental reversal of the carry backdrop, we acknowledge that the technical environment of market caution, heavy long risky asset positions and tight valuations mean pressures could remain for some time."   

The Thai baht, which has been caught in a two-tier market since the government imposed currency controls in December, gained about 0.3 percent to 35.43 per dollar onshore <THB=>.   

But it was volatile in offshore trading <THB=W>, moving between 33.05 and 34.10 per dollar.   

The Bank of Thailand on Wednesday cut its benchmark 1-day repurchase rate by 25 basis point to 4.5 percent, as expected. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0742 GMT

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Calm prevails before U.S. jobs data
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were little moved on Friday, with trade thin as some markets closed for a holiday and dealers waited for U.S. jobs data later in the day for direction.  

South Korean markets are shut for the local thanksgiving Chusok holiday, Taiwan is closed for the Mid-Autumn Moon Festival and Chinese markets have been shut all week.  

The Indian rupee <INR=IN> hit fresh four-month highs around 45.56 per dollar on robust foreign inflows into local stocks.  

Most traders said they preferred to stay on the sidelines before the U.S. non-farm payrolls report at 1230 GMT, which could shed some light on the interest rate outlook after data this week stoked speculation that the next U.S. rate move could be a cut.  

Economists polled by Reuters expect the data to show the U.S. economy created 125,000 new jobs in September against 128,000 jobs in August.  

"There is a bit of a downside risk to payrolls," said Jimmy Koh, head of economics and treasury research at United Overseas Bank. "The reason for a rally in stocks that we are seeing is that the next Fed move is more likely to be a cut then a hike."  

The Dow Jones industrial average <.DJI> hit a record closing high on Thursday and the S&P 500 index <.SPX> rose to 5-1/2-year highs. Analysts say the U.S. stocks rally bodes well for Asian equities and currencies despite signs of a U.S. slowdown.  

WEAK YEN SHRUGGED OFF  

The dollar rose almost 0.4 percent to 118.15 yen <JPY=>, heading towards this week's 5-1/2-month peak at about 118.40 yen.  

Yen weakness initially weighed on the regionals but by late trade most of them had pared early falls.  

The Thai baht <THB=> was up slightly at 37.53 per dollar, the Philippine peso moved to the firm side of 50 per dollar <PHP=> and the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> was steady at 9,200 per dollar.  

Indonesia's benchmark interest rate may fall to between 9.0-9.5 percent by year-end from 10.75 percent currently, central bank deputy governor Aslim Tadjuddin said on Friday.  

Some analysts say the prospect for further rate cuts should bolster foreign demand for local debt and the rupiah, while traders said that with rate cuts priced into the market the currency should remain in a range.  

"Bank Indonesia is doing the right thing in cutting rates as inflation is low," said a Jakarta trader. "When rates reach a bottom, we could see a reaction in the market, but until then there shouldn't be much reaction."  

In the Philippines, dealers said they remained wary of central bank intervention to curtail strength in the peso, which hit its highest level in more than four years earlier this week.  

"Because exporters are worried that if the peso strengthens further they will be hurt, the central bank has occasionally been coming into the market," said a Manila dealer.  

The Singapore dollar hugged a narrow 1.5860-1.5842 range versus the dollar, with focus on Tuesday's Monetary Authority of Singapore meeting.  

The MAS, which conducts its monetary policy through the Singapore dollar, is widely expected to maintain a policy allowing a modest and gradual appreciation of the currency. "With inflation just 0.7 percent year-on-year in August, there is an outside chance of a (very SGD-negative) switch to a neutral stance on SGD," Westpac senior currency strategist Sean Callow said in a research note.  

But he added that with the Singapore and global economies still firm, the central bank does not sound as if it is ready to change its stance.

title: Philippines  Arroyo: No Direct  Intervention  In  Forex  Mkt
text:
MANILA (Dow Jones)--Despite complaints from exporters that a stronger peso is hurting their competitiveness, Philippine President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo on Thursday dismissed the possibility of any direct intervention in the currency market.  

Instead, Arroyo said in a nationwide televised address that the government will provide assistance to exporters to cut their costs and maintain their competitiveness.  

"The central bank which makes exchange rate policy doesn't agree to (direct) intervention," said Arroyo. "So our intervention will be in other ways to reduce the cost of exporters." [ 23-03-06 0632GMT ]  

She said government financial institutions will help provide cheap financing to exporters, while government offices will have to streamline export regulations.  

"The appreciation of the peso helps the majority, but we must still protect our exporters," Arroyo said.  

Improved revenue and a narrower budget deficit have boosted the peso's value against the dollar in recent months. Since the end of September - when Arroyo quashed an effort to impeach her - the peso has risen against the dollar by around 10%, with the greenback falling from PHP56.01 to a 3 1/2-year low of PHP50.88 early this month.  

At midday Thursday, the dollar was at PHP51.16.  

The Philippine Exporters Confederation has publicly urged the government and the central bank to adjust economic policies to balance the interests of other segments of the economy with those of exporters and of the families of 8 million overseas workers who send dollar remittances home.

title: Philippines  Ctrl Bk: Will  Intervene  In Mkt Only If Needed
text:
MANILA (Dow Jones)--The Philippine central bank said Tuesday it will continue to allow market forces to determine the peso-dollar exchange rate, but it is ready to provide liquidity to smooth extreme volatility in the spot currency market.  

Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Governor Amando Tetangco told a government-sponsored investor briefing that there is "scope for occasional official action in cases where extreme movements in the peso threaten the inflation target."  

The central bank projects inflation next year will ease to 4.4%-5.8%, from a projected 7.5%-8.3% range for this year. The official target is average inflation of 4%-5% for both years.  

Currency traders suspect that the central bank has been buying U.S. dollars in recent weeks to boost its reserves. The central bank had refused to comment.  

The central bank expects the dollar to average PHP55-PHP57 this year after an average of PHP55.09 in 2005. However, the dollar fell to a three-year low of PHP51.57 Monday.  

Filipinos in higher paying jobs overseas are expected to boost remittances to $11.8 billion this year, 10% more than the estimated $10.7 billion in 2005. In the 11 months to November 2005, remittances rose 27% over the same period the year before, to $9.7 billion.  

The central bank is forecasting gross international reserves for 2006 to be between $18 billion and $18.6 billion, compared with an end-2005 level of $18.495 billion. At the end of January, reserves were already at an all-time high of $20.504 billion due to fresh government borrowing and gains in the central bank's overseas investments.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Weakness on US rate view seen brief
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 2 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were broadly weaker on Thursday, retreating from the previous day's multi-year peaks as markets pushed the dollar higher to price in more U.S. rate rises.  

But most analysts said weakness in Asian currencies would be short-lived because flows into regional equity markets were strong and positioning in favour of the regionals was still light.  

The dollar rose to a seven-week high above 118 yen <JPY=> and also rallied against the euro <EUR=> and other European currencies as interest rate markets priced in further monetary tightening in the United States this year.  

The Federal Reserve raised the fed funds rate on Tuesday for the 14th time in 19 months and hinted further rises could follow.  

The South Korean won <KRW=> dropped a percent on the day to around 974 a dollar, pulling further back from Wednesday's eight-year peak around 957.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> and the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> were also big losers. The Singapore dollar slipped to the weaker side of 1.63 per U.S. dollar, ceding more than a cent from the previous day's high.  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> rose early to 52.03 per dollar, its strongest level since May 2003, and then slipped. It has risen about 1.8 percent since Jan. 23, buoyed by expectations of foreign portfolio inflows and a possible upgrade in the country's credit ratings.  

Markets in China and Taiwan were closed for Lunar New Year holidays.  

Sean Callow, Westpac Bank's currency strategist, said the dollar's rebound was no surprise.  

"The market did get a little bit carried away with the notion that the dollar should decline as soon as the Fed even hints at finishing tightening.  

"There is no guarantee that they have finished hiking yet and that the yield story will be broadly supportive of the dollar overall," he said.  

Still, the strength of economic fundamentals would support currencies such as the won, ensuring their losses were limited, Callow said.  

"Dollar/won could track higher in the short-term but it is hard to argue for a major pullback on any of the won crosses. The fundamental story for the won is very strong," he said.  

INTERVENTION

Analysts suspected central banks in Korea, India, the Philippines and Singapore had intervened this week to rein in the strength of their currencies.  

"They are never going to sit passively while markets take their currencies stronger against the dollar," Tim Condon, ING's currency strategist said.  

"They are always going to be dollar defenders but I suspect that means they slow but not reverse the pressure," he said, while citing the strength of flows underpinning Asian currencies.  

South Korean foreign exchange reserves jumped $6.5 billion in January, the biggest monthly gain in 14 months, which dealers said indicated heavy dollar-buying intervention by the Bank of Korea.  

Yet, the commerce ministry said on Wednesday the central bank had been complacent and had allowed the won to strengthen rapidly.  

This week, the won hit an 8-year high near 8.14 per yen <JPYKRW=R>, as Asian currencies outperformed the yen.  

ABN AMRO Bank's Shahab Jalinoos said the outperformance against the Japanese currency would persist.  

"This reflects the fact that low-yielding yen is currently a global funding currency in a risk-loving environment, while Asian currencies are beneficiaries of risk-seeking global capital seeking returns in their asset markets," he said in a note. title: Emerging Asia  FX -Broadly firm, rupiah in focus after rate move
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 6 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were broadly firm against the dollar on Tuesday, boosted by gains in regional equities and optimism about economic growth in the region.  

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> hit a one-month peak at about 9,910 per dollar as investors cheered changes to the cabinet's top economic positions, but it dropped back slightly after Bank Indonesia delivered a smaller-than-expected interest rate rise.  

The central bank raised the BI rate <BIPG>, its target rate for one-month certificates <BISBI01>, by 50 basis points to 12.75 percent to contain inflation, which is at a six-year high.  

This disappointed some in the currency market who had been looking for a rise of between 75 and 100 basis points.  

Still, analysts said sentiment was likely to stay upbeat after President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono named respected former Finance Minister Boediono as his chief economics minister, replacing Aburizal Bakrie.  

Planning Minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati moves across to take on the finance portfolio from Jusuf Anwar.  

"Indonesia has been raising interest rates and hiring and firing the right people, so it is on the right track," said JPMorgan currency strategist Claudio Piron. "The rupiah is likely to close up on the day but it will give up some of its gains."  

The South Korean won <KRW=><KRW=KTFC> gained more than a third of a percent to 1,033.0, boosted by foreign buying in the local equity market, whose index <.KS11> hit an all-time high.  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> added a quarter of a percent to a three-week high of 33.405 per dollar, helped by expectations that the victory of Taiwan's opposition party in local government elections at the weekend would spur more foreign fund inflows.  

Its success has been welcomed by financial markets because the opposition is viewed as having a more conciliatory approach to China, the island's top trading partner.  

GROWTH OPTIMISM  

Analysts said favourable economic data meant Asia's currencies were holding up well against the dollar.  

"We are getting stronger-than-expected numbers for the third quarter and the export numbers are also showing that growth will be a bit better going into the first quarter despite high oil prices," said Jimmy Koh, head of economics and treasury at United Overseas Bank.  

Thailand's economy expanded 2.2 percent in the third quarter from the previous three months, beating market forecasts, data on Tuesday showed.  

Optimism about the economic outlook and rising short-term interest rates in Singapore helped push the Sing dollar <SGD=> to a two-month peak of about 1.6830 per dollar.  

Three-month rates <SGDF=> have risen to their highest level since early 2000. Traders said the upward pressure on rates was aimed at raising the appeal of local assets as interest rates around the region rise.  

"There is very strong macro data, a very strong push higher in domestic yields and a general recognition of the fact that the Sing dollar is cheaper against the basket," said Mirza Baig, a currency strategist at Deutsche Bank in Singapore.  

Dealers in the Philippines said central bank intervention to cap the peso's strength had undermined the currency in early trade.

title: Philippine Ctrl Bk: Scope For Occasional  FX Intervention
text:
MANILA (Dow Jones--The Philippines' central bank won't hesitate to intervene in the local currency market if a weakening peso is seen pushing inflation sharply higher.  

The peso has been under pressure the past several weeks on political concerns and worries over the economic impact of high world oil prices.  

"The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas will maintain a market-determined exchange rate with scope for occasional official action in cases where extreme movement in the peso threatens the inflation target," central bank Governor Amando Tetangco told a midyear economic briefing Monday.  

Tools used by the central bank to quell volatility on the foreign exchange market include raising key overnight rates, adjusting commercial banks' reserve requirement or directly buying or selling dollars on the Philippine Dealing System.  

At the last monthly rate-setting meeting of the central bank's policy-making Monetary Board held two weeks ago, key overnight borrowing and lending rates were left unchanged at 7.00% and 9.25%, respectively.  

That time, the central bank said it wanted to ensure adequate liquidity to fuel economic activity. The central bank also said domestic inflationary pressures were driven by supply factors, particularly rising oil prices, thus policy tightening wasn't merited.  

Tetangco said last month that the central bank expects the inflation rate for August to range between 6.6% and 7.1% on year compared with the previous month's 7.1% amid a slower increase in food prices.  

In afternoon trade, the dollar averaged PHP56.121 compared with Friday's close of PHP56.10.

title: Peso at 5-½ month low, hit by politics and firm dlr
text:
SINGAPORE, June 30 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso extended a three-week long slide to hit a 5-½ month low on Thursday as heightened political tension and broad-based dollar strength took a toll on the currency.  

The peso <PHP=> reached 56.25 per dollar, a level last seen in early January and close to its lifetime low of 56.45.  

The peso has shed 2.8 percent in the three weeks since controvery erupted over recordings of a conversation between President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo and an election official during last year's elections.  

This week Arroyo admitted the voice on the tape was hers, saying it was an error in judgement and she did not intend to influence the results of the election. On Wednesday, she also said her scandal-prone husband would leave the country.  

Yet calls for her to quit have risen and left-wing groups have planned a rally in Manila on Thursday.  

"This is not anything new," said Rovic De Guzman, head of trading at Union Bank of the Philippines, referring to the rally.  

"But the market is quite emotional as it is, and we have the dollar rally against the rest of the region," he said.  

Traders said there was talk that the central bank may have intervened earlier to defend the peso.

"The peso is reacting to non-economic factors," acting Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Governor Amando Tetangco told Dow Jones Newswires in a text message. "Based on macroeconomic fundamentals, it should be trading better."  

He refused to respond to questions about whether the central bank was intervening, saying only: "We continue to monitor the market."  

At the noon break Tuesday, an hour before a congressional hearing on the alleged wiretap recordings purporting to show President Gloria Arroyo conspired to rig last year's elections, the U.S. dollar averaged PHP55.88, higher than its PHP55.745 close Monday.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Down as China, G7 expectations pared.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Jan 31 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were pushed
lower on Monday as markets scaled back their expectations for
an imminent Chinese yuan revaluation and for the upcoming Group
of Seven nations' meeting to put more pressure on the region.
    That happened after fresh comments from Chinese top
officials suggested they were in no hurry to reform the yuan
regime, and the U.S. dollar found support ahead of key data and
a Federal Reserve  policy meeting.
    Traders braced for a volatile week that will end with the
Group of Seven nations' meeting in London on Friday and
Saturday and could see U.S. rates raised by another 25 basis
points.
    U.S. Treasury Undersecretary John Taylor added to the
pressure on regionals with his remarks that there was no need
for the dollar to crash and that the G7 statement would not be
different from the one issued last year in Florida.
  


 Officials
from China, India and other emerging economies have been
invited to talks with the seven industrialised nations.
 
    The Korean won fell from near Friday's 7-year high of 1,023
a dollar to around 1,026.
    The Singapore dollar fell about a quarter percent to 1.64 a
dollar and then trimmed losses. The Thai baht and Indonesian
rupiah were down.
    There was talk of intervention in Singapore and in the
  

Philippines, where the peso barely moved after its rapid 2.3  

percent gains in 3 weeks, helped by a 12 percent rally in  

stocks  

Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist with UBS, said even if  

the G7 called on Asia to share in the adjustment of the massive  

U.S. trade deficit by letting currencies rise, the region would  

not oblige readily.  

"Even if the rhetoric is stepped up on level to  

burden-sharing, I believe it will not be very significant for  

currency moves."  

"What is central for Asian authorities is that economic  

growth in most areas is clearly off the peak. They will  

continue to intervene to protect against sharp appreciation in  

their currencies, thereby trying to keep exports competitive,"  

he said.  

The Philippines released data on Monday showing annual  

gross domestic product grew 6.1 percent in 2004, the quickest  

pace in 15 years. But growth in the last quarter of 2004 was  

disappointing, and analysts warned the currency market was  

probably overestimating potential investment inflows and  

remittances.  

DOLLAR SUPPORTED  

Meanwhile, the see-sawing on the prospects of China  

revaluing its virtually pegged yuan continued, with China's  

deputy central bank governor Li Ruogu dashing expectations by  

saying China did not have the capacity to address global  

economic imbalances and was not willing or able to do it.  

The premium on one-year yuan in non-deliverable forwards  

was down to 3,850 points, pricing in 4.9 percent gains,  

compared with 5.6 percent on Friday.  

Global oil prices fell, with U.S. oil below $47 a barrel,  

after OPEC producers left output unchanged and Iraq's election  

passed without disruption to oil exports.   


 
    "The dollar will bounce this week," said Claudio Piron,
currency strategist with JP Morgan.
    "Oil prices are lower and that should help the dollar. The
Fed FOMC will be delivering 25 basis points and positioning in
Asia is very aggressive," he said.
    YEN-WON CROSS
    Piron said the north Asian currencies would suffer, but
that markets would be divided on whether to buy the won against
the yen. The yen-won cross rate showed the yen at 9.89 won.
    Markets have been torn between the urge to buy the yen-won
  

cross below the 10 mark - which they believe is the highest  

level for the won Korean authorities can tolerate - and the  

belief that South Korea will not intervene heavily, since the  

government is running out of bonds to offset the intervention.  

Traders waited for data on foreign exchange reserves from  

Korea for evidence of intervention in January and confirmation  

of their view that Korea intervened less in order to stabilise  

its bond markets.  

The finance ministry's announcement on Friday that it would  

issue 5 trillion won in fiscal bonds in February, however,  

frustrated some won bulls. That came after Korea said it would  

cut down on the amount of treasuries issued in February.

text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, March 23 (Reuters) - Local politics, again at
the fore of Asian currency trading on Tuesday, weighed on the
Indonesian rupiah, Philippine peso and Taiwan dollar.
    Analysts said the recent political and election surprises
in South Korea and Taiwan had turned investors wary on other
parts of the region where elections are due -- Indonesia and
the Philippines.
    The Singapore dollar        and the Korean won
  were higher, following the yen        after security
threats undermined the U.S. dollar.
    Those concerns arose after Israel killed the spiritual
leader of the Hamas militant group and as Pakistani troops
remain locked in battle with a group of suspected al Qaeda
fighters.
    Meanwhile, the Indonesian rupiah        continued falling
in the run-up to parliamentary elections in early April and, at
8,590 per dollar, its losses so far this year were over two
percent.
  


    The Philippine peso        languished near Monday's
all-time low of 56.45 per dollar because of mounting anxiety
ahead of the May elections, although it won some reprieve from
data showing the February fiscal deficit was within the target.
    "In places where there have been elections they have all
been surprises, Malaysia on the upside, Taiwan and Korea
considerably on the downside," said James Malcolm, currency
strategist with JP Morgan.
    Malcolm was referring to the landslide victory for
Malaysian Prime Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi's ruling
coalition, the recent impeachment of South Korean President Roh
Moo-hyun and Taiwan's disputed presidential election.
 
     "It makes people nervous about the other risks in Asia,
particularly Indonesia and the Philippines," Malcolm said.
    The hangover of President Chen Shui-bian's narrow election
victory on the weekend preceded by a puzzling assassination
attempt continued to hurt the Taiwan dollar on Tuesday.
    It recovered on suspected central bank intervention and
  

after Chen's Democratic Progressive Party proposed a revision  

of the election law to allow a recount of votes if the margin  

of difference was too low.  

Central banks have been intervening to defend currencies in  

the Philippines and Taiwan this week but, as the recent rises  

in the won showed, they were probably more tolerant now of  

currency appreciation, Malcolm said.  

"Central banks will be much be less active, both because of  

dollar/yen and that there's a lot less speculative element in  

the market at the moment," he said.  

"It is a more conducive environment for allowing currency

appreciation."

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Peso falls, baht steady in light trade.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Jan 22 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso eased on
Thursday while the Thai baht moved little, with most Asian
regional currency markets shut for the Lunar New Year holidays.
 
    Financial markets in Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore,
Indonesia, Malaysia and Taiwan were closed on Thursday.
    Markets will reopen in Indonesia on Friday. Singapore,
South Korea, Hong Kong and Malaysia will reopen on Monday and
Taiwan will resume trade on Tuesday.
    The peso fell by about a quarter percent to 55.68 per
dollar, from Wednesday's local close of 55.56.
    Dealers in Manila said the peso fell as local companies
bought U.S. dollars in the absence of any significant inflows
of that currency.
    The baht was glued to a tight range of 39.0 to 39.05 per
dollar, as only a few dealing rooms were active in Bangkok.
  


    "There were no offshore names and even our local customers
were out of the market because of the holiday," said a dealer
at a local bank in Bangkok.
    The dealer said the baht might stick to a narrow range
around the 39 per dollar level on Friday as well, but some
action was likely next week.
    "There is interest, both local and offshore, to push the
baht higher," the dealer said.
    "But players will be careful as they have already seen the
central bank in the market this week," he said, adding that the
Bank of Thailand had helped pull the baht to 39.08 on Tuesday.
    Intervention was also suspected in the Philippines where
  

dealers said the Philippines central bank had bought pesos to  

pull the troubled currency off two-month lows it had hit on  

Tuesday.   


 
    The peso, Asia's worst performer in 2003, is expected to
suffer more losses ahead of presidential elections in May.
    A three-month election campaign in the Philippines will
formally start on February 8.
    Many analysts fear that electioneering could weaken the
  

budget and prompt foreign lenders to ask for much higher  

interest rates on loans to the country, Asia's most active  

borrower of dollars outside of Japan.   


 
    But for the next few weeks, dealers said, the U.S. dollar's
global decline might help put a floor under the peso.
    The peso touched an all-time low of 55.85 per dollar in
  

November last year, and many dealers expect that level to be  

tested again as the import season in the second quarter kicks  

in.   


 
    In contrast, traders are bullish on the baht, which
strengthened by about nine percent against the dollar in 2003.
    Many analysts expect the baht to strengthen towards 38 per
dollar and beyond in 2004, despite several capital controls
imposed by Thailand last year to curb the currency's rise.
    They expect authorities in Thailand, one of Asia's fastest
  

growing economies, to lower their resistance to currency

gains.
