title: UPDATE 1-Manila c.bank says can provide  forex  liquidity.
text:
MANILA, Aug 25 (Reuters) - The Philippine central bank said on Monday it stood ready to pump liquidity into the financial system as the country's currency plunged to fresh 31-month lows. 

 "We will provide liquidity as necessary. That policy has never changed," Deputy Governor Amando Tetangco told reporters when asked whether the bank would intervene in the foreign exchange market to stem the peso's slide. 

 "Our policy continues to be the same - to essentially let market forces determine the exchange rate." 

 The peso  was quoted at 55.40/44 on Monday afternoon, perilously close to its all-time low of 55.75 in January 2001 when Joseph Estrada was ousted from the presidency in an army-backed popular revolt. 

 Jitters over a failed uprising by renegade soldiers on July 27, a court-ordered suspension of the central bank governor and money laundering accusations against the husband of President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo have combined with seasonal dollar demand to put the peso under heavy pressure in the past two weeks. 

Central bank officials have denied it has been injecting funds into the market, although traders say the bank has intervened on a number of occasions. 

 The Philippines has a limited ability to support the peso as its gross foreign reserves stand at just over $16 billion. 

 The continued slide in the peso has revived market talk the central bank may consider hiking its overnight rates or making other monetary policy moves. 

 The bank's monthly policy meeting will be held on Thursday. 

 To deter speculation in the peso before the Iraq war, the central bank hiked the reserve requirement for commercial banks to eight percent from seven percent on March 20, squeezing an estimated $224 million in liquidity from the financial system. 

 Governor Rafael Buenaventura said recently the peso's weakness was a temporary phenomenon and that hiking overnight rates not an appropriate response. 

 In July, the central bank surprised the market by cutting policy rates for the first time since March 2002. 

 The cut of 25 basis points took the overnight borrowing rate to 6.75 percent and the lending rate to 9.0 percent - their lowest levels in more than 11 years.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Focus shifts to stocks from security.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were shored
up on Monday morning by rising stock markets in the region and
some relief after the weekend passed without any militant
attacks.
    The Korean won                   was knocking at a key
resistance at 1,175 and the Taiwan dollar  reached its
strongest in a month. Korean stocks  rose to an
eight-month high and Taiwan's shares  were furthering
gains after hitting 14-month highs last week.
    Indonesia's markets were closed for the National Day
holiday, but in thin offshore deals the rupiah  was
quoted higher. Markets had sold the currency last week on
security fears after the capture of Muslim militant Hambali in
Thailand and the bombing of a Jakarta hotel earlier this month.
    The Singapore dollar        was steady, but sentiment on
the currency was bullish after some proposed changes to the
city-state's pension systems.



    Singapore's Straits Times Index        hit a 13-month high,
resuming an rally that was broken on Friday. Prime Minister Goh
Chok Tong said on Sunday that workers should expect
contributions to the national pension fund to drop to 30
percent from the current 36 percent.
    "The strengthening of the Sing dollar does not surprise me.
It has been too weak, trading close to the mid-point of the
basket for the last few months," said Peter Redward, currency
strategist with Deutsche bank.
    The Singapore dollar is managed in an undisclosed
trade-weighted band, and analysts estimate it is allowed to
move around 1.5 to 2.0 percent on either side of a mid-point.
    "We believe that based on the magnitude of the current

the relatively strong performance of the Straits Times Index
versus the S&P 500  and the low interest rate

close to the top end of the band," Redward said.
 
    JP Morgan calculated the mid-point of their U.S.

    "We would not recommend going long U.S. dollars until spot
falls below 1.7450," JP Morgan said in a report.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Down Late; Peso At New 4-Mo Low
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Philippine peso slid to a fresh four-month low Tuesday, still weighed by a failed mutiny by junior army officers over the weekend. 

 Most other regional currencies were weaker following the yen's overnight fall to a one-month low against the dollar. 

 The South Korean won was steady as corporate dollar sales offset the impact of the weaker yen, while foreign equity inflows helped lift the New Taiwan dollar, but that rise was tempered by central bankintervention. 

 The effect of the mutiny in the Philippines continued to be felt in the local currency market, with the dollar rising as high as 54.750 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System. 

 The U.S. unit trimmed gains to end at a fresh four-month closing high of PHP54.670, up from PHP54.380 Monday. 

 Earlier, Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said the monetary authority isn't selling dollars to support the weak peso Tuesday. He said the peso's slide will "not significantly" affect the country's inflation outlook. 

 Later in the session, Buenaventura said the peso is expected to recover to PHP53 to the dollar in the fourth quarter of 2002 when export earnings and investments improve. 

 He said the seasonal rise in importers' requirements for dollars and the weaker performance of regional currencies have undermined the peso. This was exacerbated by the mutiny on Sunday and also by the escape of suspected Indonesian terrorist Fathur Rohman Al-Ghozi from a Philippine jail July 14. 

 Analysts expect the central bank to defend the peso at PHP55 to the dollar. If left unchecked, the peso could move to "uncharted territory" and that would put pressure on domestic interest rates and affect the government's debt servicing, said Philip Wee, a market strategist at Singapore's DBS Bank. 

 Bank of America said the weekend mutiny "posed only a tiny threat to the government" but "may have reminded the world that political risk in Emerging Southeast Asia may be on the verge of another comeback." 

 "Perception of such risk is already important in differentiating between the markets - however, the risk is for even greater differentiation as 2004 approaches," the bank said in a research note. Both Indonesia and the Philippines will hold presidential polls next year. 

 Elsewhere, the dollar ended against the South Korean won at 1,178.7, barely changed from KRW1,178.8 Monday. 

 Exporters continued to sell dollars, but traders were reluctant to try to push the currency lower for fear the central bank might step in to support the dollar, market players said. 

 Comments by a key Bank of Korea official early Tuesday that the current dollar/won level isn't hurting exports much had little impact on the market. Traders said the remark didn't give a clear direction for the dollar's move against the won. 

 Against its Taiwan counterpart, the U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.380, down slightly from Monday's NT$34.388. Trading volume totaled US$526 million, up sharply from US$236 million in the previous session. 

 Foreign equity inflows, stimulated by a recent relaxation of rules for foreign investors, continued to put pressure on the U.S. currency, leading the central bank to intervene, though not as heavily as it has done in some recent sessions, traders said. 

 Foreign investors were net buyers of NT$2.99 billion in shares Tuesday. 

 Rising month-end dollar demand from local importers pushed the Indonesian rupiah lower despite suspected intervention by the central bank to support the local unit, dealers said. 

 The dollar ended at 8,610 rupiah, up from IDR8,530 Monday. 

 The government's official announcement not to renew the multibillion-dollar bailout program with the International Monetary Program next year had little effect on the market, as the decision was widely expected, dealers said. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7528 late in Asia, up from S$1.7480 late Monday. 

 The U.S. dollar was at 42.01 against the Thai baht, up from THB41.99 previously.

MANILA -(Dow Jones)- The Philippine Central Bank said Monday it isn't intervening in the currency market, allowing market forces to dictate the peso-dollar exchange rate after Sunday's failed rebellion by renegade soldiers.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Torn between weak US dlr and weak won.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 7 (Reuters) - Asian currencies stalled on Friday, torn between a falling dollar after U.S. President George W. Bush reinforced market opinion that a conflict in Iraq is imminent and persistent weakness in the South Korean won. 

 The U.S. dollar fell to a four-year low against the euro after Bush said diplomacy was in its final stages. He said refusing to use force to disarm Iraq would be an unacceptable risk and that he would seek a U.N. resolution authorising such action within days. 

 That helped the Singapore dollar, Thai baht and Taiwan dollar off their lows, but these currencies dithered as the won stayed near its three-month low of 1,220, which was struck in offshore deals. 

 The yen also hesitated on fears of intervention, and markets were taking few chances ahead of another U.N. inspectors' report on Iraqi compliance later on Friday. 

 David Simmonds, markets strategist with Royal Bank of Scotland, said the sudden offshore fall in the won caught players by surprise, and spurred more won selling. 

 The won was pressured by the risks from North Korea, amplified by Thursday's deployment of U.S. bombers to a Pacific island and news the North is preparing to launch a missile. 

 "It is interesting. Dollar/Asia started off pretty well bid this morning but there hasn't really been a particularly significant follow through," said Simmonds. 

 Some said the pressure on the dollar as war risks mount would be the more dominant factor for regionals. 

 "The dollar should be under more pressure. Besides the yen, peso and won, most of the Asian currencies will maintain their strength," said Thio Chin Loo, strategist with BNP Paribas. 

 SGD LOSES TO BAHT 

 The Singapore dollar came off a one-week low of 1.7380 per dollar, although analysts said it remained in the weaker half of the undisclosed trade-weighted band authorities manage it in. 

 The Thai baht followed, at a more leisurely pace, to 42.51/55 per dollar from around 42.65. 

 The cross rate showed the Singapore dollar was gradually weakening against the baht, having moved to 24.47 baht per Sing dollar from 24.65 in a week, a trend analysts have been anticipating. 

 "The Sing dollar belongs in the weak half of the policy band because of growth concerns. And, it has outperformed currencies such as the Taiwan dollar and Thai baht in the past 12 months, relative to the dollar," Simmonds said. 

 Simmonds said the similarity of Singapore's and Korea's exports also meant it competed more than others in the region for export competitiveness with the won. Thailand's robust growth and fiscal position were also giving the baht an edge, he added. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR SURPRISES 

 The Taiwan dollar surprised traders by rallying from a low of 34.72, in line with southeast Asian currencies, rather than staying weak with the won, defying market belief that the fortunes of the North Asian currencies were intertwined. 

 The won posted a 13-week closing low in onshore deals, while Korean stocks also extended a three-day losing streak. 

 The popular yen-won cross moved up to near 10.4, the highest since November 2001. 

 "A combination of negatives such as higher oil prices, a weaker economy and greater security risks in the peninsula have shifted market psychology enough for dollar/won to de-couple strongly with dollar/yen," UBS Warburg said in a report. 

 "Though the cross has displayed a strong mean reverting tendency towards 10.0, we believe the rate could go even higher under the current circumstances," it said. 

 The Philippine peso maintained a tight range as it retested the two-year low of 54.85 per dollar it struck on Thursday, with sentiment still negative after Tuesday's deadly bombings in the southern Philippines. 

 Traders suspected the central bank was intervening to provide dollars around 54.85. The central bank said on Wednesday it would provide liquidity if markets became too volatile. 

 The central bank denied intervening on Thursday, and again on Friday. But it has also been using moral suasion, asking banks to ease their dollar purchases beyond genuine needs. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR AT 0845 GMT Change on the day

title: Philippine Stocks, Peso Seen Tumbling Wed On Davao Blasts
text:
MANILA -(Dow Jones)- The Philippine peso and stocks are expected to tumble Wednesday after a bomb explosion in an international airport in Davao, a thriving southern city, aggravated the shaky security situation in the country. 

 A powerful bomb hidden in a backpack killed at least 19 and wounded about 150 people when it ripped through a crowded waiting area just outside the Davao airport on Tuesday. A U.S. missionary was among those killed. 

 Minutes after, a second bomb exploded in Tagum City, an hour's drive from Davao City. 

 "Wednesday will be a very bad day for the peso as players become wary of more violence," said a currency trader with a foreign bank in Manila. 

 The country's stock and currency markets were already closed Tuesday when the bombs exploded, but Philippine bonds immediately underperformed on news of the Davao explosions. 

 The country's EMBI+ widened seven basis points to 555 basis points over Treasurys, while its 2025 global bond lost 7/8 to 100 7/8 bid. 

 The peso recouped some of its recent losses to close at PHP54.500 to the dollar Tuesday as the market heaved a sigh of relief that the country may escape sanctions after legislators pledged to amend the country's anti-money laundering law. 

 Traders believe that the breakthrough in the talks to amend the anti-dirty money law will be offset by the latest bombing incident in the south, which could delay the dollar's pullback. 

 The stock market is also expected to take a beating Wednesday, with the Philippine Stock Exchange Index possibly moving towards its 1010-point immediate support. 

 "The bombing incident will definitely damage the country's image further and erode domestic investors confidence," says AB Capital Securities economist Jose Vistan. "The market will definitely undergo a correction now." 

 The main stock market index closed up 1.44 points, or 0.1%, at 1025.99 Tuesday, bringing its total gain to 2.6% since Feb. 27. 

 Philippine central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura refused to project the fallout on the peso of the bombings. "We will have to see what happens," he told Dow Jones Newswires. 

 Asked if the central bank would intervene to support the peso, Buenaventura replied: "We will see." 

Currency watchers are certain the peso is in for a hammering on worsening security situation. The Davao blasts just came in days after a car bomb exploded in another airport in Mindanao at the height of the fighting between Muslim rebels and the military. 

 "We're talking of a very big city and a vital facility such as an airport. It will definitely create a lot of pressure on the peso," said Roland Avante, treasurer with Chinatrust Commercial Bank (Philippines) Inc. 

 Avante said a possible intervention by the central bank should prevent the dollar from hitting key level PHP55. The peso has been lingering at its 25-month low in recent days. 

 The stock market is also expected to suffer. 

 The 30-company Philippine Stock Exchange composite index closed 1.44 points higher Tuesday at 1025.99, adding to the cumulative gain of 24.28 points during the last three days. 

 "Expect the index to test the 1000 support," said Jonathan Ravelas, chief strategist with Banco de Oro Universal Bank. "This is really bad." 

 Other traders believe this development won't trigger a substantial decline because most investors have been on the sidelines anyway. 

 "There will be some selling but I don't think the 1,000 support will be breached. There are very few buyers in the market in the first place," said Eagle Equities president Joseph Roxas. 

 Over the last few months, the local financial market has been battered by a string of bad news including the threats of war in Iraq, a further widening of the government's budget deficit and a possible sanction by the Paris-based Financial Action Task Force against money laundering. 

 -By Ditas Lopez and Cris Larano, Dow Jones Newswires; 63-9185006312; ditas.lopez@dowjones.com

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Won Ends Winning Streak
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- -Asian currencies were hemmed in within tight ranges Wednesday with few leads to spur market players into new positions as the major units, especially the dollar/yen, gave limited guidance. 

 Participants were also reluctant to make any strong bets ahead of the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday in the U.S., starting Thursday. 

 The South Korean won, the Philippine peso and the New Taiwan dollar were slightly weaker; the Singapore dollar and the Thai baht were little changed; while the Indonesian rupiah was modestly higher. 

 "It's been rather rangey. People are not taking strong positions either side (of the dollar versus regional currency trades) as the dollar/yen is not doing much," said a trader at a European bank in Singapore. 

 There were small amounts of buying but they weren't sufficient for the currency pairs to break out of their narrow trading bands, he added. 

 The South Korean won ended a four-day winning streak, hurt by dollar demand from local importers, which helped the U.S. currency erase early losses, traders said. 

 The dollar closed at 1,207.6 won, marginally up from KRW1,206.1 Tuesday. 

 The dollar initially headed south, hitting a trough of KRW1,202.5 as market players sold the currency following continued foreign buying of local shares. 

 But importers started buying dollars later in the session, which helped the U.S. currency reverse track to rise to an intraday high of KRW1,207.9. 

 "The market was directionless Wednesday. Local importers' (won) selling and exporters' (won) buying largely affected the market without any big market-moving factors," said a trader at Bank of America. 

 Meanwhile, the New Taiwan dollar was softer as offshore traders took profits on long positions that they had held for some time, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.820, up from NT$34.773 Tuesday, after trading between NT$34.735 and NT$34.823. 

 Trading volume was sharply higher at US$512.5 million, compared with US$285 million in the previous session. 

 In the Philippines, suspicion that the Philippine central bank has been intervening to support the peso kept many banks wary of further accumulating dollars, traders said. 

 The peso earlier this week sank to a new 16-month low on concerns about the country's swelling budget deficit. 

 The dollar ended at 53.600 on the Philippine Dealing System, marginally up from PHP53.590 Tuesday, after moving between PHP53.550 and PHP53.600. Trading volume nearly halved to $62.5 million from $113 million in the previous session. 

 Several traders said the central bank probably sold around $20 million to $30 million worth of dollars at PHP53.60 Wednesday. The central bank couldn't immediately be reached for comment. 

 The market is awaiting third-quarter domestic product data, scheduled to be issued at 0200 GMT Thursday. Many economists expect the pace of on-year growth to have slowed to around 3.9% in the third quarter, from 4.5% in the second. 

 The Indonesian rupiah recovered from initial losses as state banks were suspected to have sold dollars on behalf of the central bank to support the local currency. 

 The dollar ended the Asian trading day at IDR8,975, down from IDR8,990 Tuesday. 

 Earlier, the dollar rose to an intraday high of IDR9,010 as interbank players covered short dollar positions ahead of the end of the month. 

 Bank Indonesia was then believed to have sold dollars to cap the U.S. unit's rise, effectively dragging it down below the psychologically-important IDR9,000 level, dealers said. 

 Some foreign banks also sold dollars, likely on behalf of investors that were buying assets held by the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency and needed the local currency for payment, they added. 

 The Singapore dollar was fairly steady toward the end of the Asian trading day, but gained ground during the European session. 

 As of 1040 GMT the U.S. currency was quoted around S$1.7652, down from S$1.7672 late Tuesday and S1.7674 near the end of the Asian session. 

 For most of the time, the local dollar was following the yen's gyrations against the dollar, traders said. 

 Some market participants said the Singapore dollar may be flirting with the higher end of the Monetary Authority of Singapore's policy band, within which it guides the local dollar. 

 "U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar remained well bid despite U.S. dollar's overnight weakness, perhaps reflecting the wide recognition that SGD (Singapore dollar) is approaching the extremely strong portion of the existing trading band," Bank of America said in a research note Wednesday. 

 The Thai baht was hardly changed at THB42.44 at the close of Asian trading hours, from THB43.42 Tuesday. It was trapped in a tight THB43.38-THB43.44 band during the session. 

 Trading volume was extremely thin as most offshore players were on the sidelines ahead of key economic data to be announced in Europe and the U.S. overnight, and the U.S, Thanksgiving holiday that starts Thursday. 

 Economic growth projections for the year from the Finance Ministry earlier Wednesday had little impact on the market as they were within the 4.5% to 5% range it had forecast earlier. 

 The ministry said it expects 2002 GDP growth of 4.8%, as a strong domestic economy pushed third-quarter growth to an estimated 5.4% over the year-ago period. 

 GDP growth in the fourth quarter is estimated at 4.8%, said Wisudhi Srisuphan, director-general of the ministry's Fiscal Policy Office.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Speculation steps up pressure.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Speculative buying of dollars in the forward markets on Friday piled pressure on Asian currencies already beset by worries over growth, foreign investor aversion and a dithering yen. 

 Many regionals hit multi-month lows, although central bank intervention helped take the heat off the sliding Taiwan dollar and Korean won. 

 A rally on Wall Street gave the dollar some early bounce, as did adjustments ahead of market holidays in the United States, Hong Kong and Japan on Monday. 

 But profit-booking dollar sales helped regionals off their lows, even though the yen hit four-month lows against the dollar after the Bank of Japan left monetary policy unchanged. 

 "Understandably there is some position-squaring as people close out before the weekend," said Tim Fallowfield, head of currency trading at ING Barings. 

 And speculative buying had increased in recent sessions, taking Asian regionals further down, he said. 

 "For a month now, we've been seeing domestic oil companies buying dollars aggressively and foreign players take investments out. And now, speculative money too has come into these currency markets," Fallowfield said. 

 The speculation was largely in the non-deliverable forwards. Longer-tenor forwards on the Taiwan dollar reversed to positive on the pressure, while in Thailand one-year swap points in the offshore market surged to 74/77 points from a low of 50 on Thursday. 

 Traders said the heaviest intervention was seen in the Taiwan dollar, which hit an intra-day low of 35.22 while catching up with losses in other regionals after a holiday on Thursday, amid weak stocks and foreigners selling equities. 

 "In the near-term, the risks are still for the pair (US dollar-Taiwan dollar) to go up but the pair has to break 35.30, which is expected to be another strong resistance, in order to move further higher," Bank of America said in its market note. 

Central bank support for the Philippine peso was less obvious. Though it came marginally off an intra-day low of 52.855, traders merely suspected some covert intervention. 

 Morgan Stanley's downgrade of Philippines' external debt to underperform, announced on Friday, could have played a part in driving the peso down, traders said. 

 STOCKS HIT THAI BAHT 

 A two percent fall in Thai stocks depressed the Thai baht , leading markets to ignore recent upgrades in economists' growth outlooks and rating agency Fitch's upgrading of its outlook for Thailand to positive this week. 

 It fell to a six-month low of 43.88 in morning deals, and was unable to move too far away from there through afternoon trade. 

 The Singapore dollar hit an early low of 1.7951, a level last seen four months ago, before recovering slightly on suspected unwinding of some option contracts and spent the day in a dull range 

 Thursday's startling drop in Singapore's third quarter GDP started the push against the currency, and raised concerns that other regional economies may show similar deceleration. 

 The Korean won was volatile, hitting a five-month low of 1,266 per dollar before a central bank statement expressing worry at the slide helped it recoup some of its losses. 

 The weak yen weighed on the won, although it was supported by speculation that the inflows from a sale of a $230 million stake in state-run Korea Tobacco and Ginseng Corp through global depositary receipts had hit the market. 

 "Sentiment on won is likely to remain negative in the near-term, given the risk aversion in the financial markets. The dollar could test 1280 level in the near-term," Bank of America said, recommending long dollar positions against the won. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR AT 0900 GMT Change on the day

title: WRAP:Philippines In  FX  Swap Pact Talks With China, Korea
text:
MANILA -(Dow Jones)- The Philippines is in talks with South Korea and China for bilateral currency swap arrangements to bolster its dollar buffer against future financial market shocks, a senior Manila monetary official said Monday. 

 The official, who asked not to be named, said the pact with South Korea should be completed by the end of May. 

 "This is an additional arsenal that we can depend on but we are still finalizing the amounts," said the official, adding that swap lines would likely be under $3 billion each. 

 Last July, the Philippines concluded a bilateral swap agreement with Japan, giving it a potential $3 billion credit line to defend the peso if it comes under speculative attack. 

 The swap arrangements are part of a broader effort by some Southeast Asian nations to forge similar pacts with the region's strongest economies: Japan, South Korea and China. 

 Two years ago at a meeting in Chiang Mai, Thailand, the 10-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or Asean, launched the currency-protection initiative to strengthen economic and financial cooperation in the region. 

 Kwon Tae-shin, director general of the international finance bureau at South Korea's Ministry of Finance and Economy, said talks have been ongoing with the Philippines for five or six months regarding the swap arrangement. 

 The monetary official said talks with China for a timetable to open negotiations are underway. 

 Finance ministers from Asean and the so-called "plus three" group are scheduled to hold a meeting next weekend in Myanmar. 

 Analysts said the swap arrangement shouldn't impact on South Korea's foreign exchange market or economy. 

 "Frankly, there will be no impact on the current economy," said Oh Suktae, an economist at Citibank in Seoul. "The economic relationship with the Philippines isn't that deep. We cannot say that it is small, but it is not significantly big enough to effect the overall picture." 

 Oh added that the move could be a step toward bigger agreements with all Asian nations, however. 


   Defending The Peso If Renewed Attack



For the Philippines, swap lines should enable the central bank to
defend the peso without depleting currency reserves that are already
among the lowest in the region. Gross international reserves totaled
$16.3 billion at the end of February, compared with double that in
Malaysia.



Under the swap scheme with Japan, the central bank may borrow dollars
in exchange for pesos as collateral to meet unusually heavy demand for
dollars on the peso market.



The monetary official noted that before funds can be disbursed from
the facility approval must be given by the International Monetary Fund
in the form of a "seal of good housekeeping." As matters stand, the
Philippines doesn't have a loan program with the IMF, but economic and
financial targets are periodically reviewed by the Fund in a monitoring
program.



Much further down the road, bilateral agreements may eventually be
signed between the Philippines and other Asean countries, such as
Malaysia, the official said.



The swap agreement with Japan hasn't been utilized, with the
Philippines using its existing reserves in recent intervention to quell
speculative pressure on the peso.



After spending around $2 billion in an ultimately futile defense of
the peso shortly after the outbreak of Asia's 1997-1998 financial
crisis, Manila's monetary managers have generally used intervention as a
last resort.



Even so, expanding the swap lines to cover commitments from South
Korea and China are important defenses against any future speculative
attacks on the peso.



For the past several months, however, improving economic, financial
and political fundamentals have kept the peso on an even keel against
the dollar of between PHP51 to PHP52.



The dollar averaged PHP51.139 in early trading Thursday.



-By Amethyst Ma and Laura Pohl, Dow Jones Newswires; 632-885-0288;
alastair.mcindoe@dowjones.com

crisis, Manila's monetary managers have generally used intervention as a
last resort.

Korea and China are important defenses against any future speculative
attacks on the peso.



For the past several months, however, improving economic, financial
and political fundamentals have kept the peso on an even keel against
the dollar of between PHP51 to PHP52.

title: Asia Markets -  Currencies , stocks easier on air strikes.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Asian currencies and stocks 

 eased on Monday following the overnight air strikes against 

 Afghanistan by the United States and Britain in retaliation for 

 the September 11 attacks on New York and Washington. 

     The bombing and missile strikes, which may mark the 

 begining of a long military campaign, were well-anticipated but 

 still raised concerns over economic and political implications 

 and fallout. 

     The markets slipped amid those concerns but as the strikes 

 lacked a shock element and Tokyo was closed for a national 

 holiday, the downside was limited. 

     "The fact that the military response has started was not a 

 major surprise and then Tokyo is out....the markets are much 

 quieter," said David Simmonds, Salmon Smith Barney's regional 

currency strategist. 

     The yen traded in a narrow range around the 120 mark as 

 players marked the dollar down, reflecting their reluctance to 

 take positions amid the uncertainty. 

     Major Asian equity markets dipped with Hong Kong's Heng 

 Seng down 2.7 percent by midday, Seoul's KOSPI ending off 1.15 

 percent and Taiwan's TAIEX down 1.82 percent. 

     AUTHORITIES ON ALERT 

     Even more cautious than the market players were the 

 region's central banks, some of whom announced their intention 

 to step into the market to quell any panic. 

     The Bank of Korea was the first to issue a warning it would 

intervene to stem excessive volatility in the currency  market. 

 Taiwan's cabinet pledged support to its stock market through 

 its stabilisation funds. 

     But while the North Asian central banks were more concerned 

 about the economic implications, analysts said authorities in 

 Indonesia and the Philippines may be more concerned about the 

 political fall out of the U.S.-led operation "Enduring 

 Freedom". 

     The Indonesian rupiah fell through the 10,000 mark to a 

 10-week low of 10,550 as radical Islamic groups in Jakarta 

 threatened to hunt foreigners and destroy foreign targets. 

     Bank Indonesia said it planned to intervene in the foreign 

 exchange market but would avoid hiking interest rates to prop 

 up the rupiah. 

     Dealers in Jakarta earlier said Bank Indonesia sold around 

 $2-3 million through brokers at the 10,300/10,350 level. 

     VULNERABLE CURRENCIES

     Analysts said similar worries would dominate trade in the 

 Philippines. The peso fell just shy of the 51.60 per dollar 

 level where the central bank was expected to intervene. 

Currency vulnerability for both Indonesia and Philippines

 will make the much-needed lowering of key interest rates 

 difficult. 

     The Philippines had cut its key overnight rate by 25 

 basis-points only last week hoping for inflationary pressure to 

 ease and the peso to stabilise around 50-51 range by the end of 

 the year. 

 The key overnight borrowing rate now stands at 8.75 percent 

 and lending rate at 11 percent.

title: Emerging  FX  - Mixed bag, yen and c.banks watched.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were a 

 mixed bag in late trade on Wednesday with the market 

 wrongfooted by intervention from Japan and by local central 

 banks. 

     The regionals had followed the yen firmer early but turned 

 tail when the Bank of Japan stepped in to sell yen on at least 

 two occasions lifting the dollar away from the 117.00 level. 

     This is the second time this week the BOJ intervened to 

 stem the yen's rapid appreciation. However, the action was only 

 a partial success with the dollar unable even to hold 118.00 

 yen. 

     The regional currencies also had to weather central bank

intervention of their own. 

     In the Philippines, the central bank was rumoured to have 

 aggressively sold U.S. dollars to countered losses in the peso 

 caused by demand for the U.S. currency to settle maturing deals 

 in the non-deliverable forward market. 

 The Indonesian central bank also offered dollars to curb 

 the rupiah's slide which resulted from active dollar demand 

 from local banks and companies. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar drifted below the key 1.7400 market after 

 the BOJ intervention prompted dealers to mark the dollar higher 

 and some players to cover short positions. 

 Dealers said there was no sign of intervention from the 

Monetary Authority of Singapore so far, but there was talk the 

 MAS has left dollar buying orders open at 1.7340. 

 Charts show the Sing dollar is trading around its 14-day 

 moving average of 1.7419, and also that there is a gap up to 

 1.7500 left after last week's plane attacks which the currency

 was likely to fill sooner or later. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht was a touch firmer at 44.15, but still locked in a 

 tight range of 44.10-44.24 after gains inspired by foreign 

 stock buying were countered by exporter dollar offers above 

 44.20. 

     Foreign investors had been net buyers of Thai stocks since 

 last Thursday. 

     On the macro front, central bank chief economist Atchana 

 Waiquamdee said the volatile world political and economic 

 situation may leave Thailand with lower than expected economic 

 growth in 2002. 

 "If the world situation persists and worsens, we could see 

 a technical recession in 2002, when the economy contracts for 

 two consecutive quarters," she said. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah briefly dropped below 9,700 for the first time 

 since August 2 on the back of aggressive dollar buying from 

 local banks and companies, including one oil importer. 

 But the currency crawled off its lows after Bank Indonesia 

 sold the dollar at around 9,700 and some local firms took 

 profits on the dollar. 

 BI had said earlier on Wednesday that it was considering 

intervening in the foreign exchange market to prop up the 

 rupiah. But dealers said the amount of its dollar sales was 

 small. 

 Deputy central bank governor Miranda Goeltrom also told 

 Reuters there was a "likelihood" that benchmark SBI interest 

 rates would fall further. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso closed lower at 51.40 to the dollar in the onshore 

 market against 51.370 on Tuesday despite central bank

 dollar-selling intervention. 

     Market players needed the U.S. dollar to settle their deals 

 in the NDF market. 

     Dealers in Manila said central bank dollar sales accounted 

 for almost half of the total market turnover on Wednesday which 

 was around $73.50 million. However, the central bank later said 

 they had not intervened. 

Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said separately 

 he was quite comfortable with the current level of the peso.

the central bank and the yen's resilience provided support for



the local currency.



    The won closed at 1,296.50 to the dollar against the



Tuesday's close of 1,296.9.



    The central bank on Wednesday cut its target for the



short-term call rate by 50 basis points to 4.00 percent,



joining a global monetary easing to minimise impacts from U.S.



attacks on the world economy.

title: UPDATE 1-Arroyo after visiting Mahathir - "I'm like that".
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 9 (Reuters) - Philippine President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo wound up a three-day visit to Malaysia in a fighting mood on Thursday, saying she was ready to step up action against speculators, crime syndicates and Abu Sayyaf rebels. 

 With a truce signed with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) packed in her bags, along with an agreement with Malaysia to fight piracy in the seas, Arroyo's briefing to reporters at the end of her maiden state visit was full of vim. 

 The petite 55-year-old saw traces of herself in the "plain talk and common-sense" of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, the last of a generation of southeast Asian strongmen. 

 "I'm much like that too," said Arroyo, whose eight months in charge of the sometimes unruly Philippine democracy contrasts with Mahathir's 20-year grip on power. 

 There will be no ransom negotiations with the Abu Sayyaf, Arroyo said. "That's ruled out. Negotiating to come into the fold of the law, that's all right," she said. 

 The Abu Sayyaf, which is holding more than 20 hostages, including Americans, is now the only organised group still fighting in the mostly Muslim southern Philippines after the truce signed by the MILF in Kuala Lumpur this week. 

 "With the Abu Sayyaf the idea is to stop giving in," Arroyo said. Earlier this week the Philippine army said it aimed to remove the threat from Abu Sayyaf kidnappers by November. 

 The rebels are holding two American missionaries and claim to have killed a third American. 

 Arroyo said the tough message was also getting through to Manila's crime syndicates as law enforcement agencies were solving crimes faster than they did under the rule of her predecessor, Joseph Estrada. 

 Estrada is currently facing corruption charges and his alleged links to crime syndicates was a factor in his downfall in January. 

 SPECULATORS BEWARE 

 Arroyo also had a warning for currency speculators. 

 Asked whether the Philippines might resort to fixing its exchange rate or imposing capital controls, as Mahathir had done at the height of the currency crisis in 1998, she said: "I can't rule that out. I don't envision it, but I don't rule it out." 

 Arroyo has urged her central bank to restore the peso to 50 per dollar by the year end and protect its value. 

 But she said the central bank remained independent to run policy and she was not giving it orders. 

 The peso was trading around 53 to the dollar on Thursday, and has depreciated by over four percent since the start of the year. 

 Arroyo said she would be reluctant to impose capital controls, but would keep her options open. 

 "I'm not ruling out anything, a la Mahahtir," Arroyo said, though soon after she spoke Finance Secretary Jose Camacho said the Philippines was committed to free trading of the peso. 

 Arroyo said plans were on track to raise seven billion pesos from privatisations, and that sales of state-owned prime real estate could boost revenues. 

 While admiring Mahathir's handling of the financial crisis three years ago, Arroyo refused to become embroiled in the controversy over the sacking and jailing of Anwar Ibrahim, Mahathir's former deputy and finance minister. 

 Estrada had upset Mahathir by meeting Anwar's wife, Wan Azizah Wan Ismail, but Arroyo said the Philippines maintained a policy of non-intervention and she would not make the same mistake if Anwar's wife sought a meeting. 

 "Being a guest of the prime minister, if he so much as hinted he would not be happy, I would not got through with it." 

 Arroyo, who came to power following street demonstrations and backing from the military, hinted she aimed to win the presidency through the ballot box next time. 

 "I eligible," she answered when asked if she planned to run in 2004.

currencies due partly to the financial crisis in Argentina, as well as
from domestic factors.

title: Emerging  FX -Yen losses hurt, politics grip rupiah.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 28 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were caught in the yen's downdraft late on Monday, which provided players with an excuse to add to their long dollar positions, dealers said. 

 The euro strengthened at the expense of the yen after talk of central bank intervention kept investors on alert in a market thinned by holidays in London and New York. 

 Political concerns also added to the region's woes. Indonesian President Abdurrahman Wahid warned in a nationally televised speech that any attempts to oust him would break Southeast Asia's most populous country apart. 

 In Thailand, the interest rate tussle between the government and central bank dragged on. A local newspaper reported that the government was preparing to order the central bank to force up deposit rates by 1.5 percentage points to spur spending. 

 But Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra denied the report, saying he had never ordered the central bank to do so. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah wilted past 11,500, briefly hitting one-month lows of 11,720, as Indonesia's leadership crisis dragged on. 

 The market showed little reaction to President Wahid's comments, which stopped short of carrying out his threat to declare a state of emergency. 

 Wahid is scrambling to save his presidency as parliament is set to meet on Wednesday to decide whether to press ahead with a special impeachment session of the top legislative body. 

 Jakarta dealers said the rupiah escaped further losses because local corporates had little appetite for dollars around these levels and state banks were also spotted selling dollars around 11,650. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht settled in a well-worn 45.56-45.62 range, caught between buying by government-linked exporters and selling from offshore banks, Bangkok dealers said. 

 The continuing battle between the government and central bank over interest rates weighed on sentiment. 

 Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said the government would decide on the best level for interest rates after the central bank reports on its policy review on June 4. 

 Deposit rates currently stand at around two to three percent, with lending rates at seven to eight percent. Thai banks are unwilling to lend given their mountain of non-performing loans. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar struggled in the wake of poor economic data, hitting 32-month lows of 34.50 as the central bank let up its usual dogged defence in late trade. 

 Singapore dealers said the central bank sold up to $1.5 billion to slow the currency's fall, beginning its intervention early in the session around 33.495. But it later let the local dollar go in the face of heavy demand for dollars and the disappointing economic data. 

 After the close, the bank said it would enter the market to "maintain order" if necessary, attributing the local dollar's sharp fall to "untrue rumours". 

 While it had been bracing for bad news, the market was still glum over first quarter gross domestic product data issued after the close on Friday. The economy grew by a mere 1.06 percent on year, against forecasts of 3.25 percent. 

 The top economic planning agency said earlier in the day the economy slowed in April with no recovery in sight. Its index of leading indicators in April slipped 0.5 percent on month to 93.3. 

 Looking ahead, the Taiwan dollar could see some relief as the market is heavily long of dollars. Charts showed dollar/Taiwan looking hugely overbought, with a 14-day relative strength index reading of 98. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso dipped against Friday's 50.50 close, though it was off its day's low of 50.96. Local corporates seeking to repay foreign debt bought the dollar on dips towards 50.60. 

 Manila dealers said it was also weighed by ongoing political uncertainty coupled with weekend news of gunmen believed to be Muslim rebels seizing 20 people in a tourist resort in the southern Philippines. 

 The market was also eyeing a special Congressional session to debate a key power reform bill, viewed as a litmus test of the government's commitment to reform. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR The Sing dollar was in limbo, stuck in a tight 1.8080-1.8118 range over the course of the day, but dealers said the mood was hurt by growing tension in Indonesia and the Philippines. 

 Local banks and U.S. names were offering the dollar at around 1.8110, stirring jitters about possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, which admitted it had intervened in the market earlier this month to support the Sing dollar. 

 "At any rate, people want to buy the dollar with all sorts of reasons from the Philippines, Indonesia to Taiwan, but they can't because of intervention fears," a European bank dealer said. 

 Given such fears, dealers expected the Sing dollar was unlikely to weaken beyond 1.8180 in the near term. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won closed near the top end of its Monday trading range of 1,293.2-1,298.0 despite the yen's retreat, buoyed by exporter dollar offers and some fund inflows. 

 But the upside was capped amid caution ahead of major economic data this week, including April industrial output on Tuesday and the May consumer price index on Thursday. 

 Economists polled by Reuters forecast industrial output fell 0.6 percent last month from March because of dwindling exports and sluggish domestic demand. 

 Inflation is expected to be tame due to seasonal factors. 

 "We expect negative month-on-month headline inflation for the first time this year. Declines in fruit and heating oil prices are likely to be the main course," Salomon Smith Barney said. 

 "Quite stable CPI figures should be favourable to the bond market. But headline inflation tends to be modest in May because of the seasonal stabilization in agricultural food prices," the bank said in a report.

title: Emerging  FX  - Bounce back as yen jawboning helps.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 5 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were steadier in late trade on Thursday with a rebound in the yen providing some breathing space. 

 The yen traded at its highest level this week, hovering around 124.00 per dollar after Japanese officials made concerted efforts to talk it up. 

 It hit a two-and-a-half year low of 126.84 per dollar on Monday and brought down with it regional currencies amid concerns Japan's political and policy gridlock would make it difficult to snap out of its economic troubles. 

 Some analysts said recent declines in the regional currencies were excessive and there should be some dollar correction soon, although a meaningful turnaround might not take place until the second half of this year. 

 "(The decline) in March had been overdone and obviously was precipitated by the dollar/yen effects," said Arthur Woo, economist at HSBC. 

 "But our house's view is that this will eventually reverse probably not immediately but toward the second half of the year when the relief will come for most of the currencies in the region," he said. 

 The fact that recent hefty losses in regional currencies have raised the hackles of Asian central banks also dampened dollar demand a bit. 

 Korea said aggressive measures were needed to stabilise currency markets, Thailand implicitly confirmed it did intervene to stave off baht volatility and the Philippines said the peso would not drop to 52 per dollar. 

 Markets in Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong were closed for a one-day holiday, keeping overall activity rather subdued. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH The rupiah got little solace, hovering at just above three-week lows of 10,710 in relatively thin trading. 

 Jakarta dealers attributed the fall to solid corporate demand for the U.S. dollar with auto manufacturing companies, chemical and oil firms and state-owned enterprises snapping up an estimated $30 million in total. 

 Dealers said Bank Indonesia offered cold comfort to bears as its sales of around $10-15 million in the morning from 10,700 to 10,680 failed to support the downside. They added the rupiah should breach immediate support of 10,710 in the not too distant future as companies and banks have more appetite for the U.S. dollar. 

 Analysts said the higher SBI rates at the central bank's weekly auction reflected the authorities' effort to drain liquidity from the market and hence indirectly discourage the dollar buying. The rate on one-month SBIs rose to 15.79 percent from 15.58 percent at Wednesday's auction. 

 They added hopes for the IMF to approve Indonesia's reform programme and disburse a stalled $400 million loan would remove a key risk element for the rupiah. 

 A mission from the IMF will visit Jakarta as early as next week to review Indonesia's programme, a Japanese government official said. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht trod water cautiously, caught between strong corporate demand for the dollar and fears of central bank intervention. 

 The central bank said it had dealt with the baht's recent weakness, using both spot and forward market mechanisms. 

 The currency also drew mild support from news Thailand had posted a trade surplus of about $700 million in March. 

 "But in the immediate term, the baht's direction would depend largely on the yen. If the yen moves toward 122-123, for example, the baht's upmove could be steep because the market is excessively long of the dollar," said a Singapore dealer. 

 Baht funding costs offshore eased, with the one-month forward rate dipping to 35/65 satang per dollar from 60/70 satang in the morning. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR The Sing dollar tracked the higher yen and hit session highs of 1.8060, repairing most of the damage done by Monday's fall to decade lows of 1.8230. 

 Some cited speculation of capital inflows on talk a planned sale of Singapore's number two cellular operator Mobile One was attracting foreign operators. 

 Industry sources said companies expressing interest in M1 included Britain's Vodafone Group and Australia's Telestra Corp . 

 They estimate M1, a mobile phone arm of Keppel Telecommunications and Transportation , could be valued at between S$2-3 billion. 

 But dealers said the rise would be short-lived as banks and companies were looking to buy dollars on dips at around 1.8050. Analysts are also less sanguine about the outlook of the Sing dollar given slowing electronics exports and the deteriorating economic situation overall. 

 Salomon Smith Barney cut its three-month Sing dollar forecast to S$1.83 from S$1.74. 

 The government is due to release a revised forecast for growth in 2001 and a preliminary first quarter growth figure on April 10. The government currently estimates the economy would grow 5-7 percent in 2001. 

 Salomon downgraded Singapore's growth forecast for 2001 to 5.0 percent from 5.3 percent. Analysts said lower-than-expected figures would certainly bring the dollar/Sing back to above 1.8150. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso touched a low of 50.29 before finishing onshore trading little changed from its Wednesday close of 50.16. 

 Dealers in Manila said the peso traded in a tight range for most of the day helped by a steadier baht and a firmer yen. But the upside was capped by reluctance to unwind dollar longs on wariness about the near-term regional outlook. 

 The central bank said it was not in the market to support the peso and predicted the currency would not fall to 52 per dollar, though it saw volatility for the next two to three months. 

 It central bank decided not to cut overnight interest rates at its weekly policy meeting despite flat inflation growth from February to March. March inflation was an expected 6.7 percent. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 No trading was reported in the Taiwan dollar offshore non-deliverable forward market with financial markets in Taipei closed for the Ching Ming holiday. Trade will resume on Friday. 

 Dealers in Singapore said one-month NDFs were steady at 0.130/150 and three-month at 0.330/375. 

 The Taiwan dollar on Wednesday closed at a 13-week low of 32.979 against the U.S. dollar, from Tuesday's 32.90. 

 Dealers said the Taiwan dollar's direction on Friday would depend on overnight movements in the yen and U.S. equity markets. 

 Any turn of events in the continuing row between China and the U.S. over a U.S. spy plane and its detained air crew would also have an impact on sentiment. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The Korean won was bid higher in thin offshore markets with Korea's financial markets closed for a holiday. 

 Offshore dealers expected the won to recoup some lost ground when the market reopened due to a stronger yen and the central bank's remarks. 

 The central bank said in a statement on Thursday that aggressive measures were needed to stabilise the won. 

 The currency ended at a fresh 30-month low of 1,365.20 per dollar on Wednesday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed As Peso Remains At Center Stage
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 


   HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- The Philippines peso remained at center stage
in Asian currency trading Friday as President Joseph Estrada's
political troubles pushed it to new lows.


 Once again, the peso's troubles pulled down currencies in neighboring Southeast Asian markets, with the Indonesian rupiah and Thai baht falling in sympathy. The Singapore dollar was weaker much of the session but edged up late in the day. 

 The New Taiwan dollar also fell after a government decision to halt work on the island's fourth, and controversial, nuclear power plant. 

 On the peso, Rebecca Patterson, currency strategist with JP Morgan, said: "Our yearend target (for the U.S. dollar) has been THB52.00, but the risks to this target are getting larger by the minute." 

 The U.S. dollar was trading at PHP51.07 late Friday, up from PHP50.34 Thursday, having hit a high of PHP51.30 earlier in the day. 

 Dealers say they had been on the lookout for supportive intervention from the Philippines central bank, but none materialized. 

 And none may in the works, judging by central bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura's comment that "monetary tools shouldn't be used to address non-monetary problems." 

 "It leaves one wondering what they're up to," said Patterson, adding that market watchers are still expecting action from the monetary authority, if only to control the move in the currency, rather than to stop it. 

 The peso's plunge spelt trouble for the other Southeast Asian currencies as well. The Thai baht was trading at THB43.67 to the U.S. dollar late in the day, putting the U.S. unit up a touch from THB43.665 late Thursday. 

 JP Morgan's Patterson said so long as the peso is in trouble it will be difficult for the baht to change direction. But she added there's been some decent two-way flow in the baht, and it's not under the same pressure as the peso. 

 She said the U.S. currency could get up to THB45.00, although in far less dramatic fashion than the fall of the peso. 

 Against the Indonesian rupiah, the U.S. dollar moved up to IDR9,050, compared with IDR9,030 late last session. Against the Singapore dollar, it was trading slightly lower at S$1.7524, from S$1.7540. 

 Further north, the Taiwanese currency was having some trouble Friday after the ruling Democratic People's Party said it would stop construction on a fourth nuclear power plant in Taiwan. 

 The move has "revived concerns about political infighting between the KMT and the DPP," said Chi Lo, regional economist with Standard Chartered Bank, adding "with the scrapping of the plan, the battle is over but not the war." 

 Against the island's currency, the U.S. dollar was trading at NT$32.135 late Friday, up from NT$32.09 late last session. 

 The Korean won was up marginally, meanwhile, with the U.S. dollar trading at KRW1,134.8, compared with KRW1,136.5 late last session.

title: Philippines  Buenaventura: Ctrl Bk Not  Intervening
text:
MANILA -(Dow Jones)- Philippine Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said Thursday the central bank wasn't intervening in the currency market when the peso hit a new record low of 50.30 pesos to a dollar in early trading. 

 0443GMT 

 Buenaventura said the central bank will issue a statement later Thursday, but he declined to elaborate on what its contents will be. 

 The statement, however, may well be connected to earlier comments made central bank Deputy Governor Alberto Reyes that the central bank will require all foreign exchange corporations to submit documents detailing all their currency transactions over $10,000, in a move aimed at quelling speculation on the currency market and as a measure to combat money laundering. 

 Reyes said the move applies to all foreign exchange corporations and the units and affiliates of banks. 

 He said "speculative activity" on the currency market has pressured the peso and the measures should curb this. 

 -By Ditas Lopez, Dow Jones Newswires; 632-885-0288; ditas.lopez@dowjones.com

text:
MANILA -(Dow Jones)- The Philippine Central Bank said it isn't intervening to support the peso, which fell Tuesday to a record low against the dollar of PHP49.10. 

 Buenaventura, talking briefly to reporters, attributed the peso's latest losses to the weakness in regional currencies. 

 Asked if the central bank is planning further measures to support the peso, he replied: "We might do something." 

 Traders said continuing concerns over the political crisis triggered by corruption allegations against President Joseph Estrada are pressuring the peso.

title: Philippines  fin min says c.bank  intervened  in mkt.
text:
MANILA, Oct 16 (Reuters) - The Philippines central bank has again intervened in the foreign exchange market on Monday, finance secretary Jose Pardo said. 

 When asked how much dollar liquidity the bank supplied, he said "not much." 

 At 0334 GMT the peso was quoted at 48.73/78, after earlier slumping to a new record low of 49.00 to the dollar. 

 Pardo, a member of the central bank's monetary policy board which was meeting again on Monday, said the peso's slide was just an "emotional reaction," by the market, describing the central bank's action as "justified intervention of sorts." 

 "It's (the intervention) temporary..just to calm (the market). 

 The bank has consistently pumped dollars into the forex market recently in order to try to stem excessive foreign exchange volatility.

title: Philippines  c.bank says no  intervention  on Monday.
text:
MANILA, Oct 9 (Reuters) - Philippines central bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said the bank stayed out of the market on Monday even as the peso slumped against the dollar once more. 

 "I don't think so..the peso is just tracking the regionals," he said, replying to a query if the bank had provided dollar liquidity. 

 The bank has provided liquidity a number of times in the past few weeks, so as to stem excessive moves in the exchange rate. 

 At 0800 GMT the peso closed at 46.550 having touched a low of 46.555 during the day, nor far off its all-time low of 46.61 on October 4. The currency ended Friday at 46.395.

title: Emerging  FX -Mixed but jittery on oil price, stocks.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Asian currencies turned 

 mixed after an easier start amid continued worries over rising 

 oil prices and on fears of capital outflows from local stock 

 markets. 

     "Given the moves in the equity markets overnight and the 

 oil prices pushing up higher, we are likely to see weakeness 

 across the boards today," said Rebecca Patterson, regional 

currency strategist at J.P. Morgan. 

     Patterson said the downside for some of the regionals could 

 be limited but only on fears of intervention by authorities. 

     On Monday largely ignored encouraging data released by some 

 of the countries. 

     "What we are seeing today is very sentiment driven market 

 and if there are what the market perceives as negative events 

 tend to get more magnified and events that could be taken as 

 positive are ignored," a dealer at a European bank said. 

 The euro struggled to keep afloat a touch above its 

 Monday's life low, but dealers see high chance of the currency

 testing another trough below $0.8500 in near term. 

 The yen was hovered close to 107 to the dollar after 

 Dallas Fed President McTeer's said he sees little risk of U.S. 

 "hard landing," but added risks to U.S. economy still tilted 

 toward higher inflation. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso wobbled close to the key psychological support of 

 46 to the dollar and dealers said only fear of intervention by 

 the Philippines central bank could keep players from testing 

 that level. 

 "There is already talk that the central bank is in the 

 market but no one is sure. Given the levels such confusion is 

 not surprising," a dealer at a European bank said. 

 Dealers said worries about a fresh military campaign 

 launched by Manila against Muslim rebels in the south of the 

 country and a deteriorating fiscal balance would also keep the 

 peso under pressure. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The momentum of outflows from Taipei stock is likely to 

 keep the local dollar under pressure, but trading was likely to 

 be cautious after Monday's aggressive central bank

intervention. 

 Dealers said rising oil prices and the weakness of the 

 equity market has not only hurt sentiment but has raised 

 concern about the outlook of the economy. 

 "Foreign funds are leading the selling in the stock market 

 which suggests that foreign investors are getting a bit 

 sceptical about the country's economic outlook or probably the 

 political scene," a dealer said. 

 On Monday foreign investors were net sellers of T$1.807 

 billion in domestic equities, extending Saturday's net selling 

 of T$53 million. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht retained its bearish tone due to persistent dollar 

 bids from both offshore and onshore parties amid talk a few 

 large funds were covering short dollar positions. 

 Several dealers in Singapore said they did not expect to 

 see any strong dollar pullback until the U.S. unit reached 

 42.50 which was the next target. 

 But some argued that recent high baht funding cost in the 

 offshore market should substantially slow down a pace of the 

 decline. 

 One-month dollar/baht offshore forwards were quoted around 

 +15.5/+20.5 satang/dollar compared with +17.0/+22.0 early on 

 Monday. 

 "If the dollar/baht gets to 42.50, I expect to see a flurry 

 of profit taking there. We favour selling the dollar at that 

 level for 42.20," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar retreated alongside the regionals and the 

 battered euro which is believed to account for a sizeable chunk 

 in its trade-weighted basket of currencies. 

     Singapore's positive export data released on Monday was 

 clouded by bearish sentiment prevailing in the region. 

     Its non-oil domestic exports surged 27.3 percent 

 year-on-year on August, beating the most bullish estimate, on 

 the back of strong demand in electronic products from the U.S. 

 and Europe. 

 Dealers said the currency was likely to move in a narrow 

 range of 1.7450-1.7485 this week as players started to be 

 cautious about potential central bank intervention. 

 Bank of America said if the Sing dollar managed to break 

 through 1.7485, the next target would be 1.7500 in the 

 near-term. KOREAN WON -2 

 The won regained its composure after falling sharply 

 alongside local stocks on Monday, with local dealers expecting 

 the unit to move between 1,127-1,135 during the day. 

     Analysts said the current weakness was driven mostly by a 

 collasped deal between Ford and Daewoo Motor. 

     "But the market will move on. The government will be forced 

 to do something about this. Moreover, South Korea still has 

 very strong external balances which should be supportive to the 

 won," said a dealer in Singapore. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 Dollar profit taking helped lift the rupiah above the 8,700 

 mark, but not the market gloom. 

 The dollar has now returned to the neutral zone on the 

 14-day relative strength index, indicating there could be room 

 for further downside for the rupiah. 

 Salomon Smith Barney suggested that once the rupiah 

 retreated to 8,550, players should start building long dollar 

 positions again.

title: Emerging  FX  - Unnerved by bomb-shaken rupiah, yen.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 14 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah tanked 

 in early trade on Thursday following a powerful bomb blast at 

 the Jakarta Stock Exchange, dragging down other regional 

currencies. 

     At least 15 people were killed by the car bomb on 

 Wednesday, which sent bad vibes to a market already infested 

 with negative news. 

     "The market is sentiment-driven. People are rushing to cut 

 losses after these currencies skidded through one support after 

 another," said a dealer at one U.S. bank in Singapore. 

     "But for various reasons, I don't think they will keep 

 sliding. Intervention fear in the Philippines, offshore baht 

 liquidity squeeze, and an increase in oil revenues in Indonesia 

 should provide some support," he said. 


    The yen	  languished below the 107 level in the



absence of positive news to boost it.



    The euro	  was mired near overnight lows against the



dollar, with the market expecting only little support from an



ECB policy-making meeting on Thursday.



    All 55 economists polled by Reuters earlier this week



predicted the ECB would hold rates steady.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    The rupiah sank to its worst level in more than a month on



the back of solid dollar demand from both offshore and onshore



players.



    The Wednesday bombing came on the eve of the resumption of



former president Suharto's graft trial, which many feared could



trigger violence by his supporters.



    "It might probe 9,000 in the immediate term. The sentiment



is really bad. But I hope things will settle down in the near



future because this clearly is a reaction to a specific



incident," said Simon Flint, regional currency strategist at



Bank of America.



    Bank of America suggested investors stay long on



dollar/rupiah.



    The pair is looking heavily overbought, with a reading of



82 on the 14-day relative strength index (RSI). The overbought



line is 70.



    THAI BAHT	



    The baht fell to 41.83 overnight -- a level not seen since



August 31, 1998 -- after a fall below 41.70 prompted players to



cut losses.



    Strong dollar demand for commercial reasons and



short-covering activity are expected to keep downward pressure



on the baht, dealers said.



    However, the unit was unlikely to breach a key support of



42 without bouts of profit taking as exporter offers were seen



around 41.80-41.90.



    Regional factors and political uncertainties in the runup



to the Thailand's next election are likely to put the currency


on the defensive in the near-term.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Sing dollar was weighed by the plunging rupiah and the



weak euro which drifted near its overnight low.



    Dealers said if the rupiah breached the 9,000 psychological



support or the euro sank further, the Sing dollar could test



its July 24 year-low of 1.7515 soon.



    "All eyes are now set for the 1.7515 mark, but there's also



fear of intervention by the authorities," a dealer at a



European bank said.



    KOREAN WON	



    The won kicked off the first trading day of this week on a



bearish note, taking its cues from weak local stocks and the



easier yen.



    South Korea's financial markets were closed on September



11-13 for a Thanksgiving holiday.



    Traders said the won would move between 1,110.5 and 1,114



on Thursday, with the upside capped by expected dollar demand



from importers after the three-day break.



    PHILIPPINE PESO	



    The peso slipped as the decline in regional currencies


worsened market sentiment already negative on the Philippines'



deteriorating economic and political situation.



    Dealers said a large budget deficit, a long-running and



embarrassing hostage crisis and negative perception of the



government's handling of policies were likely to keep the peso



under pressure.



"Intervention or rate hikes by the authorities have given



the peso only temporary boost. It has further room to



depreciate," a dealer at a European bank said.



The central bank has intervened several times since last



week and raised key domestic interest rates by a full



percentage point effective on September 11.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar nudged lower due to a weaker yen and



fears of capital outflows sparked by increased selling of local



stocks by foreign funds.



Foreign equity funds, whose attitude is a leading indicator



of the market trend, were net sellers of T$3.817 billion in



local stocks on Wednesday, taking their net selling over the



last seven sessions to T$17.915 billion.



    Dealers said the unit was likely to trade in a 31.10-31.13



range on Thursday.

title: Philippine Stocks - Factors to Watch - Sept 7.
text:

 Renewed weakness in the peso and the slump in the Nasdaq overnight will likely spur selling in Philippine shares.

title: Philippines  Buenaventura: Ctrl Bk Hasn't  Intervened  Tue
text:
MANILA -(Dow Jones)- Philippine Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenventura said the peso's fall against the dollar Tuesday was due to losses in other regional currencies. 

 Buenaventura, speaking to Dow Jones Newswires from Hong Kong, reiterated that the exchange rate will remain market-determined, and said the central bank hasn't intervened in the session so far to support the peso. 

 At the noon trading recess, the dollar averaged 45.488 pesos on the spot market, up from PHP45.30 at the previous close. The dollar reached an intraday high of PHP45.595, its highest level since PHP46.50 Jan. 7, 1998. 


Traders blamed the peso's fall on losses in the Thai baht, which is
closely tracked in Manila, tight dollar liquidity and the generally
bearish sentiment for the Philippines.
- - 05/09/00 05-49G



Asked if the central bank is targeting a specific peso-dollar rate,
Buenaventura replied: "We have no rate in mind...we will just have to
use our judgment."



Buenaventura said he expects the dollar to retreat to between PHP42.40
to PHP43 later in the year, with the peso partially underpinned by
programmed foreign direct investments and loans from multilateral
sources.



"I still maintain that the peso - and other regional currencies - will
correct," he said.



Even so, with investor confidence in the Philippines at a low ebb,
many currency watchers expect the peso to continue trending lower over
the rest of the year.



The peso has been under near constant pressure this year on concerns
over President Joseph Estrada's leadership - and particularly
perceptions of a resurgency in cronyism.



The Muslim insurgency in the south, as well as a number of economic
worries, such as slowing exports and the likelihood that the
budget-deficit target will badly overshoot, are also rattling the
market.



Buenaventura's comment that the central bank hasn't intervened so far
Tuesday may raise some eyebrows in the market, as traders believe the
authority did sell dollars early in the session to stop PHP45.50 being
breached.



Buenaventura reiterated that the central bank was prepared to supply
dollars during liquidity crunches but this didn't occur Tuesday morning.
The exchange rate, he said, is "still market determined."



Buenaventura said the "good news" that U.S. interest rates have
stabilized has been largely ignored by the region's currency markets,
which have focused instead on political developments in Indonesia,
Thailand and the Philippines.
