title: Philippine peso wobbly on corporate demand.
text:
MANILA, Aug 31 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso fell again on Thursday as month-end corporate dollar buying added to lingering concerns over the drawn-out crisis with Moslem rebels in the south. 

 After opening stronger at 45.075, the peso reversed direction and slid to 45.137 to the dollar at the close, against 45.087 at Wednesday's finish. 

 "Since it's month-end, a lot of corporate demand came out. There's a lot of buying from certain sectors because it's imports season," a trader from a local bank said. 

 Banks also sold the peso owing to jitters over the potentially depressing effect on investment and the economy of all the media attention being showered on foreign tourists kidnapped by Moslem rebels in the southern Philippines, another trader said. 

 Traders said the central bank intervened to keep the peso from breaching the 45.15 to the dollar level, which they said could prompt the currency to slide all the way to the previous year-low of 45.20. 

 And for the second day in a row, central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura denied the bank had intervened by selling dollars to support the beleagured peso. 

 "We were not there," Buenaventura told reporters. 

 Yet traders continued to assert it had. 

 "He would deny it but we think he was (the central bank had intervened) at 45.14," a trader from a foreign bank said. 

 The volume of trades through the Philippine Dealing System totalled a moderate $93.5 million, down from $137.8 milion on Wednesday when banks also pointed to central bank intervention. 

 The peso is expected to trade in the 45.10 to 45.20 range against the dollar on Friday.

title: Philippine peso down early, takes cue from baht.
text:
MANILA, July 26 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso opened softer on Wednesday as it followed the weak Thai baht due to the absence of fresh factors in the local market. 

 One trader said the local currency might test its 45 to the dollar psychological barrier later in the day. 

 Others, however said they expected some banks to take profits at this level. 

 By 0130 GMT, the peso was quoted at 44.90/44.95 to the dollar. It opened at 44.86 from its closing of 44.755 on Tuesday. 

 Turnover was $10 million. 

 "The peso is being pressured by the baht," said one trader, adding the baht was quoted below the 41 level early on Wednesday. 

 The baht slid to a 10-month low of 41 per dollar on Tuesday after the central bank in that country said it would keep interest rates low and showed no sign of intervening to support the currency. 

 The currencies of the Philippines and Thailand sometimes follow each other because they have the same export markets. ((Dolly Aglay, Manila newsroom, +632 841-8936, fax +632 817-6267; manila.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Philippine peso ends weaker in line with region.
text:
MANILA, July 25 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso , already battered by fears of a slowing local economy and the Moslem insurgency problem, ended lower on Tuesday in step with the Thai baht and other regional currencies. 

 Traders said dollar buying by firms covering their month-end import requirements and debt settlements also pulled down the peso. 

 The peso settled at 44.755 to the dollar from Monday's closing of 44.60. Earlier, the peso hit a day's low of 44.76. 

 Turnover was higher at $118.60 million from the previous $108 million. 

 One trader said he believed that Philippine central bank intervened in the spot market again on Wednesday through two foreign banks. 

 "I think it sold $25 million at 44.65 to 44.70," the same trader said. 

 Other traders, however, said there was no reason for the central bank to intervene as the peso took a cue from the baht and other regional currencies in the absence of fresh local news. 

 The baht slid to a fresh 10-month low of 41 to the dollar in afternoon trade on Tuesday after a central bank official in that country said the authorities were monitoring its movement but failed to say they would intervene to support it. 

 The currencies of the Philippines and Thailand sometimes follow each other because they have the same export markets. 

 One trader said he expected the peso to trade between 44.65 and 44.85 to the dollar on Wednesday. ((Dolly Aglay, Manila newsroom, +632 841-8936, fax +632 817-6267; manila.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Philippines ' Buenaventura: No  Intervention  On Spot  Market
text:
MANILA -(Dow Jones)- Despite renewed losses in the peso Tuesday, the Philippine Central Bank said it isn't intervening in the market to support the currency. 

 "It's a waste of time and money," governor Rafael Buenaventura told reporters, reiterating the authority's policy of only selling dollars on the spot market in the event of heavy speculative pressures against the peso. 

 In afternoon trading Tuesday, the dollar averaged PHP43.567 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP43.530 at the previous close. The greenback hit a day-high of PHP43.60, setting a fresh 21-month high against the peso. 

 Shortly after the outbreak of Asia's 1997 currency crisis, the Philippine Central Bank lost a costly battle defending the peso from speculative attack. Since then, it has generally allowed the peso-dollar rate to be determined by the market. 

 Buenaventura attributed the peso's decline Tuesday to weaker regional currencies, led by the Indonesian rupiah. 

 However, traders say the peso is also weak on a raft of economic and political concerns, including low local interest rates, a slowing economy and national security worries. 

 To be sure, the narrowing differential between U.S. and Philippine interest rates has prompted a significant shift towards dollar-denominated investments. Although U.S interest rates were kept unchanged last month, the Philippine central bank effectively lowered its overnight borrowing rate from a flat rate of 10% to a three-tiered system that offers a lower rate for funds in excess of PHP5 billion. 

 -By Amethyst Ma, Dow Jones Newswires; 632-892-5590; amethyst.ma@dowjones.com

title: Philippines  Buenaventura Says Not  Intervening  In  Forex
text:
MANILA -(Dow Jones)- Philippine Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said Monday the central bank isn't intervening in the currency market to support the peso. 

 Buenaventura, speaking to reporters, said the authority also isn't targeting a specific exchange rate, a comment indicating that it remains committed to a market-determined peso despite recent heavy losses in the local currency. 

 The peso hit a fresh 19-month low against the dollar of PHP41.880 in afternoon trading Monday. 

 Some currency traders believe the central bank may have indirectly supplied dollars to the market at around PHP41.80 to support the ailing peso. 

 Buenaventura said the central bank is considering further raising its overnight borrowing rate to help stabilize the peso, stopping short of saying how large a rise the authority is eyeing. 

 "It's an option we are looking at and it's an option we will discuss with the banks," Buenaventura said. 

 Buenaventura said the central bank will meet this week with the Bankers Association of the Philippines, the umbrella organization of the country's 53 commercial banks, to discuss the impact of a another increase in the central bank's overnight borrowing rate. 

 "There's really a basis for higher interest rates, but if we don't have to (raise the overnight borrowing rate), we won't," Buenaventura said. 

 The central bank raised its overnight borrowing rate by one percentage point to 10% last week to help support the peso and to align the key rate with higher U.S. interest rates. 

 -By Amethyst Ma; 632-892-5590; amethyst. ma@dowjones.com

title: Emerging  FX  - Limp in cautious trade, baht sags.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 15 (Reuters) - Asian regional currencies

 remained soft in late Monday trade, though volumes thinned 

 ahead of a key decision on U.S. interest rates. 

     Players stayed on the sidelines before a Federal Reserve 

 meeting on Tuesday, widely expected to result in a 50 basis 

 point rate hike. 

     Major currencies were relatively steady as markets focused 

 on the Fed meeting as well as talk of European Central Bank

 interevention to help the euro. 


    The euro	  held near Friday's two-week highs against



the dollar.



    Against the yen, it	     was holding just shy of



Friday's four-week peaks just above 100.



    The dollar was trading near 109 yen	  with cooled



enthusiasm for Japanese equities. The Nikkei average



fell 0.25 percent on Monday, stuck near six-month lows hit last



week.



THAI BAHT



The baht slipped through its key 39.20 per dollar support,



partly because of the rupiah fallout.



Dealers said the baht was being sold as a proxy due to poor



liquidity in the rupiah. Chartists said it could test 39.50



soon now that 39.20 was broken.



Clouded by the region's bearish tone, the baht barely drew



support from positive news on the non-performing loans and debt



restructuring front.



The Bank of Thailand said on Monday that total



non-performing loans carried by the Thai financial sector fell



to 37.02 percent of total loans in March from 38.09 percent in



February.



KOREAN WON -2



The won shed early gains on late dollar short-covering and



strong dollar buying in the non-deliverable forward (NDF)



market.



    Dealers in Seoul said weakness in the yen and other Asian


currencies prompted won selling in overseas forward markets.



    Traders said the government's purchase of $100 million in



the foreign exchange market to pay off its foreign debt also



helped to offset the won's gains.



    The won is expected to trade between 1,113 and 1,116 on



Tuesday, staying hostage to moves in overseas forward markets.



    The chief of Korea's Financial Supervisory Commission said



in late trade the economy could face trouble unless corporate



and financial restructuring is completed by the end of the



year.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah was still weighed, testing seven-month lows at



8,750 per dollar as pessimism over Indonesia's economic and



political prospects persisted.



Indonesia reported first quarter gross domestic product



growth of 3.21 percent year-on-year, below market expectations



of 4.2 to 6.5 percent growth.



Indonesia also said GDP growth in the second quarter was



likely to be less than one percent compared to the first



quarter.



President Abdurrahman Wahid said he had never promised he



would act to boost the rupiah if it did not rebound by Monday,



denying comments made last Friday.



    Wahid had said the government had a plan to prop up the


currency if it did not rebound by Monday.



    Support was seen pegged at Friday's low of 8,750 per



dollar, while resistance was at 8,345.



    PHILIPPINE PESO	



    The peso dipped against the dollar in sympathy with other



regional currencies.


Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura told reporters



the central bank did not intervene on Monday.



    In the debt market, the Philippines' benchmark 91-day



Treasury-bill rate fell at the weekly auction on Monday despite



expectations of higher local rates due to a looming rise in



U.S. rates on May 16.



    The rate, used by banks to price loans, dropped to an



average of 8.69 percent against last week's 8.746 percent.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Sing dollar drifted lower alongside its regional



counterparts and the yen, but wariness of central bank

intervention kept it supported the right side of 1.73 per



dollar.



Eddy Kong, chartist at MMS Standard & Poors put near-term



support for the Sing at 1.7310-20, with resistance at



1.7240-45.



    The market is focused on Singapore's first quarter economic



report due later in the week.



    "Undoubtedly, the first quarter growth would be strong



(around 7.0 year-on-year) on the back of strong manufacturing



output," SEB Merchant Banking said in a report.



    "But with a recent survey showing businesses are less



optimistic about the economic outlook, investors would be



looking out for the composite leading index for further



confirmation," the report said.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar was easier as losses in domestic stocks



and withdrawals of foreign capital in local equities dampened



sentiment.



    Dealers said although the central bank was in the market to



prop up the unit, the intervention was light.

title: Emerging  FX  - Domestic factors rule, baht slides.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 3 (Reuters) - Regional currencies were 

 directionless in early trade on Wednesday, guided mostly by 

 domestic and technical factors with Tokyo closed for the Golden 

 Week holiday. 

     The baht dipped further on sales from large investment 

 houses and broad-based dollar short covering triggered by its 

 fall below 38.25 on Tuesday, dealers said. 

     The dollar is expected to retain its bullish tone against 


the yen	    and the euro	    in the near-term as strong



U.S. new home sales in March reaffirmed the outlook for higher



U.S. interest rates.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    Tuesday's news of President Wahid pledging no more cabinet



reshuffles failed to provide a boost to the rupiah and it still



traded on the weaker side of the 8,000 level early Wednesday.



    Dealers said dollar/rupiah remained firm above 8,000, with



the recent highs of 8,075 in sight.



    Political uncertainty following the sacking of two of



Wahid's economic ministers last Thursday sent the rupiah to six



month lows.



    KOREAN WON	     -2



    The Korean won was a little firmer against the dollar in



early trade on Wednesday as players looked to unwind dollar



positions, wary of possible inflows from foreign investors



buying local stocks, dealers said.



"Players are watchful of possible dollar inflows from



foreign equity investment in recent sessions," said a foreign



bank dealer.



    Dealers forecast the won would move between 1,109 and



1,110.6 on the day.



    The Finance Ministry reiterated its warning on Wednesday



that the won's rapid rise against the dollar was not desirable



given Korea's dwindling trade surplus and the dollar/yen moves.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Singapore dollar fell on a steady slope in early trade



on Wednesday, though its pace has somewhat eased as it inched



closer to the psychologically important level of 1.7200 where



dealers were nervous about possible intervention by the MAS.



    Dealers said the overall strength of the US dollar was



helping to push down the Singapore unit.



    They said the market saw 1.7200 as pivotal, because the



Sing dollar had not closed above that level since March 8



    Some retreat was expected on profit-taking though support



was seen at 1.7100, dealers said.



    PHILIPPINE PESO	



    The peso barely drew support from robust export data and



talk of potential central bank's intervention to prop up the



unit.



    The Philippines' exports in March rose 10.6 percent from



the same period last year to $2.988 billion. The January-March



exports were up 9.6 percent year-on-year.



    Dealers said the central bank was unlikely to allow the



peso to drop below 41.30 where stop-loss orders and active



hedging activity are likely to emerge.



    THAI BAHT	



    The baht came off against the dollar on heavy sales from



major investment houses, dealers said.



    The unit was also pressured by dollar short-covering and



stop-loss orders as the dollar/baht looked set to test



resistance of 38.50 where exporter offers are lined up.



    Chart suggested the baht could head toward 38.65 if the



38.50 level is broken. Some houses suggested clients reassess



the trend only when the baht pulls back to 37.90.

    But dealers expected the unit to be underpinned by comments



from Moody's Investors Service that its outlook for Taiwan Aa3



foreign and local currency ratings remains stable despite



recent political uncertainties.

than by political developments.

title: Philippine Peso Ends Higher On Dollar Inflows
text:
MANILA -(Dow Jones)- The Philippine peso closed Thursday higher against the dollar, buoyed by dollar liquidity as some foreign and offshore banks unwound long-dollar positions, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 41.12 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, down from Wednesday's PHP41.13. The U.S. currency averaged PHP41.129, lower than PHP41.172 in the previous day. 

 Volume rose to $163 million from $150.5 million. 

 Traders don't see any fundamental reason behind the peso's latest strength, given the weaker regional currencies and the lingering political concerns over the Philippines, leading many to suspect the central bank has intervened to support the local currency. 

 "It's up (peso) because of intervention," said a trader for a foreign bank, echoing a widely-held suspicion in the central bank is injecting dollars in the market to defend the peso after it hit a six-month low of PHP41.20 early this week. 

 The central bank denied it's selling dollars through some foreign banks to prop up the sagging peso. "No, we were not in the market," Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said. 

 Still, the selling pressure the dollar is encountering at or close to the PHP41.20 level has forced some of those with long-dollar positions, particularly offshore banks, to unwind their positions. 

 "It appears the peso won't be allowed to breach the PHP41.20 for the moment, so some offshore banks are reducing their long positions," said trader with another foreign bank.

title: Philippines  Buenaventura Says CB Not  Intervening
text:
MANILA -(Dow Jones)- Philippine Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said Wednesday that the peso-dollar rate continues to be market-oriented and the authority isn't intervening to support the local currency. 

 "Let the market believe what it wants to believe," Buenaventura told Dow Jones Newswires, commenting on market talk that the central bank has supplied dollars to the market to relieve pressure on the peso. 

 In morning trading Wednesday, the dollar averaged 41.179 pesos on the spot market, up from PHP41.150 at Tuesday's close. 

 Tight dollar liquidity and strong demand for the U.S. currency from domestic corporations and offshore funds, coupled with concerns over the political situation in the Philippines, have kept the dollar above PHP41 for the past few trading days. 

 Buenaventura said he expects the peso-dollar rate to be "fairly stable" Wednesday and said the peso market isn't out of kilter with the trend of regional currencies. 

 In morning trading Wednesday, regional currencies were mixed, but the Thai baht, which is closely tracked on the peso market, was weaker against the dollar. 

 Buenaventura said that at a certain level, which he didn't name, dollar-selling will likely kick in on the peso market and help strengthen the local currency. 

 Buenaventura noted with approval March's "good" inflation rate was lower than expected. 

 As reported, inflation in March rose 3.3% on year, far lower than many economists' forecasts of around 3.8%. 

 "The good news is that the inflation rate is rather below the range and with the peso stable vis-a-vis regional currencies, perhaps there is no need to raise overnight rates, but I'm not ruling it out," he said. 

 Earlier this week, Buenaventura said March's inflation data will determine whether it's necessary to raise policy rates at Friday's meeting of the Monetary Board. 

 The overnight borrowing rate, the central bank's main tool to control domestic liquidity, is at 8.75%.

title: EMERGING MARKET  FX -Baht respite, zloty sub-parity.
text:
LONDON, Sept 29 (Reuters) - The Thai baht drew breath on Wednesday amid confusing signals from the central bank, while equally mixed pointers from the National Bank of Poland left the zloty below its basket parity. 

 The buoyant Czech crown tested fresh resistance levels against the euro, but South Africa's rand eased slightly after this week's sharp rise on the back of surging world gold prices. 

 Kenya's shilling fell sharply on fears that government attempts to woo the International Monetary Fund were not going well. 

 Emerging Asia was mixed as the dollar hovered just below 107 yen, with the Philippine peso continuing south on expectations of further baht weakness. 

 The Thai currency found some respite, firming slightly but staying on the weak side of 41 to the dollar after assistant central bank governor Cherdthawee Chareonpitak said it should not drop below 40, based on economic fundamentals. 

 Speaking in Singapore, Deputy Prime Minister Supachai Panitchpakdi chimed in with the same message that fundamentals justified a stronger baht. 

 Only a day earlier, Thailand's deputy central bank chief, Tanya Sirivedhin, said the central bank saw a range of 41-42 baht per dollar as "acceptable". 

 "The problem with the central bank is that they're trying to manipulate a level, and that's always problematic," said Gerry Celaya, senior forex technical analyst at American Express Bank in London. "We still think it's going to go towards 42." 

 The peso opened at an 11-month low of 41.20 to the dollar, although it retraced some ground after President Joseph Estrada said he was not ruling out intervention. 

 Analysts said the Philippines was more concerned at the speed of the peso's slide than its actual level against the dollar, as a soft currency would support exports. 

 "We don't think (Estrada) has any great affection for a mega-strong FX," Celaya said. "It's really the pace of things and the fact that people are actually talking about it that's upset them." 

 MIXED SIGNALS IN POLAND 

 The zloty, which slipped to around 0.12 percent below its basket parity on Tuesday, eased further on Wednesday to settle around 0.29 percent below the midpoint. 

 Some analysts blamed the slide on political uncertainty after news that the junior partner in the coalition government could ask for the dismissal of Prime Minister Jerzy Buzek. 

 But others said it was drifting ahead of Friday's balance of payments data for August, and was still taking its cue from Tuesday's comments by central bank governor Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz that the zloty would hover around the centre of its trading band in the near term. 

 Recent signs from Poland's central bank have been mixed, with another member of its Monetary Policy Council saying last week he saw the zloty ending the year at 3.0-4.0 percent above parity, and the currency has shown mild volatility as a result. 

 "Politics in Poland really hasn't appeared to enter into market equations this year," said Juliet Sampson, emerging market currency strategist at Bank of America in London. 

 "Major cabinet shakeups are unlikely and there will be an impact (on the zloty) only if it looks like the coalition will break up." 

 The Czech crown was challenging strong resistance at 35.60 to the euro and analysts saw it firming further. 

 "The bias has to be on strengthening, given FDI (foreign direct investment) flows, the strong current account and trade picture and the fact that we've seen no intervention from the central bank," Sampson said. 

 The Kenyan shilling lurched beyond 77 to the dollar amid fears that the government was making poor headway in trying to persuade the IMF to resume lending to the cash-strapped East African country. 

 Finance Minister Chris Okemo is leading a mission to Washington in a bid to convince the IMF to start negotiations on a resumption of lending, which was cut off in mid-1997 in protest at official corruption.

title: ASIA  FOREX -Jolted by domestic woes, dlr demand.
text:
0830 GMT - Most regional currencies extended their losses 

 in late trade, ignoring the yen's resilience amid growing 

 confidence Japan would not win wider backing in its efforts to 

 rein in the rising yen. 

     Trade was thinned by a Japanese holiday but the dollar 

 slipped as far as 103.44 yen as remarks by U.S. officials 

 dampened fears the G7 would come up with a plan for joint 

intervention at this weekend's meeting. 

     New York Fed President William McDonough said current 

 dollar/yen levels are not a concern for the U.S. economy, while 

 U.S. Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said the dollar would 

 do "fine" as long as U.S. fundamentals remained healthy. 

     Asian currencies charted their own -- mostly southbound -- 

 course amid a raft of comments by regional central bank

 officials, with Thailand and the Philippines assuring the 

 market they did not plan to intervene. 

     *** The Thai baht slid through a series of supports, 

 falling through the key 41.00 per dollar level in late trade on 

 persistent dollar demand from companies needing to make foreign 

 loan payments. 

     The central bank said it was monitoring the baht, but it 

 had not seen any sign of a speculative attack and had no plans 

 to intervene. 

     It attributed the baht's recent decline to low domestic 

 interest rates and limited dollar supplies as exporters 

 withheld dollars due to low premiums in the swap market. 

     The market has also turned slightly more bearish about 

 Thailand in the wake of weaker than expected second quarter 

 growth. 

     The IMF said Thailand should grow 4.0 percent this year and 

 next but sounded warnings over the banking sector. 

     Banking reform was proceeding in the right manner but was 

 taking longer than expected, the IMF's director for Thailand 

 Ranjit Teja said. 

     *** The peso took its cue from the weak baht, sliding to 

 40.59, its lowest level in 10 months. 

     The peso has mirrored the Thai currency's moves of late as 

 the two countries compete in export markets. 

     Dollar demand from corporates and institutional investors 

 cutting their exposure to economies which are seen as holding 

 higher Y2K risks have also contributed to the peso's decline. 

     The Philippine central bank said it was not about to 

intervene as the peso's fall was in line with general weakness 

 in the region. 

     July production numbers for manufacturing fell year on 

 year. The government said the value of the production index 

 dipped 0.7 percent from July 1998, while its volume fell 4.6 

 percent. 

     Net sales for July rose 3.1 percent year-on-year mainly due 

 to price hikes in petroleum products. 

     *** The rupiah slid to the wrong side of 8,600 per dollar 

 as thousands of students clashed with security forces in 

 Jakarta and Surabaya, protesting against a new security law 

 they argue gives the military even more power. 

 Indonesia's parliament passed a watered down version of the 

 original draft on Thursday as police fired tear gas and warning 

 shots over the heads of students protesting in central Jakarta. 

 There was trouble in East Timor too, with Indonesian troops 

 accusing U.N. forces of firing warning shots at them, a charge 

 denied by the commander of the British contingent of the 

 multinational force in the territory. 

     Brigadier David Richards said Indonesian troops had fired 

 shots near his soldiers on Thursday. 

     The central bank said it expected a rupiah rate of 6,850 to 

 7,600 to the dollar by end-1999, while year-on-year inflation 

 was seen falling to between three and five percent. 

     It said it was sticking to its 1999 GDP forecast of minus 

 two to zero percent and end-year one-month SBI interest rate of 

 10 to 12 percent. 

     The IMF said overnight it expected the Indonesian economy 

 to contract by 0.8 percent this year - much less than the 4.0 

 percent decline it expected half a year ago - and to grow 2.6 

 percent in 2000. 

 *** The Taiwan dollar was barely changed, with dealers 

 confident the central bank would maintain investor confidence 

 after Tuesday's huge earthquake, which has killed 2,100 people. 

     Liquidity was given an added boost after the central bank

 injected T$600 million worth of funds into the banking system. 

     The government said August industrial production rose 9.03 

 percent year-on-year but September output was likely to be 

 affected by the quake. 

     August export orders rose 9.73 percent year-on-year. 

 Economists surveyed by Reuters had forecast on average a 7.98 

 percent rise. 

     Taiwan has lowered its 1999 GDP forecast to 5.5 percent in 

 1999, compared with previous estimates of 5.74 percent. 

     *** South Korea's forex market is closed until Monday for a 

 national holiday which runs from September 23 to 25. 

     Seoul dealers saw the won firming after the holiday, given 

 expected demand for dollars from corporates and banks. 

     Demand would be triggered by principal and interest 

 payments of mid-term foreign loans in early October.

title: EMERGING MARKET  FX -Asia in a rut with yen.
text:
LONDON, June 14 (Reuters) - Emerging Asian currencies eased on Monday in tandem with the softer yen, but analysts said they would remain stuck in a benign rut until the Japanese currency made a bigger shift up or down. 

 The Indonesian rupiah bucked the trend, lifted once more by post-election optimism. 

 Emerging European currencies were quiet, with the Hungarian forint slipping off the top of its 4.5 percent-wide trading band in stilted trade and the Polish zloty drifting ahead of expected privatisation inflows. 

 The Czech crown barely flickered at retail sales data seen by analysts as broadly positive, although it remained on an upward course against the euro. 

 Most Asian currencies were slightly down on late Friday levels as the Bank of Japan intervened repeatedly to sap the yen's upward push against the dollar, fearing excessive currency strength could harm its economic recovery. 

 Dollar/yen dipped below 118 in Asian trading but surged to a peak of 120.85 on the intervention. It eased back slightly in the London morning, but fresh yen gains were limited by fears the Japanese central bank may have left orders to sell yen beyond its own time zone. 

 Analysts said players were still looking for pointers on the possibility of a U.S. interest rate hike when the Federal Reserve's policy making body meets at the end of this month. 

 Eyes will be on Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, who is due to speak at 1400 GMT on Monday on the impact of high technology on jobs, wages and living standards, and on U.S. May consumer price and industrial production data published on Wednesday. 

 But analysts said emerging Asian currencies would stay range-bound, trading mainly on their own merits, until dollar/yen made a clear break through 118-117.50 or 122-123. 

 "With the Bank of Japan aggressively intervening to prop up dollar/yen, regional curencies look unable to make headway against the greenback near term despite the threat of a U.S. rate hike," analysts at Standard Chartered said in a note to clients. 

 This would not necessarily be unwelcome, analysts added, as stability against the dollar would help keep inflation in check and ease fears of dented export competitiveness in countries such as South Korea, Thailand and the Philippines. 

 But some suggested the Bank of Korea, which intervened three days running last week to cap the won's rise, might still be uncomfortable with current levels despite Monday's weaker turn. 

 "The Bank of Korea hasn't been shy about showing its hand, and that's going to continue," one currency analyst said. 

 "I don't think they really like it here between 1,180 and 1,160 (to the dollar). If dollar/yen stays in the 118-120 range I'm pretty sure the Korean authorities would rather have the won between 1,180 and 1,220." 

 The rupiah continued its upward push in volatile trade, breaking through 7,500 to the dollar bid for the first time this year, as political horsetrading got under way to form a new coalition government after last Monday's general election. 

 "The rupiah is in its own little world," said Gerry Celaya, senior forex technical analyst at American Express Bank in London, adding that a squeeze on outstanding long dollar positions could lift the currency further towards 7,300. 

 Counting remained very slow, with only one-third of the results in. The opposition Indonesian Democratic Party-Struggle (PDI-P) was well ahead with just under 38 percent of the vote, with the ruling Golkar party trailing in third place. 

 In Europe, commercial dollar orders knocked the forint down to around 2.22 percent above its basket parity from last week's steady 2.25 percent, the ceiling of its trading band. 

 Dealers said a 50-basis-point cut in the central bank's overnight repo rate, and a 25-basis-point cut in the two-week deposit facility, had no immediate effect on the currency. 

 The zloty firmed slightly to be quoted at 3.57 percent above parity around 1015 GMT, from Friday's 3.41/3.31 percent, but the market was still waiting for imminent privatisation inflows to lift the currency towards its next resistance at four percent above the mid-point. ** Following is a table of key emerging market exchange rates, including the change versus late New York trade the previous day and the change in the year to date.. ** The Czech, Polish, Hungarian and Slovak currencies, formerly quoted against the mark, are now quoted against the euro to reflect new market norms. title: ASIA FOCUS - Chronology of Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 3 (Reuters) - The following is a chronology of Asia's financial crisis. 

 1997 

 Jan 23 - Leading South Korean steel maker Hanbo Steel Corp defaults on loans, the first of a string of major corporate failures in 1997. 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency comes under attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 The Philippines is affected. The central bank raises the overnight rate to 13 percent and dumps dollars. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thai finance minister. Resignation has immediate impact in the Philippines, where the overnight deposit rate rises to 15 percent. 

 June 27 - Thai central bank suspends operations of 16 cash-strapped finance companies and orders them to submit merger or consolidation plans. 

 June 30 - Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh assures the nation in a televised address there will be no devaluation of the baht. 

 July 2 - After a failed defence of the Thai baht, Bangkok floats its currency and calls on the IMF for "technical assistance". 

 The baht is effectively devalued by about 15-20 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah starts to crumble. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support. 

 July 24 - Asian currency meltdown. The rupiah, baht, ringgit and peso slump as confidence in the region deteriorates. 

 August 11 - In Tokyo, the IMF unveils a rescue package for Thailand including loans of $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of a managed exchange rate. The rupiah plunges. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bail-out package, bringing it to $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 20 - Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad tells delegates of IMF/World Bank conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Around this time the South Korean won also begins to slump in value. 

 Oct 27 - Asian jitters spill over on to world stock markets. The Dow plunges 554 points, its largest single-day point loss ever. 

 Oct 31 - Indonesia's IMF package is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 1 - Indonesia shuts down 16 troubled banks. 

 Nov 5 - IMF approves a $10 billion loan for Indonesia as part of the massive international package. 

 Nov 17 - Korea abandons its defence of the won, which rapidly falls to 1,000 to the dollar. 

 Dec 4 - IMF approves a $21 billion loan for South Korea, part of a bail-out package that will total nearly $60 billion. 

 Dec 8 - Thailand closes 56 of 58 previously suspended finance companies. 

 1998 

 Jan 8 - Representatives of the IMF and South Korea agree to a 90-day rollover of short-term debt. 

 Jan 12 - Peregrine, one of Asia's largest independent investment banks, collapses under a mountain of bad loans to Indonesian borrowers. Shares fall sharply in Hong Kong, China and Singapore. 

 Jan 15 - IMF managing director Michel Camdessus and President Suharto sign an agreement strengthening economic reforms. 

 Jan 22 - The rupiah collapses. It is dealt at 17,000 to the dollar at one stage. Bank Indonesia intervenes and drives the currency back to end at 11,800. 

 Jan 27 - Indonesia announces a temporary freeze on debt servicing. 

 Jan 28 - International creditor banks and the South Korean government say they have agreed on a plan to exchange $24 billion of short-term debt for new loans maturing in one, two and three years. 

 Jan 30 - U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warns Asia's financial crisis could spread. 

 Feb 14 - The IMF threatens to cut off the bail-out fund for Indonesia over its plans to introduce a currency board. 

 Feb 26 - Indonesia's borrowers and lenders begin negotiations on rescheduling at least $70 billion in private off-shore debt. 

 March 1 - Indonesian President Suharto says reforms prescribed by the IMF have not worked. 

 March 4 - The IMF approves release of the third tranche payment from Thailand's package and commends the Thai government for its economic reforms. 

 March 6 - IMF says its board will not discuss Indonesia's economic reform programme before April, effectively delaying a $3 billion payment initially expected by March 15. 

 March 23 - Indonesia nearly doubles interest rates to boost the rupiah and control inflation. 

 April 1 - Japan begins steps aimed at liberalising its financial markets to make them "free, fair and global" by 2001. Tokyo share prices fall, the yen dips and Japan's central bank governor pronounces every economic indicator bad. 

 April 2 - The chairman of electronics giant Sony, Norio Ohga, says the Japanese economy is on the verge of collapse. 

 April 3 - U.S. ratings agency Moody's lowers its outlook on Japan's sovereign debt to negative from stable. Asian currencies fall sharply on the news. 

 May 7 - Fears that riots in the Indonesian city of Medan will spill over into a wider social crisis send regional stocks into retreat. 

 May 11 - India stuns the world with announcement of three underground nuclear tests. Pakistan stocks tumble 3.52 percent while India's National Stock Exchange index slides 2.55 percent. 

 May 13 - The United States imposes economic sanctions on India and Japan suspends some loans. 

 May 14 - Mobs rampage through Jakarta and students demand Suharto's resignation. Indonesia's worsening crisis takes centre-stage for Asian markets, several of which suffer sharp losses. 

 May 15 - Suharto returns home from a Group of 15 summit in Egypt amid signs he is losing his 32-year grip on power. 

 May 21 - Suharto steps down under strong pressure and is succeeded by former deputy president B.J. Habibie. Markets enjoy a limited rally. Jakarta stocks surge more than three percent. 

 May 25 - South Korean shares plummet 6.78 percent despite a lifting of foreign ownership limits on stocks. Most other Asian markets shrug off Seoul's fall. 

 May 26 - Seoul's KOSPI share index continues to dive, losing a further six percent, hurt by a looming recession and labour unrest. 

 May 27 - Asian markets are hammered as the yen falls against the dollar and amid mounting fears of economic recession. Hong Kong stocks plunge more than five percent after Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa warns of possible recession. 

 May 28 - Pakistan conducts nuclear tests. 

 May 29 - The dollar rockets to a seven-year high of 139 yen on fears of a possible nuclear arms race in Asia and after news that Japan's unemployment rate hit 4.1 percent in April, its highest level since the end of World War Two. 

 Recession looms in much of Asia. Hong Kong reports that its gross domestic product contracted two percent in first quarter of 1998. About the same time Indonesia and Malaysia also report their economies contracted in the first quarter. 

 June 1 - Pakistani stocks plunge 12.38 percent as traders get their first chance to react to sanctions imposed after the country's nuclear tests. Asian markets are hit as nuclear tension adds to a cocktail of domestic problems. 

 June 5 - International lenders and Indonesian companies reach a deal to reschedule the country's massive corporate debt. 

 June 8 - The yen falls past 140 to the dollar, sending a shudder through Asian markets. Signs that Japan and other leading economies are unlikely to intervene to support the unit sap confidence further. 

 June 10 - China's central bank governor warns that the weak yen is having a severe impact on Beijing's foreign trade, raising fears that China may devalue its yuan currency. Markets across Asia tumble, led by a near five percent fall on Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index. 

 In Taiwan, the local dollar hits new 11-year lows and the Australian dollar plummets past 59 U.S. cents. 

 June 11 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin all but rules out the possibility of joint intervention by major industrial powers to bolster the yen. He says the weak yen reflects the state of the Japanese economy. 

 June 12 - Economic Planning Agency says Japan's gross domestic product fell by an annualised rate of 5.3 percent in the first quarter, signalling recession. The yen dives towards 145 to the dollar as hopes fade of official intervention. 

 June 17 - The U.S. joins Japan in selling the dollar in favour of the yen. 

 The action takes markets by surprise and the yen rises to a high of around 134 at one stage from a level of some 142.50 prior to the intervention. 

 June 19 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin tells Reuters he is not expecting high level meetings in Tokyo to produce specific new action plans on the economy. His statements put further pressure on the yen. 

 June 20 - Top finance officials from the Group of Seven meet in Tokyo and vow to cooperate as appropriate in the currency markets. 

 June 23 - IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus calls the yen fall a "crisis within the crisis". 

 June 25 - Indonesia and the IMF sign another letter of intent - the fourth. The letter says that Indonesian GDP is expected to contract by at least 10 percent in 1998 and says the rupiah will stabilise at around 10,000 by the last quarter of 1998. 

 June 26 - Malaysia cuts bank statutory reserve requirements to eight percent from 10 percent. 

 June 29 - For the first time, South Korea closes banks, shutting five ailing operations in a major step towards meeting the mandate of the massive IMF rescue package. 

 July 2 - World Bank approves $1 billion loan disbursement to Indonesia, another $6 billion to arrive from international donors. 

 Japan Prime Minister Hashimoto and the ruling Liberal Democratic Party agree to adopt bridge bank system to tackle the country's massive bad loans. 

 July 4 - Foreign Minister Keizo Obuchi hints at permanent tax cuts. 

 July 8 - Hashimoto vows to seek permanent tax cuts and an overhaul of the tax system, but reveals no details. 

 July 9 - South Korea announces its intention to double this year's budget deficit in a bid to stimulate the economy. 

 July 12 - The ruling LDP is trounced in Upper House elections, winning only 44 seats, well short of a majority and 17 less than the 61 it had held prior to the election. 

 South Korea's Financial Supervisory Commission imposes involuntary restructuring on conglomerates, or chaebols, directing eight banks to pick about 16 chaebols for the exercise. 

 July 13 - PM Hashimoto announces his resignation and cancels planned official visits to France and the United States. 

 July 14 - Tens of thousands of South Korean workers down tools to protest against wage cuts and layoffs, part of the massive corporate restructuring programme. 

 July 15 - IMF approves immediate $1 billion loan payment to Indonesia. 

 July 16 - Striking Korean workers return to work, but warn of further protests if necessary. 

 Indonesia revises 98/99 budget to reflect the deteriorating economy, assuming a rupiah/dlr rate of 10,600. 

 Foreign governments announce their agreement to reschedule the country's $54.4 billion in sovereign debt. 

 July 20 - Protests begin at Hyundai's factory in Ulsan, striking workers pitch tents. 

 July 23 - Record 7.0 percent unemployment in South Korea, with more than 1.5 million unemployed. 

 July 24 - Obuchi wins 225 votes out of 411 in LDP voting to become LDP president and, almost certainly, prime minister. 

 July 29 - Moody's Investors Service warned that it may downgrade credit ratings of Thai banks due to poor results. 

 July 30 - Parliament formally names Obuchi prime minister; he then announces his new cabinet. 

 August 3 - Thailand unveils 25 point plan to salvage its economy at the start of two weeks of talks with the IMF. The plan includes measures to create jobs and stimulate the economy, and is later endorsed by the IMF. 

 Indonesia launches debt rescheduling agency to aid the country's debt-ridden companies. 

 August 6 - New Japanese prime minister Obuchi announces a plan to vary tax cuts according to existing tax brackets, and says he will ask parliament to approve cuts worth more than six trillion yen ($41.3 billion). 

 August 14 - The Hong Kong government intervenes in the local stock market, buying stocks to squeeze out investors accused of playing the currency and interest rates against the stock market. The Hang Seng Index soars 8.47 percent. 

 August 17 - Russia effectively devalues the rouble and declares a 90-day moratorium on some foreign debt. The next day, Asian markets slide. 

 Thousands of Hyundai Motor workers rally near the South Korean company's main factory complex in Ulsan, suspending production in protest over layoffs. Police stand ready for action. 

 August 25 - Hyundai workers return to work after a union-brokered agreement to limit number of layoffs. 

 August 26 - IMF approves $1 billion loan to Indonesia. 

 August 31 - Wall Street suffers its second-largest point loss in history, plunging 6.37 percent and sparking another series of stock market routs in Asia. 

 IMF approves $900 million loan payment to South Korea. 

 Sept 1 - Malaysia imposes new foreign exchange controls to contain speculation and restrict capital flows. The IMF warns that the move may undermine investor confidence. 

 Sept 2 - Malaysia announces that the ringgit will be fixed at 3.80 to the dollar indefinitely. 

 Wall Street stages its second-largest comeback in history, sparking off a rally in Asian markets. 

 Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is sacked. Police state that Anwar is under investigation over allegations made in a banned book, "Fifty Reasons Why Anwar Cannot Become Prime Minister". 

 Sept 3 - South Korean riot police storm plants owned by Mando Machinery Corp., the country's largest auto-parts producer, to end a strike over planned mass layoffs.

title: ASIA MARKETS - Get a little help from the yen.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 14 (Reuters) - Asian markets had a mixed end to the week on Friday with a recovery in the yen offsetting lingering concerns about developments in Russia. 

 All the regional currencies posted slight gains, ranging from 0.2 percent to just over two percent in thin volumes. 

 HONG KONG STOCKS LEAD THE REGION HIGHER 

 Hong Kong stocks soared to a sharply higher close fuelled by short-covering sparked by a firmer Japanese yen and as fears faded of an attack on the Hong Kong dollar over the long weekend, brokers said. 

 The Hang Seng Index rallied 564.27 points, or 8.47 percent, to end at 7,224.69. It was the ninth biggest points gain for the blue chip index. 

 RUPIAH STRENGTHENS AHEAD OF INDEPENDENCE DAY 

 The Indonesian rupiah started the day weaker but by late afternoon had posted two percent gains on its late Thursday levels as the market preapered for the long Independence Day holiday weekend in Jakarta. 

 The early weakness in the rupiah was attributed to nervousness over the prospects for rioting or other forms of street protest to coincide with the national holiday. 

 On the banking front Indonesia has confirmed that the so-called interbank exchange offer by Bank Indonesia and Indonesian banks of eligible debt for new loans will go ahead as scheduled on August 25. 

 According to Bank Indonesia, around $2.7 billion of external bank debt, as well as a large amount of derivatives and other debt obligations, have been tendered by overseas creditors for exchange. 

 THE RINGGIT FIRMER BUT MARKETS WATCH STOCKS 

 In Malaysia the ringgit was a little firmer but traders were keeping a close eye on the KLSE after yesterday's more than five percent drop to 10-year lows. 

 Rating agency Fitch IBCA said it expected Malaysia's non-performing loans to peak at around 25 percent of total loans against the 20 percent peak forecast by the government's National Economic Action Council. Fitch also estimated bank recapitalisation needs at 20 billion ringgit. 

 Fitch IBCA assigned a long term rating of BBB-to Malaysia on Thursday. 

 THAILAND UNVEILS BANK REFORM PACKAGE. 

 The Thai baht was basically steady with the market digesting a bank reform package announced dueing the morning session. 

 The details of the package show the central bank is effectivley going to nationalise the worst performing institutions via a debt for equity swap. 

 The Bangkok share market liked what it heard and rallied by over three percent with investors targetting the large capitalised banks like Bangkok Bank or Thai Farmers Bank. 

 Thailand's foreign reserves stood at $26.8 billion as at August 7, unchanged from a week earlier but against $27.5 billion on July 24, the Bank of Thailand said. 

 The International Monetary Fund, which sponsored a $17.2 billion bailout package for crisis-hit Thailand, has suggested that the country maintain minimum foreign reserves of $26-28 billion this year. 

 SINGAPORE'S ASIAN DOLLAR MARKET CONTRACTION SLOWS 

 In Singapore the government released figures showing the sharp deterioration in the Asian dollar market was beginning to slow. The Asian dollar market shrank by $1.5 billion in June after declining $14 billion in the first five months of 1998. 

 Over the 12 months of the Asian financial crisis the Asian dollar market has contracted to $484 billion from $560 billion in June last year. 

 PESO FIRMS WITH A LITTLE CENTRAL BANK HELP 

 The Philippine peso closed firmer at its intra-day high underpinned by the central bank's dollar selling through foreign banks and the gains of other regional currencies. 

 "There was still central bank intervention through the two foreign banks. They must have sold some $50 million and they were selling at various rates," said a trader from a foreign bank. 

 The peso ended at 43.05 to the dollar against the previous session's close of 43.21. 

 The Philippines this week has raised official interest rates sharply and intervened regularly to support the currency to little effect. 

 KOREAN MARKETS HELPED BY YEN RECOVERY. 

 The Korean won was a touch firmer helped by the yen's recovery while Seoul stocks rose 0.53 percentage point with traders there still worried about Russia's outlook. 

 Officials of South Korea's top five business groups agreed on Friday to try to sign letters of intent for restructuring by the end of August to advance the process, a business lobby group said. 

 The top five business conglomerates, Hyundai, Samsung, Daewoo, LG and SK Group, agreed with the government last week they would submit business swap plans by the end of August. 

 Government officials have said the big deal plans would involve most of the country' major industries suffering from overcapacity and overlapping investments. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

text:

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  suffer as Korean won slides.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 1 (Reuters) - The South Korean won fell to a new low on Monday as the market awaited details of an international bailout package for the economy. 

 A wave of dollar purchases pushed the won and several other currencies to greater depths as European markets opened. 

 Dealers said selling pressure stemmed from worries over the terms of the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) loan to help rescue the South Korean economy. 

 Some feared the IMF would want to impose very tough conditions, such as much higher interest rates which would hit economic growth. 

 "If conditions are very restrictive, then I would expect more pressure on the won," said Andy Tan, general manager at Standard & Poor's/MMS in Singapore. 

 Others worried a mooted US$20 billion rescue package might not be enough to deal with South Korea's woes. 

 "A $20 billion dollar loan seems to have calmed the (won's) fall somewhat, but the market's fear is that this isn't enough," a dealer with a European commission house said. 

 The won fell to 1,182/1,188, off from 1,173 around midday. 

 "It was relatively quiet but some large orders (for dollars) brought about big price moves," a dealer with a local bank said, noting the general trend to reduce Asian exposure. 

 Tan said the next resistance point for the won against the dollar was 1,200 with the currency at some risk of sliding past that mark, depending on the reform policies that the IMF demanded in exchange for the rescue package. 

 Other Southeast Asian currencies were also on the defensive with no reprieve due to strong corporate dollar demand. 

 While the two-day Asian finance ministers meeting in Kuala Lumpur, which started on Monday, was closely watched the market was disappointed it offered no immediate remedies. 

 The ministers stopped short of endorsing a separate standby facility to complement the IMF. 

 Instead, they backed an agreement reached recently in Manila that nations would provide aid on a case-by-case basis. 

 Traders reacted by buying the dollar against regionals. 

 Thailand's baht slipped to new lows with offshore falling to 41.30 against the dollar, before bouncing back to 41.05. 

 The onshore rate dropped to 40.80, against 40.60 earlier. 

 Dealers blamed the baht's offshore price fall on unabated foreign demand for dollars ahead of year-end debt requirements. 

 "There are so many factors for the baht's weakness. It's year-end dollar demand to repay debt and tight volume trading," said one dealer with a U.S. financial institution. 

 She added that Moody's Investors Service downgrade of Thai sovereign debt last week had also raised the cost of borrowing. 

 Elsewhere, the Indonesian rupiah fell on sustained regional weakness with spot at 3,720 against the dollar compared with 3,665/3,675 on Friday. 

 The Malaysian ringgit was hit by large dollar orders late in the session after large losses in the stock market. 

 Kuala Lumpur's key share index ended down 3.11 percent to 528.45 as the market reacted to trading curbs placed on five stockbroking companies over the weekend. 

 "There was some talk that 12 other broking firms would be placed under those same curbs," one dealer said earlier. 

 Dollar/ringgit was lifted to a high of 3.5800 on large orders for dollars, but eased back to 3.5650. 

 The ringgit was at 3.5250 during the early afternoon. 

 Meanwhile, the Philippine Peso clawed back to 34.90 against the dollar, against 35.30. Speculation the Philippines central bank intervened to sell dollars at 35.30 was not confirmed. 

 The Singapore dollar drifted along with regionals to 1.6045, against 1.5940/60 earlier. Dealers said the raising of prime rates by some local banks late on Monday was mostly discounted. 

 Taiwan's dollar recouped slightly to T$32.10, up from T$32.395 but remained sluggish with its ailing stock market. 

 Dealers said currencies and stocks responded to the ruling Nationalist Party's surprising weekend loss in local polls, which could trigger a renewed outflow of foreign funds. 

 Taiwan's main share index fell 5.09 percent on Monday. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was almost unchanged at 7.7309 against 7.7300 earlier in the day.

title: Philippines /Singson -2: Minimal  Central Bank Intervention
text:
Singson said the peso's steady appreciation has been achieved with minimal central bank intervention. 

 Singson noted that interest rates are also starting to soften, with the yield on the benchmark 91-day Treasury bill declining to 15.928% at this week's government securities auction from 16.341% at the previous auction. 

 Similarly, he said, interbank rates have dropped sharply, with the weighted average interbank call loan rate Tuesday at 13.1% compared to 42.5% on Nov. 6. 

 The central bank's priority is to see more exchange rate stability, which would pave the way for interest rates to fall further, Singson said. 

 He noted that various factors are at work in strengthening the peso, including significant remittance inflows from overseas Filipino workers and the bulk of local commercial demand for dollar having already been met. 

 Furthermore, Singson said, 'apparently banks are also responding to the call for less aggressive foreign exchange trading, which could be counter-productive to banks' overall interests in the long run.' 

 Singson also noted that the regional currency situation has become calmer.

title: Key dates in Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 24 (Reuters) - A dramatic week on the Hong Kong stock market, with a savage fall followed by a partial recovery, is the latest development in a string of financial crises across East Asia. 

 The following are key dates: 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency is hit by a massive attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 The Philippines is affected. The central bank raises the overnight rate 1-3/4 percentage points to 13 percent and dumps dollars. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thailand's finance minister. 

 The resignation has immediate financial impact in the Philippines, where the overnight rate rises to 15 percent. 

 June 27 - The Thai central bank suspends operations of 16 cash-strapped finance companies and orders them to submit merger or consolidation plans. 

 June 30 - Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yonchaiyudh assures the nation in a televised address there will be no devaluation of the baht. 

 July 2 - The Bank of Thailand announces a managed float of the baht and calls on the International Monetary Fund for "technical assistance". 

 The announcement effectively devalues the baht by about 15-20 percent. It ends at a record low of 28.80 to the dollar. 

 In Manila, the central bank is forced to intervene heavily to defend the peso. 

 July 3 - The Philippine central bank raises the overnight lending rate to 24 percent from 15 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. The intervention works and the currency hits a high of 2.5100/10 after a low of 2.5240/50. 

 July 11 - The Philippine central bank says in a statement it will allow the peso to move in a wider range against the dollar. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah is starting to be affected. In a surprise move, Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support under fast-track regulations drawn up after the 1995 Mexican crisis. 

 July 24 - Currency meltdown. 

 The ringgit hits 38-month low of 2.6530 to the dollar. Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad launches bitter attack on "rogue speculators". 

 The Hong Kong dollar remains steady, but territory later reveals US$1 billion was spent on intervention during a period of two hours on an unspecified day in July. 

 July 26 - Mahathir names hedge fund manager George Soros as the man responsible for the attack on the ringgit. He later brands Soros a "moron". 

 August 5 - Thailand unveils austerity plan and complete revamp of finance sector as part of IMF suggested policies for a rescue package. Central bank suspends 48 finance firms. 

 August 11 - The IMF unveils in Tokyo a rescue package for Thailand including loans totalling $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 13 - The rupiah begins to come under severe pressure. It hits a historic low of 2,682 to the dollar before ending at 2,655. The central bank actively intervenes in its defence. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of managing the exchange rate through the use of a band. The rupiah plunges to 2,755. 

 August 16 - An unnamed Beijing source tells a local Hong Kong newspaper that China is prepared to use US$50 billion to defend the Hong Kong dollar. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. The package now totals $16.7 billion. Brunei later adds $500 to the bailout package, bringing it to a total of $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 4 - Carnage in the Philippine peso continues. It falls to a record low of 32.43 to the dollar before central bank intervention helps it up slightly to end at 32.38. 

 Ringgit breaks through 3.0000 to the dollar barrier. 

 Mahathir delays several multi-billion dollar construction projects. 

 Sept 16 - Indonesia says it will postpone projects worth 39 trillion rupiah in an attempt to slash the budget shortfall. 

 Sept 20 - Mahathir tells delegates to the IMF/World Bank annual conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral and should be stopped. 

 Sept 21 - Soros says "Dr Mahathir is a menace to his own country". 

 Oct 1 - Mahathir repeats his siren call for tighter regulation, or a total ban, on forex trading. The currency falls four percent in less than two hours to a low of 3.4080. 

 Oct 6 - The rupiah hits a low of 3,845. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 14 - Vietnam, bowing to months of pressure on its dong currency, doubles the permitted trading range to 10 percent either side of the daily official rate. 

 Oct 17 - Malaysia presents a belt-tightening budget to try to stop the economy sliding into recession. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. The Hang Seng index plunges 23.34 percent to 10,426.30 by Thursday's close, after 13,601.01 the previous Friday. 

 The Hong Kong dollar is linked to the U.S. dollar at an official rate of 7.8 to one. After the turmoil in Southeast Asian markets, the heat is on the Hong Kong dollar.

title: Philippines De Ocampo-2:Sees Stabilization At Basement Level

In Manila, Philippine stocks plunged to a record low Thursday, swept by a region-wide selloff following another downgrade for Asian shares by a U.S. investment bank. 

 The 30-share Philippine Stock Exchange Index lost 96.06 points, or 5%, closing at 1,832.91, its lowest level since the country's two stock markets were unified in 1994. 

 Asked if the massive sell-off across the region had been 'washed out' by Thursday's events, de Ocampo said 'it's not very easy to tell.' He said the sell-off was being encouraged by the 'continuing perception' of currency instability in the region, the need for Thailand to put into effect its economic reform program and the strength of the U.S. economy, which siphons off investment capital. 

 'So I think that it's likely to be stabilizing once it begins to appear that the prices of the stocks here have reached bargain basement levels,' he said. 

 De Ocampo said the Philippine decision to float the peso had proved a success. 

 'It has depreciated a little bit less in spite of the fact that there has been minimal intervention from the Central Bank of the Philippines and we have been able to preserve our reserves,' he said. 

 De Ocampo said that in the long run, significant changes needed to be made, chief among them 'greater information transparency' and 'better monitoring systems.'

title: SE Asian  Currencies  In Renewed Falls As Pessimism Deepens
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Southeast Asian currencies
dropped across the board against the U.S. dollar during

title: Key dates in Southeast Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 8 (Reuter) - Indonesia's announcement on Wednesday that it will seek assistance from the International Monetary Fund was the latest development in Southeast Asia's financial crisis. 

 The following are key dates: 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency is hit by a massive attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 The Philippines is affected. The central bank raises the overnight rate 1-3/4 percentage points to 13 percent and dumps dollars. 

 May 16 - Thailand says foreign speculators will have to "pay the price" for their attacks by buying back the baht from the more expensive swap market. 

 Again the Philippines is affected. The overnight rate is hiked seven percentage points to 20 percent and the central bank sells more dollars. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thailand's finance minister. 

 The resignation has immediate impact in the Philippines. There, the central bank had cut the overnight rate in the morning to 12.75 percent from 13 percent. But after the resignation announcement it jacks it back up to 15 percent. 

 June 27 - The Thai central bank suspends operations of 16 cash-strapped finance companies and orders them to submit merger or consolidation plans. 

 June 30 - Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yonchaiyudh assures the nation in a televised address there will be no devaluation of the baht. 

 July 2 - The Bank of Thailand announces a managed float of the baht and calls on the International Monetary Fund for "technical assistance". 

 The announcement effectively devalues the baht by about 15-20 percent. It ends at a record low of 28.80 to the dollar. 

 In Manila, the central bank is forced to intervene heavily to defend the peso. 

 July 3 - The Philippine central bank raises the overnight lending rate to 24 percent from 15 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. The intervention works and the currency hits a high of 2.5100/10 after a low of 2.5240/50. 

 July 11 - The Philippine central bank says in a statement it will allow the peso to move in a wider range against the dollar. The IMF backs the move and Managing Director Camdessus says he would recommend the IMF board approve the Philippines' request for an extension of its Extended Fund Facility (EFF). 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah is starting to be affected. In a surprise move, Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support under fast-track regulations drawn up after the 1995 Mexican crisis. 

 July 24 - Currency meltdown. 

 The ringgit hits 38-month low of 2.6530 to the dollar. Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad launches bitter attack on "rogue speculators". 

 The Singapore dollar hits 32-month low of 1.4738 to the dollar. 

 The Hong Kong dollar remains steady, but territory later reveals US$1 billion was spent on intervention during a period of two hours on an unspecified day in July. 

 July 26 - Mahathir names hedge fund manager George Soros as the man responsible for the attack on the ringgit. He later brands Soros a "moron". 

 August 5 - Thailand unveils austerity plan and complete revamp of finance sector as part of IMF suggested policies for a rescue package. Central bank suspends 48 finance firms. 

 August 11 - The IMF unveils in Tokyo a rescue package for Thailand including loans totalling $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 13 - The rupiah begins to come under severe pressure. It hits a historic low of 2,682 to the dollar before ending at 2,655. The central bank actively intervenes in its defence. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of managing the exchange rate through the use of a band. The rupiah plunges to 2,755. 

 August 16 - An unnamed Beijing source tells a local Hong Kong newspaper that China is prepared to use US$50 billion to defend the Hong Kong dollar. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. The package now totals $16.7 billion. 

 August 27 - Brunei adds $500 million more to Thailand's bailout package, bringing it to a total of $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 2 - A falling equity market helps push the Philippine peso to a record low of 30.90 to the dollar. 

 In Jakarta, the rupiah ends at 3,045. 

 Sept 3 - Indonesia announces measures to revive investor confidence in the country, including scrapping a 49 percent limit on foreign purchases of shares at initial public offerings and a hike in luxury taxes. 

 The package has little impact on the rupiah. 

 Sept 4 - Carnage in the Philippine peso continues. It falls to a record low of 32.43 to the dollar before central bank intervention helps it up slightly to end at 32.38. 

 Ringgit breaks through 3.0000 to the dollar barrier. 

 Mahathir delays several multi-billion dollar construction projects. A controversial measure to ban short selling in 100 key stocks will also be withdrawn. 

 Sept 16 - Indonesia says it will postpone projects worth 39 trillion rupiah in an attempt to slash the budget shortfall. 

 Sept 20 - Mahathir tells delegates to the IMF/World Bank annual conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral and should be stopped. 

 Sept 21 - Soros says "Dr Mahathir is a menace to his own country". 

 Sept 22 - The forex market gives its answer to Mahathir. The ringgit tumbles more than two percent to end at 3.1220 to the dollar. 

 Sept 30 - Ringgit fall continues. Mahathir says in Chile that 1998 Malaysian economic growth would slow due to the falling ringgit. It hits a low of 3.2150. 

 Oct 1 - Mahathir repeats his siren call for tighter regulation, or a total ban, on forex trading. The currency falls four percent in less than two hours to a low of 3.4080. 

 Oct 6 - The rupiah hits a low of 3,845. Dealers are now talking of the possibility of Indonesia having to go to the IMF for help. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals firm on  central bank  fea.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 7 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies regained their footing on Tuesday as traders turned cautious about buying the dollar too aggressively amid growing talk of central bank intervention in very thin markets. 

 Bank Indonesia, which stepped in to sell dollars when the rupiah slumped to an all-time low of 3,850 per dollar on Monday, was believed to have intervened again on Tuesday. 

 Dealers said the central bank had sold dollars in small amounts, pushing the rupiah to a high of 3,475 against its opening 3,600/50. 

 But persistent dollar demand from underhedged domestic companies and offshore funds jumping on the bandwagon pushed the rupiah back down to 3,640/50 by 0455 GMT. 

 The rupiah's overnight gains after State Secretary Murdiono said the government would take steps to stabilise the rupiah, while remaining committed to free foreign exchange flows, also helped sentiment. 

 The Philippine central bank also stepped in to prop up the peso as it fell prey to pent-up dollar demand from foreign banks, diving to a record low of 35.981 per dollar. 

 Manila traders said the central bank's dollar sales from the 35.85 peso level helped turn the tide, pushing the peso back up to 34.65/75 by 0455 GMT. 

 The reimposition of a volatility band added to the market mayhem as the peso twice breached its limits before the central bank intervention, leading to trade suspensions. 

 The Bankers Association of the Philippines, which operates the electronic forex dealing system, decided late on Monday to reintroduce the band due to the peso's recent volatility. 

 It calls for a 30-minute recess if the peso moves outside a two percent limit. Upon resumption of trading, the band is narrowed to one percent and trading can be suspended two more times before being stopped for the rest of the day. 

 Elsewhere, the Malaysian ringgit recovered sharply amid rumours in Singapore that the central Bank Negara Malaysia was intervening to support the unit. 

 But Malaysian dealers said they had not detected the central bank's presence and most attributed the ringgit's rise to commercial demand and buying of the unit against the Singapore dollar. 

 "U.S. names were said to be buying about $200-$300 million in ringgit/Sing," said one Singapore dealer. 

 Dealers said the market was also plagued by fears Malaysia might implement a two-tier market, similar to Thailand's system, after Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's repeated calls for further curbs on currency trading. 

 There was confusion on foreign exchange markets when the format on a Reuters currency quotation page was mistakenly changed early on Tuesday. The changes gave the impression a two-tier market had been created in the ringgit, rupiah and peso. 

 This mistake was subsequently corrected to reflect global consolidated contributions. 

 The Singapore dollar recovered from its lows around 1.5470 to the U.S. dollar in line with the ringgit's move, but its gains were capped by buying of the ringgit/Sing cross. 

 Dealers said the market was awaiting discussion in parliament, later in the day, about the impact of the Southeast Asian currency crisis on Singapore's economy and whether steps were being taken to address it. 

 The Thai baht showed a firm bias on growing optimism about the government's finance sector reform package, due to be announced on October 15. 

 "It is a very narrow bid and offer, I think people are looking into the future for October 15 and some people think the news will come out positively," a local bank dealer in Bangkok said. Onshore baht was at 36.60/65 to the dollar while the offshore rate was at 35.65/75.

title: Philippine c. bank  intervention  tempers peso slide.

MANILA, Sept 4 (Reuter) - The Philippine peso weakened to a new low on Thursday, but a modest intervention by central bank in the afternoon propped the peso slightly at close, dealers said.

title: IMF/Philippines -3: First Time Post-Mexico Procedure Used

To protect official reserves after an aborted attempt to intervene against a speculative attack on the peso, the Philippines moved on July 11 to float the currency. 

 The IMF noted that authorities moved to extend the existing credit facility to allow passage of key tax reforms and ultimately 'to support their action to float the peso in order to discourage speculative capital flows.' 

 The IMF decision was taken under an emergency assistance mechanism created in September 1995 after a controversial $17 billion standby credit was approved to help combat the December 1994 Mexican peso crisis. It was the first time the procedures were instituted, according to the fund. 

 The IMF called the Philippines performance under the existing credit arrangement 'satisfactory.' But it also noted that while its 'macroeconomic program remained broadly on track in the first quarter of 1997, the authorities faced a number of important challenges in the second quarter.' 

 It pointed to 'increasing turbulence in the foreign exchange market, slippages in fiscal performance, and a delay in the passage of proposed tax reforms.'

title: S.E. Asia/Exchange Rates -3: End Of An Era For Region
text:
Economists agree that the recent developments mark something of end of an era. 

 'We're coming to end of a what's been a very difficult period for the region, with property and banking sectors consolidating, and hence the need for easier monetary policy,' says Angus Armstrong, chief Asia-Pacific economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Singapore. 

 'A broader moral can be drawn about foreign exchange policies in emerging economies,' says Derek Hargreaves, New York-based economist at J.P. Morgan. 'Fairly steadily, there is a drift away from regimes based on relatively narrow, publicized fluctuation bands,' he says in a recent report, noting the recent relaxation of the regime governing the Czech koruna. 

 Bernhard Eschweiler, J.P. Morgan Asia-Pacific economist in Singapore, says the Philippines risked getting itself 'caught in a trap.' 

 The Philippines had a free-floating exchange rate in theory. However, for the past two years the central bank has managed the currency so tightly it had barely fluctuated in the spot market. 

 Eschweiler said currency stability in the Philippines' 'good times' has exaggerated capital inflows, as investors took advantage of rich interest-rate spreads and negligible foreign-exchange risk. 

 But the rigid currency only exacerbated problems when investor sentiment deteriorates, as happened when the crisis in Thailand led foreigners to worry that its problems might be replicated in the Philippines. 

 Protecting currency stability meant tight monetary policy, but intervening to support the peso was circumscribed by the Philippines' modest foreign reserves of around $10 billion. Higher interest rates required to defend the peso intensified pressure on a debt-laden corporate sector. 

 Yet the Philippines financial sector is now in some trouble because of its exposure to foreign-currency loans, exactly the problem confronting Thailand now that the baht has lost more than 15% in value. 

 'The Philippines has a malady rather similar to Thailand's,' notes P.K. Basu, economist at Union Bank of Switzerland.
