title: Philippines should allow peso to fall - analysts.
text:
MANILA, July 10 (Reuter) - Pressure on the Philippine peso is reaching a stage when it may make more sense for the government to give in, end the pain, and let its currency slip a little, analysts and bankers said on Thursday. 

 The Central Bank has been adamant that the peso will not be allowed to fall against the dollar, but other government officials have been quoted this week as saying "devaluation" is being considered. The reports were quickly denied. 

 "When it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it must be a duck. Since high officials were the first to talk about it (devaluation) in a situation ripe for it, then the peso will have to depreciate soon," said Noel Reyes, analyst at Anscor Hagedorn Securities. 

 "(The Central Bank) can no longer rely on a few phone calls to bankers or a few innocuous, toothless warnings to the press against speculators to do the trick," he said. 

 If the speculative attack on the peso continues much longer, the Central Bank may have to give in and stop defending the currency anyway, Reyes said. Other analysts agree. 

Foreign exchange reserves have been depleted by repeated intervention, and interest rates raised to levels which could hurt the economy. 

 Although the government has so far steadfastly declined to say how much money it has left in its kitty, official figures last put foreign exchange reserves at just under $12 billion in May -- a bit more than three months' worth of imports. 

 Bankers estimated the Central Bank sold more than $600 million in the market on Wednesday alone to defend the peso. 

 That would easily take care of the $500 million it raised last month by issuing a Yankee bond in the United States. 

 This has been the Philippines' worst currency crisis in four years. Besides intervention, the central bank has had to raise its overnight interest rate to a high of 32 percent -- a 2-1/2 year high. 

 Many economists argue that the Philippine economy itself is in good shape and on target to become the next Asian tiger by the turn of the century. 

 Exports are booming, inflation is around record lows, the budget position of the government is in surplus and growth is likely to be at least six percent this year. 

 Even the grey peso market rate is virtually the same as the official rate. 

 So why should a currency, that has barely moved against the dollar in close to two years, suddenly have to fall? 

 Analysts say much of the speculation stems from fears -- especially among foreign investors -- that the Philippines cannot avoid being infected by the financial crisis in neighbouring Thailand. 

 Last week, the Thai authorities allowed a de facto devaluation of the baht after prolonged speculative pressure. 

 "The underlying fundamentals are pretty good...It is what they are doing to protect the currency which is worrying people," said Chris Hunt, head of research at W.I. Carr in Manila. 

 Interest rates have doubled in the past week simply to defend the peso and if they are prolonged they will inevitably cap growth. 

 "My feeling is that they (authorities) may be compelled to do something sooner rather than later," Hunt said. He added that a small drop in the peso's value would send the right message and not cause much of a shock. 

 "I think the peso will weaken. The Central Bank can't keep it up for very long," Luz Lorenzo, economist at Peregrine Securites said. 

 "Interest rates now are punitive. The question is how much they will depreciate. But they'll do it gradually," she added. 

 She said that if the peso were to drop under the current pressure to around 28 to the dollar -- a depreciation of some six percent -- it would most likely bounce back fairly quickly afterwards because of general good economic conditons.

title: Philippines  says it will  intervene  to defend peso.

 "The (Central Bank) will intervene strongly using all its available policy weapons to maintain an orderly foreign exchange market and to penalise speculators," the Monetary Board said in a statement following a regular meeting. 

 The Monetary Board is the highest policy-making body of the Central Bank and is chaired by Bank Governor Gabriel Singson.

 The head of southeast Asian currency trading at a regional bank said speculators who believe the baht move offers a good opportunity to bet against other currencies are plotting a dangerous course, because the central banks in the region will protect each others' currencies. 

 'My 17 years on the markets here have taught me that you never muck around with Asian central banks - they always win, they always protect each other,' she said. 

 'I respect the fact that Thailand has severe economic problems,' she added, but the region's central banks, equipped with large foreign exchange reserves, will only allow devaluation on their terms. 

 In May, the Monetary Authority of Singapore was among the regional central banks which joined in the Bank of Thailand's defence of the baht against a sustained speculative raid, exercising a number of bilateral cooperation agreements signed in the past two years. 

 The U.S. bank trader said that it look as if Bank Negara and the Philippines central bank have been quick to support their currencies in early dealings Wednesday. 

 'The Malaysian central bank is intervening successfully to support the ringgit, and in the Philippines, which is not an open market, the central bank has a better control on the currency than in Thailand,' he said. 'Although the Indonesian rupiah has fallen a little in the spot market, high interest rates will protect the currency,' he added.

title: INTERVIEW - Singson sees lower Philippines rates.
text:
HONG KONG, May 22 (Reuter) - Rates in the Philippines are returning to normal after last week's Asian currency turmoil, with further declines in the key overnight rate possible next week, central bank governor Gabriel Singson told Reuters on Thursday. 

 "It is down to 18 (percent) and we can bring it back down to normal next week. It depends on the market, how the market behaves," Singson said. 

 The overnight rate, raised from 13 percent to 20 percent when speculators attacked the Thai baht last week, dropped back to 18 percent on Thursday morning. 

 Speculators betting on a sudden devalution of the Thai baht precipitated widespread currency turmoil throughout southeast Asia last week, with hedge funds taking positions on the Malaysian ringgit, Philippines peso and Indonesian rupiah. 

 Coordinated central bank intervention appeared to foil the hedge funds, and Singson said that if market conditions warrant, the overnight rate will be dropped back to normal next week. 

 Singson also put forward a firm defense of the Philippines' peso, ruling out any immediate devalution. 

 "Devaluation won't work. A sharp devaluation won't solve our problems," he said. "Our exchange rate policy is to let the market decide the exchange rate and we intend to continue. My statement is unqualified." 

 Although he conceded that interest rates were high and credit growth was strong, Singson rejected any comparison with Thailand or Malaysia, where he said credit continue to grow at rates of about 90 percent. 

 In the Philippines, private sector credit growth dropped to 37 percent in the first quarter from 57 percent in all of 1996. 

 Bank indebtedness to the property sector is restricted to less than 20 percent of outstanding loans, with two recent surveys confirming total exposure of less than 11 percent. 

 If credit growth were a problem, the inflation rate in the Philippines would be higher than the 4.6 percent recorded in April, Singson added. 

 The central bank governor gave no clues on the timing of the launch of its controversial US$1.25 billion yankee bond, which was delayed in April. 

 Market conditions would determine the new date of the launch, and everything was in place to allow the Philippines to move swiftly, he said. 

 The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission registration remains valid for nine months and the roadshow has been completed, he said. 

 "This is really a judgement call and we have to decide on a daily basis. Ultimately, I have the luxury of time. I'm not in any hurry," he said.

title: Manila upgrade delights analysts, market uncaring.
text:
MANILA, May 19 (Reuter) - A ratings upgrade for the Philippines on Monday underlines what many economists and the government have been proclaiming for weeks, though largely to deaf ears. 

 The young cub among Asia's economic tigers has been battling for weeks, often unsuccessfully, to convince investors that the Philippines does not carry within it a virus about to erupt into the same illnesses that have weakened the Thai economy. 

 "I don't know why investors are still so sceptical about the Philippines economy... It's just a matter of sentiment. But it is important the Philippines shows growth is not a one-time blip," said Al Rillo, analyst at DBS Securities. 

 Moody's Investors Service earlier on Monday upgraded the country's foreign currency bonds and deposits and 11 of its top banks. 

 The news did nothing to stop the local stock market tumbling to another 17-month low, a slump triggered last month as investors decided that fears of a property glut would tear into bank profits. 

 Not so, argues the government, which points out that, in contrast to a number of its neighbours, major Philippines banks have a relatively low number of loans to property firms and certainly low enough to withstand a real estate crash. 

 "The upgrade also means that perceptive analysts could discern the strengths of an emerging market like the Philippines beyond the fashionable headlines of today that cater to fears fuelled by knee-jerk reactions and superficial comparisons," Central Bank Governor Gabriel Singson said. 

 Fears of economic chaos in Thailand have swept through the Philippines in the past week, forcing Singson to intervene heavily in currency markets and boost interest rates to two-year highs to protect the peso. 

 In fact, the surge in interest rates could have an added benefit of preventing overheating from a fast-striding economy which, despite investor gloom, is still growing at 6-7 percent a year, BNP Prime East banking analyst Marco Lucena said. 

 "Since the start we have believed that banks have quality loans and are not on the brink of following Thailand," he added. 

 ING Barings analyst Joey Cuyegkeng said the Central Bank was addressing concerns such as the speed of credit growth, the quality of banking assets and foreign currency lending. 

 "It's the overall devaluing of Asia that is keeping a lid on prices," Cuyegkeng said. 

 Some analysts and bankers hoped that the Moody's report would finally turn the tide in the country's favour. 

 "It's very good. We've been trying to show that the banking industry is not just exposed to real estate... Here's proof that we can't be compared with Thailand," said Marjo Elevado, analyst at the policy research group of the Bankers Association of the Philippines. 

 "This will make analysts realise that there's a night and day difference between Philippine and Thailand banks... The banking system has a very strong foundation," added Jose Facundo, president of BPI Capital Corp. 

 But other analysts said more proof was needed by the Philippines, which even after five years of sustained growth, had not quite managed to convince emerging market investors it was made of the right stuff. 

 Economic growth figures for the first quarter, expected to be published by the beginning of June, will be the next real test of the country's health. 

 If the figures are below expectations, the share market will certainly take another beating. 

 "We believe there is still more downside. If (the stock market index) breaks through 2,450 that would be scary. It could go into freefall,' Lippo Securities analyst Jidgette Valenzuela said. 

 The index closed on Monday at 2,509.36, a dive of 27 percent from its record high in early February. 

 DBS Securities' Rillo said a key factor undermining sentiment is not the economy at all but fears over who will replace President Fidel Ramos in next year's presidential election. 

 "In any emerging economy the political structure is important. There are still concerns that politics could undermine the economy," he added.

title: S.E. Asia Central Bks/Baht -2: Tighter Monetary Policy
text:
The Bank of Thailand was joined by the other members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in supporting the Thai central bank in its defence of the currency, Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said early Friday. The Monetary Authority of Singapore described the intervention as 'effective'. 

 But the sources said the coup de grace of the banks' operations was the squeeze in short term interest rates engineered Thursday and Friday in Thailand, Malaysia and the Philippines. 

 'I'm less impressed with the intervention and more impressed with the rise in Thailand's interest rates,' said the senior foreign exchange trader at a U.S. investment bank, speaking on condition of anonymity. '(The Bank of Thailand) dried up liquidity to punish the speculators,' he said. 

 Overt measures by the Bank of Thailand - urging domestic banks not to lend baht to offshore counterparties at rates less then 1,000% - ensured that many speculators who wanted to liquidate short positions in the Thai currency could do so only at an unacceptable cost. 

 Bank Negara has also pushed up short-term interest rates to defend the ringgit, though it was quick to deny suggestions Friday that it was penalizing offshore players in the ringgit swaps market. Bank Indonesia issued a similar denial Friday. 

 And the Philippine central bank jacked up its overnight interest rates in stages to 20% by Friday from 12% Wednesday, steadying the Philippine peso by the end of the day. 

 Regional currency dealing rooms were frantic Friday as liquidity in the forward and swap markets evaporated. 

 'The (local) banks were quoting such ridiculous spreads... basically Thailand and Malaysia were barricading their capital accounts (from offshore players),' said Chia Wooh Khien, treasury economist at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken (South East Asia) Ltd. in Singapore. 

 The sources agreed the effect of sharply higher short-term interest rates in Malaysia and Thailand had much the same effect Friday as a temporary imposition of exchange controls. 'This hasn't been a natural market,' said StanChart's Van der Wath.

title: Philippines' Ramos operated on for arterial block.
text:
MANILA, Dec 23 (Reuter) - Philippine President Fidel Ramos successfully underwent surgery on Monday for a cholesterol blockage in a main artery that could have been life-threatening, doctors and officials said. 

 Ramos, 68, was conscious and recuperating well and was likely to be discharged from hospital on Christmas Day or on Thursday, doctors said. 

 "The president just called up and said that by tomorrow (Tuesday) he wants to get back to work," Executive Secretary Ruben Torres told a news conference about three hours after the operation ended. "He wants an office set up in the hospital." 

 "President Ramos is awake, he's smiling, he's listening to radio," Jose de Venecia, speaker of the House of Representatives, told reporters. "The operation was extremely successful." 

 Raul Fores, the director of the Makati Medical Centre, said doctors discovered a cholesterol blockage "the size of a garbanzo" in Ramos's right carotid artery on the neck. 

 The carotids are the two main arteries carrying blood to the brain and blockages in them can lead to a stroke, officials said. 

 "The condition may be life-threatening if it is not removed immediately," said Health Secretary Carmencita Reodica. "That's why they decided to remove it right away." 

 Fores said doctors noticed a build-up of cholesetrol when they conducted tests on Ramos the previous weekend, when he was admitted to hospital for treatment of a throat infection. He said both Ramos and his wife consented to immediate surgery and a 75-minute operation was successfully conducted. 

 "The president is presently out of anaesthesia, awake and all vital signs are within normal limits," he said. 

 "The surgical team are confident that he may be out of the hospital either on Christmas Day or the day after," Fores said. 

 The Philippine stock market plunged at the open on news of Ramos's operation but recovered marginally by the close. The composite index closed down 1.27 percent at 3,139.92 points, off a low of 3,112.56. 

 "In markets like the Philippines where the chief executive officer is seen as a very strong and powerful leader, the market is very sensitive on news about his health. There was a lot of foreign selling," said Raul Ruiz, vice president at Sun Hung Kai Securities. 

 "The market over-reacted on news of the surgery but rebounded a little bit in midsession on news that it was successful," said Felix Barrientos, a trader at ING Barings Securities. 

 The Philippines Central Bank intervened in the foreign exchange market to stabilise the peso, dealers said. The peso was marginally weaker at 26.311/315 against the dollar at midday from a middle rate of 26.301 on Friday. 

 "The market was a bit jittery at first, but the central bank was quick to react," said Joselito Dalit, an analyst at the Asian Bank. "That stabilises the market." 

 Ramos is a fit, youthful man for his age, works up to 18 hours a day, regularly plays golf and is known to enjoy a twirl on a dance floor. But Fores said he would have to slow down and watch his diet, adding the president suffered from "the usual problems of people above 60". 

 "You get this illness from eating too much cheese and chocolates," he said. "For the first time, he has listened (to doctors advice). He realises he's got to slow down."

 But the latest data released Monday showed the central bank has been intervening less actively at the Philippine Dealing System (PDS), where banks buy and sell dollars. 

 The central bank accounted for an average of 35% of volume from January through Oct. 4. By comparison, it accounted for 55% in January alone.

title: IMF/ Philippines  Economy-4:Liquidity Rise Due To  Intervention
text:
The IMF mission will be visiting Manila for two weeks to see whether an upward revision in the Philippines monetary targets are warranted, even if inflation has been trending higher in the past three months. 

 Earlier Monday, a National Economic Development Authority official said the government had just raised its 1995 inflation target to between 7.0% to 8.0% from the original 6.5%, citing inflationary pressures from an impending oil price hike. 

 The IMF has been concerned that higher liquidity would trigger inflation. 

 'They (IMF) see also the foreign exchange that we are buying,' Singson said. 'Whatever liquidity there is, is coming principally from these purchases in foreign exchange. These are externally generated rather than internally generated - it's not really money being released.' 

 Liquidity has also been pumped up by the central bank's decision to reduce the reserve requirement of commercial banks by two percentage points to 15% at the end of May. 

 As this move was meant primarily to ease the high interest rates in April, Singson noted that the rate of the bellwether 91-day treasury bill dropped to 13.36% last Friday from a high of 15.4% in mid-April. 

 'In the months ahead, Singson expects a stable interest rate regime with the continued resurgence in economic activity absorbing the observed growth in domestic liquidity,' another BSP statement said. 

 'Monetary policy will remain supportive of economic growth but will continue to be cuatious and vigilant of any inflationary pressures'

title: Philippines Central Bank  -3:Want  Central Bank  To  Intervene
text:
Foreign exchange traders said the central bank was trying to attract people to lend at 25% so as to siphon off liquidity from the market. 

 Tightness in money supply is expected to push up interbank borrowing rates next week, which should put some pressure on the surging dollar. 

 Higher interest rates mean that it will be more expensive to carry dollars. It is also seen as inducing the unloading of some arbitrage dollars on the market in order to benefit from the higher yield. 

 Traders said the best way for the central bank to arrest the dollar's rise is to start selling more dollars on the market now. 

 'We have sold everything we can, but we can not satisfy all the dollar requirements,' said a trader for a foreign bank. 'They have to add additional supply.' 

 Despite having unloaded as much as $70 million in previous sessions, the central bank has not been a big seller Friday.
